papers.design_stakeholders: Teachers; Students & Learners
papers.abstract: This demo presents TeamLearn, a multimodal collaboration analytics dashboard designed to facilitate reflection and provide feedback on developing group artifacts during long- term collaborative problem-solving projects. By integrating meetings, documents, and collaboration experience analytics, the dashboard offers visualisations that help groups monitor participation, task progress, and collaboration dynamics. Developed through a design-based research process, the TeamLearn dashboard provides structured opportunities for reflective dialogue. The demo will showcase the dashboard’s core features and illustrate how it can be integrated into collaborative project activities.

papers.title: Improving Co-Designed Asynchronous Graduate Learning Through Network Analysis
papers.authors: Dina Samson, Jonan Phillip Donaldson
papers.design_stakeholders: Teachers; Students & Learners; Educational Researchers & Designers
papers.abstract: This design-based research study investigated student experiences in a co- designed, asynchronous online graduate course. We applied learning experience network analysis to examine 43 student reflection papers. The analysis identified seven distinct learning ecologies, each characterized by different configurations of learner agency, theoretical principles, and challenges. While two ecologies represented successful engagement, five others revealed specific struggles. These struggles included translating individual work into group collaboration and managing anxiety during transformative learning. This study shows that co-design resulted in varied learning ecologies of experiences. We proposed specific design moves for each challenging configuration. Network analysis offered a valuable method for systematically improving co-designed learning environments through responsive, theory-based support.

papers.title: Transformative Disruptions: Using Call-In Strategies To Enact Solidarity In Community Partnerships
papers.authors: Chasity Mayo, LuEttaMae Lawrence, Stephen Kwiatek, Indu Garg
papers.design_stakeholders: Special Education Teachers; Students & Learners; Educational Researchers & Designers; Community Members & Partners; School Administrators & Leaders
papers.abstract: As the Learning Sciences have continued discussing subtle nuances related to community partnerships, there has been emphasis on how to enact solidarity, healing, and care. In this piece, we reflect on our enactments of solidarity and care by sharing about moments of calling-in, which we refer to as moments of curiously challenging. We use examples from our co-design sessions to showcase how call -ins function as transformative disruptions of harmful knowledges and how these moments are situated within other relationship building practices. We call on other scholars within the Learning Sciences community to consider the complexities surrounding systemized mindsets and how to attend to harmful productions and reproductions of knowledge within community-based partnerships.

papers.title: Learning With and About AI: Building Capacity for Equitable Participation in an AI-Shaped Future
papers.authors: Ibrahim Oluwajoba Adisa
papers.design_stakeholders: Elementary / Early Childhood Teachers; Middle School Students; Educational Researchers & Designers; Community Members & Partners
papers.abstract: My research investigates how learners and educators understand, design with, and collaborate with AI systems, and how these sociotechnical interactions shape equity and participation. Using design-based research, participatory design, and qualitative and computational methods, I study AI education and disciplinary integration of AI in K–12 contexts. My work aims to design equitable learning environments, develop theoretical models of learner engagement with AI, and build cross-disciplinary approaches to teaching with and about AI. Theoretical and methodological foundations that inform my work My research sits at the intersection of the learning sciences, data science and artificial intelligence (AI) education. I am particularly interested in how educators and learners understand, design with, and collaborate with AI systems, and how these sociotechnical interactions shape equity and participation in society. In my work, I frame learning as a socially and materially mediated practice, drawing on sociocultural perspectives that conceptualize knowing as participation in activity systems rather than simply the acquisition of decontextualized concepts (Vygotsky, 1987; Wertsch, 1991). Within this view, AI tools and data infrastructures function as cultural tools (Cole, 1996; Saxe, 1991) that shape what becomes visible, what is considered authoritative, and whose perspectives are deemed valid as knowledge. I also draw on constructionist (Holbert et al., 2020; Kafai & Resnick, 1996; Papert & Harel, 1991) and design-oriented traditions that treat building computational artifacts as a powerful avenue for learning. When students build or critique AI applications and data stories, they are engaging in epistemic work that reveals their assumptions about what counts as evidence, how models relate to the world, and whose experiences are encoded in data (Vakil et al., 2022). I am particularly attentive to how young learners develop both conceptual and sociotechnical understandings of the affordances and limits of AI technologies, and how educators can support these competencies in ways that foster agency, critique, and creativity.

papers.title: Frame Alignment and Feedback in CT-ified Science Classrooms
papers.authors: Connor Bain, Uri Wilensky
papers.design_stakeholders: Science Teachers; Students & Learners; Educational Researchers & Designers; Community Members & Partners; Domain Experts & Technologists
papers.abstract: While computational thinking (CT) is an integral part of modern scientific inquiry, STEM teachers struggle to incorporate these ideas in classrooms. We report on the efforts of a design-based implementation research project in which teachers participate in a constructionist co-design process to design and then implement CT -ified STEM units in their classrooms. Using feedback teachers left on student responses from these unit implementations, we utilize a basic bag-of-words model to show that teachers did specifically attend to student learning at the intersection of CT and STEM. We then further explicate this evidence through a qualitative think-aloud interview with one of the teachers who designed and implemented a curriculum based around computational models in biology. What we find is evidence that STEM teachers in CT -ified classrooms can assess both CT and S TEM skills at the same time though this intersection still needs additional attention in terms of tools and PD for teachers.

papers.abstract: This study aims to explore the affordances of augmented reality technologies (AR) to facilitate studentsʼ product design processes in a business course. We analyze the affordances of AR in the context of a product design activity in an undergraduate classroom. The course is held in a Makerspace lab at a university campus, and it requires students to conceptualize, design, prototype, manufacture, and market new products by using 3D computer -aided design (CAD) software and 3D printing. Our study illuminates that although CAD allows students to visualize and manipulate digitally manufactured 3D objects on a 2D computer monitor surface, it does not allow them to visualize and manipulate those 3D objects in 3D space. However, AR does afford visualization and mani pulation of digitally manufactured 3D objects in 3D space which is why we investigated how do interactions with 3D models in AR impact product design processes for students.

papers.title: Teacher as Designers: Using Robotics to Integrate Computational Thinking and Science
papers.authors: Michael Cassidy, Debra Bernstein, Jennifer Cross, Karen Mutch-Jones
papers.design_stakeholders: Middle School Teachers; Students & Learners; Educational Researchers & Designers; Domain Experts & Technologists
papers.abstract: This study examines how middle school science teachers designed and implemented robotics-based units that integrated computational thinking (CT) practices following a professional development (PD) program positioning them as curriculum designers. Drawing on Waterman et al.’s (2020) and Coenraad et al.’s (2022) integration frameworks and the project’s CT framework (Bernstein et al., 2025 ), we analyzed teacher interviews, implementation logs, lesson plans, and student materials from six teachers across twelve units. Findings show that teachers implemented CT at multiple integration levels, engaging students in algorithm design, decomposition, abstraction, pattern recognition, and data practices. Teachers explored CT practices to establish foundational understanding, enhanced CT– science connections through scaffolds, and guided students to exhibit disciplinary ideas through programmable mode ls and extend understanding by collecting and analyzing data. These findings illustrate how positioning teachers as informed designers supports CT-integrated science curricula. Importance Computational technologies are essential for problem solving and collaboration in both professional and personal contexts (NRC, 2014). In STEM fields, these technologies have transformed practice through abstraction, algorithms, decomposition, modeling, simulation, and data analysis enabled by computing (Puttick et al., 2024; Weintrop et al., 2016). Preparing students to participate in such transformations requires the development of computational thinking (CT) practices, defined as “solving problems, designing systems, and understanding human behavior, by drawing on the concepts fundamental to computer science” (Wing, 2006, p. 33). Such preparation positions students to become producers, not merely consumers, of computational solutions. Yet despite growing calls to integrate CT into K –12 science classrooms, teachers face persistent challenges in designing learning tasks where CT meaningfully supports science learning (Cassidy & Puttick , 2022). Teachers are rarely positioned as designers of curricula that combine science, engineering, and computing (Margot & Kettler, 2019), leaving limited evidence on how to support them in planning, adapting, and enacting such curricula in authentic ways (Lee et al., 2020). Conceptual framework Computational Thinking (CT) Prior research offers important frameworks for conceptualizing CT integration. For example, Waterman et al. (2020) introduced a continuum of CT integration in science education, distinguishing between levels where CT exists (CT concepts, skills, and practices already present in the lesson can be called out or elaborated upon by the teacher, often without technology use), enhances (development of additional tasks or lessons that serve to deepen the disciplinary concept while making explicit connections to relevant computing ideas), and extends (redesign or expand lessons so that computing or CT practices become central to students’ engagement with disciplinary content). More recently, Coenraad et al. (2022) added the category of exhibit, which emphasizes students’ representing science knowledge through computational models. These frameworks provide a robust lens for describing the variety of ways CT can interact with disciplinary science learning. Engaging with robotics enables learners to develop CT practices while investigating core scientific phenomena, positioning robotics as a powerful context for integrating disciplinary learning with computational problem solving (Cassidy & Puttick, 2022). Through robotics, students apply key CT practices such as problem decomposition, abstraction, algorithmic design, and iterative debugging. These activities also support engagement in core science practices, including modeling, experimentation, and data collection and analysis (e.g., Sullivan & Hefernan, 2016). For the Robots in Science project, we adopted the PRADA framework (Dong et al., 2019), which emphasizes pattern recognition, abstraction, decomposition, and algorithms. To better align with the needs of 1297 science and robotics integration, we extended PRADA by including a fifth practice, Data Practices (Weintrop et al., 2016). In our framework, pattern recognition refers to identifying similarities among and within problems. Abstraction involves stripping away unnecessary details to develop a generic solution or representing a complex system through a simplified model or visualization. Decomposition is the process of breaking down data, processes, or problems into smaller, manageable parts. Algorithm design c oncerns the creation of an ordered sequence of instructions to solve a problem or perform a task. Data practices include collecting information, analyzing it to generate insights, and representing it through graphs, charts, words, or images. Professional development for teachers-as-designers Positioning teachers as designers acknowledges their capabilities as effective curriculum developers who draw on both disciplinary knowledge and classroom expertise (Penuel & Gallagher, 2009). This approach recognizes teachers’ pedagogical knowledge, their professional judgment, and their ability to innovate in response to their unique contexts (Voogt et al., 2019). When teachers design and/or adapt their curricula and instructional practices, they put disciplinary goals, student learning needs, and classroom resources at the forefront of implementation (Puttick et al. , 2025). Professional development that supports this role emphasizes strategies such as active learning, practice- based inquiry, and collaborative design, which create opportunities for teachers to engage directly with new ideas while situating them in the realities of classroom practice (Darling -Hammond, 2017; Tucker-Raymond & Gravel, 2019). Also, time is needed to be allotted for deep play with new technologies and resources (Koehler et al., 2011). Thus, teachers’ curriculum adaptations are shaped by their wisdom of practice and responsiveness to student needs (Calabrese Barton et al., 2021).

papers.title: “It’s aligned with my personal beliefs, i can do this”: How Science Educators Navigate Tensions Between Official and Counter Scripts of Science and Learning
papers.authors: Shaghig Chaparian, Olivia Ortiz, Maia Yoshida, Kam Waugh, Jasmine Ma, Ronni Hayden, Latasha Wright
papers.design_stakeholders: Science Teachers; Educators & Practitioners; Youth & Adolescents; Domain Experts & Technologists
papers.abstract: This study examines how informal science educators transform their lived experiences of migration, activism, and encounters with marginalization into pedagogical commitments focused on social justice. Drawing on Holland and Lave’s history-in-person and Gutiérrez’s third-space concepts, we explore how educators’ histories serve as mediational resources that shape teaching philosophies and reconfigure who belongs in science. Using semi- structured interviews with community scientists from Daphnia , an after -school science organization serving marginalized youth, the analysis traces how educators navigated and re - authored official and unofficial scripts about legitimate science and participation. Findings reveal that educators mobilize personal histories to create hybrid pedagogical spaces emphasizing freedom, flexibility, and epistemic justice. These third-space negotiations obscure boundaries between scientific and community knowledge, transforming science into a relational, participatory practice rooted in care and belonging. By conceptualizing informal educators as historical actors, this study highlights their critical role in social transformation.

papers.abstract: This study explores how preservice teachers engage with artificial intelligence (AI)- powered virtual students in VR classrooms, focusing on psychological distance and construal - level theory. papers.title: From Tool to Encounter: Generative AI as a Catalyst for Ethical and Epistemic Transformation in STEM Teacher Learning
papers.authors: Sophia Jeong, Sevil Akaygun, Mutlu Şen Akbulut, Ulku Seher Budak
papers.design_stakeholders: Math Teachers; Students & Learners; Educational Researchers & Designers
papers.abstract: This paper examines how generative artificial intelligence (GenAI) reconfigures teacher learning within STEM education through a posthumanist and diffractive lens. Drawing on an empirical study involving preservice and inservice teachers engaged in AI -integrated science and mathematics classrooms, the paper reconceptualizes GenAI not as an instructional tool but as a pedagogical encounter and an active participant shaping teachers’ epistemological and ethical becomings. Using data from microteaching sessions, collaborative lesson design, and reflective narratives, the study maps how teachers negotiate distributed learning and ethical response-ability as they design and critique AI -mediated learning activities. Findings reveal three entangled processes : emergent agency in classroom dialogues, distributed learning between teachers and AI tools, and ethical reconfigurations of teacher becoming. The paper proposes an onto- epistemological framework for GenAI integration that emphasizes relationality, reflexivity, and culturally responsive practice, contributing to lea rning sciences scholarship on technology-mediated teacher education.

papers.abstract: My research explores how to support K-12 science teachers’ professional development toward equitable and justice-centered teaching. Positioning teachers and students as those who decide what matters to them in their local contexts, I leverage design-based research to co-design, test, and co-refine pedagogical tools with practitioners. Through this process, I study teacher learning by drawing upon a professional identity development lens. In my most recent work, I study how to support middle school science teachers in customizing high-quality instructional materials and investigate how curriculum customization catalyzes teacher teaching. Looking forward, I hope to explore how community-based curriculum design and customization help science teachers create equitable learning experiences for their students.

papers.abstract: Science education in rural China often privileges Western epistemology, creating disconnects with students ’ community knowledge systems like Traditional Chinese Medicine (TCM). This design-based research study addresses this gap through a co-designed three-lesson unit in a rural middle school in central China. The unit on Shanghuo ( 上火, internal heat) positioned TCM and Western science as complementary systems with distinct goals, reasoning processes, and evidence criteria. Using a Knowledge Integration framework, analysis of 40 eighth-graders' responses reveals how students navigated between correspondence -based and reductionist causal reasoning without devaluing community knowledge. Students shifted from binary epistemological stances ( “TCM is superstitious” ) to purposeful differentiation, recognizing when each system serves specific purposes. Three instructional routines supported this work: organizing family knowledge as analyzable data, using parallel comparison structures, and scaffolding dual justification. Findings demonstrate that rural students possess rich epistemological resources that Western -dominant curricula render invisible, offering design guidelines for culturally relevant science pedagogy.

papers.abstract: Humanizing Institutional Landscapes of Ability Differences and Learning Cathery Yeh, Erin McCloskey, Alfredo J. Artiles, Mimi Ito How can schools, universities, and community spaces construct, reinforce, or challenge how ability differences and disabilities are understood and organized in relation to race, language, and culture? This session brings together researchers working in schools, higher education, and out-of-school settings to study, reconceptualize, and redesign institutional, programmatic, and pedagogical practices. Through an engaging, dialogic format, the panelists will share stories and artifacts from four participatory design projects and explore common themes and challenges. The goal is to grapple with institutional landscapes that unevenly distribute learning opportunities, and to consider what equitable, culturally sustaining approaches to ability differences and disabilities in learning might look like. Cathery Yeh uses participatory mapping with youth, teachers, and families to capture lived experiences, decision points, and institutional boundaries shaping access, labels, and opportunities across bilingual education, special education, and mathematics, tracing patterns of exclusion and possibility to inform asset-based intervention systems. papers.title: Trend Trackers: Building Data Literacy Through Problem-Based Learning
papers.authors: Anna Amato Shao, Jessica Ochoa Hendrix, Mandë Holford, Noelle Posadas Shang, Christopher Pollati
papers.design_stakeholders: Middle School Teachers; Middle School Students; Domain Experts & Technologists
papers.abstract: In this demo, we discuss the co-design of an interactive, problem-based science supplement called Trend Trackers. Trend Trackers aims to engage middle school students with socioscientific issues that impact cities and communities all over the world. Students take up the role of a data scientist to address public health problems within the fictional city of Springfield. In this demo, we will explore a challenge in which students are asked to design a vaccination plan to reduce the rates of flu in Springfield. Students engage in interactive and immersive activities to collect wastewater samples, measure rates of flu in the community, and generate evidence through a series of wrangling, visualization, and analysis activities. Students then share their findings and collaborate with their team to co-construct a vaccination plan for Springfield.

papers.abstract: This study examined how collaborative language empowers STEM coaches' agency through researcher -practitioner partnerships. Using Cultural -Historical Activity Theory (CHAT) to analyze the collaboration between one STEM coach and researcher, data from professional learning sessions, videos, and artifacts were analyzed through thematic analysis. Students combined visual and literary arts with electronics and coding as they reflected on oneself as a “star” in a constellation within their communities and society. papers.title: Designing Digital Enhancements for Social Emotional Skill in a Collaborative Learning Environment
papers.authors: Enruo Guo, Emily Kerzabi, Jessica Andrews-Todd, Jiangang Hao, Patrick Kyllonen, Stephen Elliott
papers.design_stakeholders: Teachers; Students & Learners; Educational Researchers & Designers; Domain Experts & Technologists; School Administrators & Leaders
papers.abstract: This study presents the design and implementation of a fifth- grade Social and Emotional Learning (SEL) curriculum within a hybrid digital collaborative environment. Using a user -centered design approach, we engaged teachers and a school administrator as co - designers over a four -month period to iteratively refine the features and tools from a collaborative learning and assessment system (EPCAL). Key design decisions, such as tailoring class analytics to SEL and integrating feedback and rewards systems, were informed by teacher input. A semester-long pilot study involving two teachers and 22 students demonstrated the feasibility of delivering SEL through a hybrid model using EPCAL. Findings highlight strong teacher engagement and meaningful student participation. This research contributes a scalable framework for hybrid SEL delivery, demonstrating how a participatory design approach can be effectively applied to curriculum and technology enhancements - an approach that can be generalized to other hybrid learning contexts.

papers.title: Co-design as Transformative Pedagogical Spaces: what zooming out teaches us about learning to co-design together
papers.authors: Michael Chang, Areej Mawasi, Angel Osorio Pizarro, Thomas M. Philip, Amani Rohana, Jool Farra
papers.design_stakeholders: Math Teachers; Educators & Practitioners; Elementary Students & Children; Educational Researchers & Designers; Community Members & Partners; Domain Experts & Technologists
papers.abstract: This symposium brings together Learning Scientists and practitioners engaged in co- design practices embedded in diverse traditions (participatory design, human- centered design, youth participatory action research, design- based implementation research, and research practice partnerships) across diverse geographies. In different ways, these collections of papers challenge two artificially imposed constraints on how many co- design spaces are (a) designed, as short, condensed, irregular, or infrequent activities, and (b) studied, as analysis primarily focused on the interactions happening within the formal co -design activities themselves. By zooming out temporally and analytically, we make visible co- design processes that are deeply context-dependent, relational, political, and ethical practices, ones that researchers and participants construct a nd hone together over longer units of time. Through our collective discussions, we show how co- design spaces are unique spaces of being, doing, and becoming, for researchers and participants alike. Objective of the session In recent years, collaborative design has emerged in the learning sciences as a key method supporting the development of learning artifacts (Yoon et al., 2016; Gomez et al., 2018). Like other design-oriented disciplines, co-design in the learning sciences seeks to surface participants’ lived experiences and needs to directly inform the design of some learning artifact. Unlike other design-oriented disciplines, co-design in the learning sciences has focused on the relational, social, and dynamic learning processes that occur within co-design spaces (Mawasi et al., 2023; Penuel, 2019; Philip et al., 2022). This burgeoning line of research from the learning sciences complicates how we design, analyze, and assess co -design spaces, particularly when time constraints often necessitate that these co -design sessions occur over short or infrequent periods. Extrapolating concrete design decisions from co- design spaces can be exceptionally difficult given the fluidity, tensions, and outright contradictions that emerge ( Chang & Philip, 2025). Here, rather than narrowly conceptualizing the telos of co- design spaces as surfacing fixed designs, we build on Rogoff’s conceptualization of “learning as a process of transformation of participation” (1994) and argue that co- design spaces must be understood as sites where participants and researchers dynamically learn to co -design together. In this way, we understand co- design as a deeply context-dependent, relational, political, and ethical practice that researchers and participants construct and hone together; design decisions thus emerge as an ever-evolving byproduct of these practices (Bang & Vossoughi, 2016; Vossoughi et al., 2021). Past work in the learning sciences offers several starting points for exploring co-design spaces as sites of mutual learning about co-design itself. McKercher (2020) argues that building conditions for co-design workshops 2274 require intentional power sharing, relationship and trust building, and creating safe spaces for participants. The relational nature of co -design spaces presents a key challenge, as co -design engagements (in practice) typically occur over a short, condensed time period (10s of hours). Such tensions, even when unintended, raise important questions for the Learning Sciences community regarding what co-design entails and how to educate participants and researchers in co-design. Prior work has begun to conceptualize co-design as co-researching with participants and youth (e.g., Clark et al., 2022), while educating learners about the research process. While past work gestures towards the deep relational work that happens in co- design processes, our understanding of how those relational processes unfold is often constrained by two artificially imposed constraints on how many co- design spaces are (a) desi gned, as short, condensed, irregular, or infrequent activities, and (b) studied, as analysis primarily focused on the interactions happening within the formal co -design activities themselves. This symposium brings together five projects that seek to zoom out from these constraints in different ways and conceptualize co -design as a pedagogical space that generates educational possibilities (Freire, 1976) for transformation and shifts in interactions, dynamics, relations, roles, and knowledge, while positioning both researchers and participants as learners of co-design. The projects offered here are hardly the only projects in the learning sciences that thoughtfully challenge those constraints; we seek to make a humble contribution by bringing together a highly diverse group of co-design projects that engage with those constraints and possibilities in creative ways. By exploring these constraints and possibilities, we collectively explore different approaches we have taken in exploring this argument, by focusing on five examples of what we consider a form of co-design research work. Across these projects, we take care to highlight the conditions for co- design, describing the process of mutual becoming and what is transformed in the process, emerging issues in the co-design process (e.g., relational trust, context, power, shifts, ideologies, axiologies), and the tensions or possibilities between desired outcomes and what was eventually achieved. This focus enables us to make the following contributions: (1) We bridge between various co-design projects in the field to recognize the multiplicity of approaches to co-design, and to refine our conceptualization of co-design. (2) We outline key challenges for conceptualizing co -design spaces in the learning sciences for both technology-mediated environments and work with educators, practitioners, and learners using participatory methods. (3) We examine the kind of learning co-design environments afford to participants and, researchers in their collaborative learning process. (4) We examine the ways co -design can be a potential space for creative and constructive exploration and deconstruction and construction of ideas, among participants and researchers with no necessarily defined outcomes needing to emerge - enabling possibilities for critical thinking, liberatory education, and fluid outcomes that create new possibilities for groups and that could be similar to group work in psychology treatments. Overall, the symposium provides guidance on addressing co- design not only as a methodological approach, but also as a learning environment design that enables diverse possibilities for learning for both participants and researchers. Each of the five projects here identifies different ways to zoom out from the typical frames used to study co-design spaces, thereby illustrating different ways that researchers and/or participants learn from each other in ways that enrich the co -design process: (1) Chang et al. zoom out from one -off co-design intensives to show how researchers and youth participants negotiate the aims of co- designing AI-for-education tools over a three -year period. (2) Mawasi et al. zoom out from the formal co- design activities and show how a team of researchers/designers, themselves operating from the margins, learn from each other in order to create co- design spaces around ethical AI that respond to the political contexts of Arab/Palestinian youth. (3) Romero & Lee zoom out from simplified descriptions of participant needs to demonstrate how decision junctures during long-term co -design processes, both big and small, shape how researchers and participants participate in co- designing math and computer science curriculum. (4) Takeuchi et al. zoom out from recent history to demonstrate how researchers and participants learn to attune themselves to the agency and teachings of the Land through mutual learning and imagining, spanning approximately 12,000 years of land stewardship by indigenous communities. (5) Ehrenfeld et al. zoom out from the seemingly convenient touchpoints between researcher and academic during co-design and demonstrate how mismatched rhythms of co-design create pedagogical and ethical tensions when researchers partner with math educators. Collectively, these projects illustrate heterogeneity in co -design research enactment across geographies, topics, and methodological choices of design- based research, and demonstrate how co -design can serve as a productive framework across disciplines, including AI in Education, Mathematics Education, and STEM Education. Together, these contributions assert the need for teams t o co-design for co- design—to continually 2275 examine and refine the very processes and relationships that make co-design possible. As a final point, to illustrate our conceptualization of co-design across these five papers, we share Figure 1, an example of tatreez, Palestinian embroidery art. The art of tatreez , as described by the United Nations Educational, Scientific and Cultural Organization (UNESCO, 2021), particularly among women, is an intergenerational and sociocultural practice whose symbols and motifs (e.g., birds, trees, flowers, and places ) carry knowledge, stories, memories, and epistemologies. It has been, and continues to be, widely practiced within Palestinian communities. By “zooming out,” the front and reverse offer two vantage points on a single, entangled practice in which the product carries the process: some makers keep the reverse deliberately neat; others show thread paths and revisions. As Palestinian women engage in tatreez , they enact several choices while being intentional about what they are creating; they often do so in community and in circles, talking with one another. Like co -design, tatreez interweaves structure and improvisation, and ties knowledge to land, relations, and stories. Made collectively—in circles and conversation—the practice is both what is created -and-process itself, a space for care and knowledge-building. Figure 1 Tatreez Tatreez (noun and verb) as co -design: form-and-process as one entangled practice. The patterned front and the reverse—whether kept deliberately neat or showing thread paths —are complementary views of the same iterative making. As in co -design, meaning emerges through interwoven structure and improvisation, situated relations, ties to land, and storytelling. Handmade by Areej Mawasi. Overview of the symposium A key theme of this year’s International Society of the Learning Sciences (ISLS) conference centers on creating learning experiences that “partner with purpose” with the communities we design with and for. However, such intentions for purposeful partnership require a nuanced understanding of the educational ecologies that shape research–practice partnerships and collaborative design efforts. These intentions also call for an acknowledgment of the resources, capacities, and constraints at play for both communities and researchers across the various cycles of design and partnership—such as temporality, sociocultural and political contexts, histories, relational dynamics, and the lived experiences of participants (e.g., Bang & Vossoughi, 2016; Ehrenfeld & Stengel, 2025; Mawasi et al., 2023). While we expect this symposium to be held entirely in person at the conference venue, we will intentionally build in the option for remote participation by presenters to accommodate emergent circumstances that affect presenters’ ability to travel. papers.title: Rise Above State-of-the-Art: Designing New Possibilities of GenAI for Knowledge Building
papers.authors: Jiayu Cheng, Vivian Leung, Yue Zhao, Chen Wang, Bodong Chen, Jianwei Zhang, Yanqing Sun, Sudarshan Kammu, Mei-Hwa Chen, Seng Chee Tan, Yee Yin Tan, Chew Lee Teo, Guangji Yuan, Xueqi Feng

papers.abstract: This symposium presents cutting- edge research that explores how Generative Artificial Intelligence (GenAI) can be leveraged to enrich human-AI collaboration in CSCL for Knowledge Building (KB). It challenges prevailing educational paradigms of ‘learning from AI’ and instead it foregrounds collaborative creation, emphasizing how GenAI can be harnessed to enrich epistemic agency empowering learners in knowledge building. Building on four decades of KB research, this symposium aims to enrich both the conceptualization and design of human- AI collaboration for knowledge advancement. Seven interrelated contributions demonstrate emergent KB -AI design approaches, including dialogic approaches that engage learners in collaborative dialogue with AI, and integrated approaches that embed AI affordances into knowledge building environments. These designs span diverse contexts from doctoral interdisciplinary research to K -12 classrooms. Grounded in a design-based approach, this symposium positions these contributions as conceptual artifacts for design advancement and envisions new KB-AI synergies that enable emerging forms of CSCL and knowledge creation.

papers.abstract: This research engages teachers as knowledge builders who create minicourses on the Knowledge Network for Innovations in Learning and Teaching (KNILT; https://knilt.arcc.albany.edu/) to support peer teacher learning around authentic issues of educational practice. A content analysis of 42 teacher -designed minicourses examined the types of knowledge addressed and the teaching methods employed to support teacher learning. The findings show that the minicourses devote substantial effort to helping teachers deepen their knowledge of teaching, student learning, curriculum content, and technology, with rich co-occurrence among knowledge themes and learning activities. papers.title: Cultivating Relational Trust in Community-Engaged Educational Research Partnerships for Environmental Justice
papers.authors: Chris Jadallah, Emily V. Reigh, Symone Gyles, Devon Azzam, Lauren Daus, Sam Burmester, Minjung Shin, Amanda Gonzaga, Danielle Harlow, Julie A. Bianchini, Hosun Kang
papers.design_stakeholders: High School Teachers; Educators & Practitioners; Youth & Adolescents; Educational Researchers & Designers; Community Members & Partners; Domain Experts & Technologists; School Administrators & Leaders
papers.abstract: Community-engaged educational research partnerships have the potential to catalyze new approaches to environmental justice teaching and learning by bringing together multiple actors with different lenses, positionalities, epistemologies, and expertise to unsettle normative approaches to educational practice. Such work, however, requires situating relational trust as central to partnership development. In this paper, we examine how relational trust was built across four different educational partnerships working toward environmental justice. We identify five themes that support developing and sustaining relational trust: (a) collectively working toward socio-ecological change, (b) naming and disrupting hierarchies, (c) purposeful processes, (d) centering relationality, and (e) redistributing resources. Theoretically, this paper advances our understanding of relational trust as central to partnership work; methodologically, it deepens our understanding of using partnership artifacts to understand partnership dynamics; and practically, it provides insights and tools for researchers who aspire to cultivate and sustain relational trust in partnership activities. Major issue(s) addressed In the face of ever -increasing environmental challenges, there is a growing need to innovate novel forms of teaching and learning that support youth and communities in understanding, interrogating, and taking action to address environmental injustice and to work toward socio- ecological well -being. Taking this as a point of departure, this paper examines community -engaged educational research partnerships as having the potential to catalyze novel frameworks, models, and approaches for environmental justice education. These types of partnerships involve collaborations that extend beyond researchers and school districts; they intentionally include researchers, youth, families, teachers, administrators, frontline communities, land workers, and other actors who are collectively working toward educational and environmental improvement. Such partnerships are uniquely positioned to support this work because they bring together people with different perspectives to jointly identify problems of practice, co-design potential solutions, and monitor their effectiveness across iterations (Bang et al., 2010; Coburn & Penuel, 2016; Ishimaru et al., 2016). Within these partnership processes, diverse sets of actors bring together different sets of expertise in order to envision, implement, and evaluate novel curricular, pedagogical, and material interventions in support of environmental justice education - from new infrastructures like green schoolyards and outdoor classrooms, to new curriculum that engages environmental justice as an anchoring phenomenon of inquiry. In examining community -engaged educational research partnerships, we focus on the construct of relational trust. Relational trust is defined here as the willingness to participate in relationships that potentially involve risk, vulnerability, and tension on the basis of interactions premised on benevolence, competence, reliability, and respect (Kolleck, 2023). Specifically, we ask, how is relational trust built in community -engaged educational research partnerships working toward environmental justice? Theoretical and methodological approach(es) pursued Theoretically, we draw on literature on research-practice partnerships (Coburn & Penuel, 2016) and participatory design research (Bang & Vossoughi, 2016) to frame our study of relational trust. From these perspectives, we understand partnerships and design processes as spaces of learning in and of themselves, where researchers, teachers, and, in the present cases, additional community-based partners collaborate across boundaries to negotiate 388 goals, engage in shared practices, and innovate pedagogical and curricular practices (Goldman et al., 2022; Morales-Doyle et al., 2025). Engaging in boundary crossing necessitates nurturing sustained relational trust. Cultivating relational trust happens over time and is a continuous process, entailing a deliberate, intentional focus on power and privilege given partners’ diverse histories, social positions, and range of prior experiences (Henrick et al., 2023; Vakil et al., 2016). When partners with diverse organizational and personal identities, structures, and routines come together, there is opportunity and risk, both of which may be amplified in work to address environmental justice given different histories of marginalization, contested meanings and values associated with the environment, and intersecting challenges that cut across political, cultural, and ecological lines (Morales - Doyle et al., 2025). This makes relational trust all the more important as an area of inquiry.

papers.title: A Design Space for Dialogic Assessment in CSCL
papers.authors: Rolf Steier, Magnus Hontvedt, Jacob Davidsen, Charlotte Beal, Morten Oddvik, Marit Solem
papers.design_stakeholders: Teachers; Educators & Practitioners; Students & Learners; Educational Researchers & Designers; Domain Experts & Technologists; School Administrators & Leaders
papers.abstract: Dialogic assessment remains remarkably unexplored as a research and design setting in CSCL. We address this gap by developing a design space to support future partnership-based work in our field. Our design space reflects a 1.5- year investigation of dialogic assessment practices and perspectives conducted through literature review work, focus group interviews with practitioners, formal and informal discussions with colleagues and prototype development work with technology designers. First, we frame the design space concept before arguing for the relevance of dialogic assessment as a potential CSCL activity. Then, we present our design space through a cumulative distillation of four relevant perspectives and seven design dimensions. Finally, we conclude by laying out an agenda reflecting how this design space can inform future work and prompt innovative assessment practices.

papers.title: Programming Self-Efficacy and Outcomes, and Programming-oriented Prompting: A Comparison of Two Human–AI Collaboration Configurations
papers.authors: Ying-Tien Wu, Yi-Hong Zeng, Ching-Hui Kuan
papers.design_stakeholders: K-12 Teachers; Higher Education Instructors / Faculty; Elementary Students & Children; Educational Researchers & Designers
papers.abstract: This study investigates the effects of GenAI -assisted programming learning on fifth graders’ computational thinking, programming self-efficacy and outcomes, and programming - oriented prompting. A total of 99 fifth graders from four classes participated and were randomly assigned to two GenAI -assisted programming instruction groups with different human– AI collaboration configurations: single student -AI collaboration (SSAC), in which each student worked individually with a computer with ChatGPT, and dyad student -AI collaboration (DSAC), in which two students worked in pairs, collaboratively using a shared computer with ChatGPT. The instruction was implemented over 6 weeks (1 class per week). This study revealed no significant difference in computational thinking between the two groups of students after GenAI-assisted programming instruction ( p>0.05). In contrast, the students in the DSAC group showed significantly higher programming self -efficacy and better programming outcomes ( p<0.05). Moreover, significant differences in the distribution of programming- oriented prompting between these two groups of students were also found ( p<0.05).

papers.title: What Children’s Books Do and Do Not Teach About AI: An Analysis Using the AI4K12 Framework
papers.authors: Feiwen Xiao, Shiyan Jiang
papers.design_stakeholders: Elementary / Early Childhood Teachers; Elementary Students & Children; Educational Researchers & Designers; Community Members & Partners
papers.abstract: Although many storybooks introducing artificial intelligence (AI) to young children are now available, their quality and educational value have not been systematically or empirically examined. This study addresses this gap by analyzing how AI- themed storybooks conceptualize and communicate foundational AI ideas, practices, and values to young learners. Guided by the AI4K12 framework, this study shows that while most books make AI approachable through friendly robots and playful visuals, they rarely explain how AI actually works. Concepts such as representation, reasoning, and learning were largely introduced as vocabulary rather than as processes, and ethical or responsible AI use was largely absent. These portrayals risk reinforcing AI as magical or infallible. The study offers implications for designing AI literacy materials for young children that balance engagement with conceptual transparency and critical awareness.

papers.title: Living the Impossible: Designing Life Happens, an AI-Supported Budget and Justice Simulation
papers.authors: Devan Walton, Haesol Bae, Jaesung Park, Yingru Zhao, Raymond Weiss, Susan Tashjian
papers.design_stakeholders: Teachers; Higher Education Instructors / Faculty; Undergraduate / Graduate Students; Community Members & Partners
papers.abstract: This paper reports on the design of Life Happens, a classroom simulation in which students manage household budgets across twelve months while encountering criminal justice– related financial obligations. Grounded in situated learning theory, the simulatio n develops quantitative reasoning and perspective -taking through authentic financial dilemmas. Initial prototypes relied on large language models, producing inconsistencies and outputs that reinforced harmful stereotypes. Informed by a trauma -aware framework, the team restructured the system into a three -layer architecture: a deterministic core, a curated event layer, and a bounded AI layer limited to brief affective text messages. This paper focuses on design principles that emerged from documented failures during deployments at a Hispanic -Serving community college and a Minority-Serving state university. Context, theoretical framing, and focus Faculty at a Hispanic -Serving community college and a Minority- Serving state university in the northeastern United States identified a need for experiential tools conveying how criminal justice involvement compounds household financial hardship (García et al., 2019). The interdisciplinary partnership brought together computer science pedagogy and criminal justice education to serve predominantly first-generation college students (Penuel et al., 2013). Institutional constraints, including limited class time, variable devices, and diverse student demographics, shaped every design decision. We conceptualize learning through situated learning theory (Lave & Wenger, 1991), which holds that knowledge develops through participation in authentic practices. Life Happens situates students within household financial management under justice- system co nstraints, requiring arithmetic computation, budgeting, and quantitative trade-off reasoning as disciplinary competencies that emerge through meaningful decision- making (Gee, 2007). Simultaneously, students develop perspective -taking as they experience cascading consequences of systemic inequities (Belman & Flanagan, 2010). This paper focuses on the simulation’s design and AI integration, tracing how concrete prototype failures led to the principled architecture presented here. Simulation design and learning affordances Life Happens positions students as household decision- makers managing limited resources across twelve simulated months. Each cycle requires allocating funds across housing, food, transportation, healthcare, and phone services. Justice -related obligations such as probation fees, court -ordered payments, and commissary contributions impose additional mandatory costs (Harper et al., 2020). Five well -being indicators update transparently based on decisions, with visible arithmetic enabling students to anticipate consequences (Chernikova et al., 2020). Quarterly reflection prompts emphasize metacognition and discussion (Squire, 2011). The system employs a three -layer architecture. The deterministic core maintains authored family compositions, income parameters, and cost data from regional economic sources, ensuring reproducibility and enabling instructor customization. The event layer introduces curated disruptions ranging from routine expenses to justice -related challenges, each with specified costs and well -being consequences. The affective AI layer generates brief text messages that translate numerical outcomes into personal narratives, adding emotional context while the core mechanics remain fully deterministic. AI integration: From unconstrained generation to bounded use Initial prototypes relied on large language models to generate family scenarios, event narratives, and financial parameters (Yan et al., 2024), producing three categories of documented failure. Generated family compositions contained logical inconsistencies that confused students and undermined budgeting strategies. AI- produced cost structures varied unpredictably across similar scenarios, making it difficult for students to develop reliable 2865 quantitative intuitions. Generated content also perpetuated harmful stereotypes about poverty and justice involvement, particularly affecting overrepresented communities (Lee et al., 2024). These failures demanded a framework for addressing stereotypes and trauma. Drawing on trauma - informed pedagogy (Carello & Butler, 2015), we committed to ensuring that scenarios allow full participation independent of personal history, that content represents systemic patterns while honoring individual complexity, and that instructors retain the ability to modify or disable any element they judge inappropriate. This framework guided the restructuring of AI’s role. Because educator control over sensitive elements is a pedagogical and ethical requirement, all factual elements became authored content maintained in versioned databases (Gibson, 2023). AI was retained solely for generating 280- character text messages formatted as communications from family members, employers, and service providers (see Figure 1). Prompts incorporate strict constraints on tone, relationship dynamics, and prohibited content, and each message passes validation filters before display. Pre - authored fallback messages activate when outputs fail validation or when instructors operate in non -AI mode (Aldrich, 2005). This bounded application introduces meaningful variation across simulation runs and supports empathy-building, all while the deterministic mechanics remain fully intact. Figure 1 The Phone Message Interface Displays AI-Generated Communications from Family Members and Service Providers. Design principles traced to practice The following principles emerged from the documented failures and institutional constraints above, and we trace each to its originating episode (Wang & Hannafin, 2005). Separation of deterministic and generative components arose because AI -generated cost s tructures produced inconsistencies that undermined learning objectives. Educator authorship of core mechanics resolved this while confining AI to a role where variability adds value and fairness is preserved. Trauma- aware content governance emerged from en counters with AI outputs that stereotyped justice-involved families. Instructor override, scenario review, and explicit content boundaries ensure that every version of the simulation actively interrogates these patterns. Privacy-conscious architecture responded to institutional review board concerns, and the minimal state approach transmits only current meter values and recent decisions (Pardo & Siemens, 2014). Redundancy and fallback systems became essential after pilot-session technical failures disrupted engagement, so pre -authored alternatives for every AI feature ensure continuity. Reflection over scoring prioritizes metacognition because early testing revealed that competitive scoring distracted students from systemic insights (Li et al., 2024). Conclusion Life Happens demonstrates that AI can enhance educational simulations when carefully bounded by pedagogical goals and equity commitments. The most consequential design decisions centered on preserving educator authority over content touching systemic inequality, trauma, and identity. These transferable principles confirm that thoughtful AI integration remains accessible across diverse educational settings when guided by clear learning objectives. 2866 References Aldrich, C. papers.abstract: Conversation-based assessments (CBAs) incorporate conversational agents into computer-based tasks to elicit evidence about learners’ knowledge and skills in a domain. We describe the design of a science conversation -based assessment incorporating AI agents that engages high school students in a scenario related to storm formation and storm prediction. We further discuss results from a usability study in which students completed the CBA task and subsequently responded to interview questions about their perceptions related to the design and usability of the task. Students generally had positive experiences with the task and its design, though challenges related to information clarity and AI interaction authenticity were noted.

papers.abstract: Many education technology(edTech) product rollouts underperform because tools are designed for schools instead of with them. In this practice paper we describe a three -month pilot where an edTech product manager, developer, and designer worked from the school, sat in classrooms, and co- created a Portfolio Analyzer with the Principal, teachers, and students. We adapted Design -Based Implementation Research (DBIR) within a Research –Practice Partnership (RPP) to run short improvement cycles: observe in class , try a change, check it in class, write it into school policy with a scope to review and iterate. The pilot saw strong use in Grades 5, 7, and 9 (~60 students, 10 teachers) with clear improvements to day- to-day usability and review flow, leading to a whole -school rollout decision. We shar e a simple, repeatable pattern for other K-12 schools and edtech teams.

papers.title: Wordless Books as Tools for Language, Identity, and Voice
papers.authors: Arlen Nava, Christine Lee
papers.design_stakeholders: Teachers; Elementary Students & Children; Educational Researchers & Designers; Community Members & Partners
papers.abstract: This paper is led by a dual language kindergarten teacher and presents insights on a multi-year participatory research study on wordless books. We discuss how wordless books can support emergent dual language learners by fostering literacy through storyte lling and creative expression. The paper highlights a case study on how wordless books can empower children to see themselves as competent readers. We argue for a broader definition of literacy that values and includes students’ linguistic and cultural resources, and position wordless books as a tool for equitable access to reading for all children. Objectives of our practice-oriented paper Over the past three years, Arlen and Christine , a dual language kindergarten teacher and a university researcher, have collaborated on a participatory design -based research study (Bang & Vossoughi, 2016) examining the potential of wordless books for young dual language learners. Our paper examines how wordless books can serve as a powerful tool for dual language literacy, empowering young learners to take agency in their oral storytelling and reading. When we think of literacy instruction in primary grade levels, it tends to focus solely on phonics, accuracy, and decoding words. This experience can provide a narrow view of literacy, and it views children as passive recipients rather than active meaning makers (Freire & Slover, 1983). It also doesn’t leave ro om for student-driven creative expression, like storytelling. For emergent dual language learners, the act of learning to read in a new language can present an extra level of pressure, setting expectations that they have to somehow quickly master both languages. Wordless picture books offer a different kind of entry point into literacy. It can remove the pressure to perform and instead invite children to build their own narratives using a variety of resources like language, tone, gestures, and imagination. Our paper shows wordless books as a resource to support children’s identities as lifelong readers and empower them by giving children agency in their storytelling. We argue that we need to move away from deficit thinking by highlighting the immense skills children already bring to the world of reading. This means that we must ultimately expand the definition of literacy by exploring ways of being a lifelong literate human being, and help children form a relationship with literature that extends beyond merely decoding words. In this paper, we present a case study that shares how a student with limited Spanish, in a dual language classroom, can communicate powerfully to tell stories when given the tools and space to do so. We follow a kindergarten student (5 year old) who used wordless books to tell stories in both English and Spanish over time. Her storytelling showed how young children can express meaning in complex and personal ways, even when their vocabulary in a second language is limited and still dev eloping. Therefore, we wonder, how can wordless picture books support student autonomy in storytelling for emergent dual language learners? Wordless books Wordless books are picture books with little to no written text. Thus, readers rely on the illustrations and images to read and tell stories. These visual stories invite readers to interpret meaning and construct narratives using their own imagination, lived experiences, and cultural knowledge (Lee, et al., 2025; Razfar & Gutierrez, 2003; Vygotsky, 1978). Our case study draws on literature that positions literacy as a meaning- making social activity. Freire and Slover (1983) argue that literacy is not a mechanical skill to be mastered, but a process of consciousness formation where learners first “read the world” before they “read the word.” His conception of reading was that it was a critical, experiential, and transformative act (Crawford & Hade, 2000). Therefore, reading is inherently social, reflective, and tied to identity, power, and context (Vygotsky, 1978). We argue wordless books can support storytelling, language development, and creative expression, and offer young learners the opportunity to reflec t on their own experiences and prior knowledge (Arif & Hashim, 2008). Wordless books open up storytelling for all children, regardless of their reading level or language proficiency. They invite students to navigate meaning using gesture, tone, facial expression, and oral language across multiple languages (Alvermann, 2002; Dehghani et al., 2013). In doing so, wordless books position students as active participants in the meaning- making process (Freire & Slover, 1983), rather than passive recipients of a fixed and scripted narrative. Wordless books also offer space for children still developing language to engage with complex ideas and express personal insights through their own narrative decisions (Arif & Hashim, 2008; Goriot et al., 2024) . For emergent dual language learners, wordless picture books offer inclusive, flexible, and linguistically accessible 2147 entry points into literacy. Children may even feel freer to communicate authentically by lifting the pressure of correctness and allowing for fluid, spontaneous storytelling. Because the narrative is not fixed by written words, students are free to interpr et and reframe the story in ways that reflect their multilingual and multicultural experiences (Crawford & Hade, 2000). This makes wordless books especially powerful in culturally and linguistically diverse classrooms, where children can exercise autonomy and agency in meaning-making, without being confined by rigid, traditional models of literacy instruction that often feel limited at a young age. Each child, regardless of language or fluency, is encouraged by the pictures in wordless books to construct their own meaning of the story, offering beneficial possibilities for use in all-inclusive learning settings. Designing wordless books into literacy curriculum The design and implementation of wordless books into our literacy curriculum came from a multi -year collaboration between Arlen and Christine. We began the work by searching for and reading research on wordless books in early literacy. We then introduced wordless books to our kindergarten (5- 6 years) classroom, and immediately realized the potential these books had for emergent readers, especial ly as a way to equitably engage and provide access to literacy regardless of the child’s background. Our initial observation of students exploring wordless books was that these books can be a powerful tool for voice and agency. This is important for dual language classrooms and multi-lingual learners because many children in a dual language classroom can often be positioned as “being academically behind” in their literacy or language skills. We took these preliminary observations and focused on designing a learning experience for children with wordless books where they can see themselves as creative meaning-makers, where they can author their own stories, and come to form a solid identity as a reader early on. In Table 1, we outline how we designed our literacy curriculum to incorporate wordless books over the academic school year. Table 1 Outline of Wordless Books in our Literacy Curriculum. Timeline Goals Description of Goals September Exposure and exploration of wordless books Children freely explored wordless books. October-November Sequence of events and details from illustrations Students did picture walks and were encouraged to pay close attention to the details in the illustrations. Based on their observations, students made conjectures about what the story was about and where they thought the story was going. December-January Perspectives in storytelling Students explored how narration and dialogue shape a story. Tried on and played with different voices for different characters. Discussed and practiced how stories can be told in first, second, or third person. February-June Wordless books as part of regular reading practices Wordless books became a regular reading activity that sparked creative and playful conversation. Students regularly chose to read wordless books during their reading time. Case study Arlen teaches in the dual language program, and Christine is a university researcher. Our research was conducted in an elementary school in Southern California, and the case we present in this paper is from Arlen’s dual language (10% English instruction and 90% Spanish instruction) kindergarten classroom. Our focal student, Camila (pseudonym), was a five year old emergent bilingual learner who primarily spoke English at home and was newly acquiring Spanish through the school's dual language program. To explore Camila's storytelling across languages, 2148 we video-recorded her storytelling with wordless books. In November 2024, Camila narrated the wordless picture book Good Dog, Carl (Day, 1985) in English, and in March 2025, she narrated The Girl and the Bicycle (Pett, 2014) in Spanish. When we look at Camila’s number of words spoken across the two video recordings (Table 2), it is no surprise that the total words spoken in English while reading Good Dog, Carl is much higher than when she read The Girl and the Bicycle in Spanish. Table 2 Total Words Spoken when Reading in English and Spanish English (Good Dog, Carl) in November 2024 Spanish (The Girl and the Bicycle) in March 2025 Total Words Spoken 261 111 Average Words Spoken per Page 8 words per page 3 words per page In both recordings, Camila is reading the wordless books to two of her classmates who were attentively listening to the story by her side. We transcribed both video- recorded reading sessions and organized the transcripts by page to arrange her narration with the visual content of the book. Together, we analyzed the two transcripts and found two emerging themes that we present in this paper (Braun & Clarke, 2022). Theme 1: Emotional expression as a storytelling strategy Across our transcripts, Camila demonstrated that emotional expression can be a powerful tool for storytelling. Throughout the Spanish storytelling transcript, Camila relied on her vocal tone, pauses, facial gestures, and nonverbal sounds (like dramatic sighs) to convey a character's or narrator's feelings. The transcript of her Spanish reading of the wordless book was rich with these emotional expressions and was a crucial part of her storytelling. Camila expressed deep understanding of the story even when her Spanish vocabulary was limited, showing how emotional gestures, prosody, and tone can support meaning- making when verbal language is still developing. In her English narration of Good Dog, Carl , Camila primarily used sentences with consistent pacing and a neutral tone. For example, she said, “Carl looks out the window. The baby sneaks out, and the dog comes by”. While this sentence is descriptively accurate of the story, her delivery and oral t elling of it resembled the cadence of classroom read-alouds, where students are taught to prioritize clarity and linear sequencing rather than emotional interpretation and creative storytelling. In contrast, her Spanish narration of The Girl and the Bicycle had nonverbal elements like tone, gesture, and diverse pacing to convey emotional depth. Earlier in the story, she asked, “¿En dónde está mi dinero? ¿Aquí? ¿Aquí?” with a rising intonation while using her whole body to mimic the action of searching for something. Her rising intonation and repetition of “¿Aquí?” created a sense of urgency and concern, as she embodied the character's anxious search for money to buy a bicycle. Later, Camila captured the character’s disappointment by using a different tone to interpret and communicate the emotional arc of the story. She paused and sighed dramatically before saying “Poquito triste,” meaning “a little sad” as she embodied the character’s emotions when she found out the bicycle was gone. Camila effectively communicated the sadness of the moment through her tone shift, softly stating “Poquito triste”, dramatic pause, and pacing. These emotional expressions added depth to the statement, expressing a feeling that extended beyond the image itself and making listeners understand the heavy moment in the story. Therefore, Camila’s use of semiotic resources effectively communicated the feelings and emotional depth of the story despite speaking fewer words – illustrating the true power of embodiment and emotional connections in rich storytelling. Theme 2: Narrative perspectives Camila's storytelling across the two transcripts also revealed a shift in narrative perspectives. When she read Good Dog, Carl in English, her point of view was in the third person, and when she read The Girl and the Bicycle in Spanish, it was in both the third person and first person perspectives. For example, in Good Dog, Carl, she said, “They open the door, and went to the Mommy and Daddy's room, and they played with makeup”. Camila stayed in the third person, narrative perspective throughout her entire reading of the story as she orally described the events of the story. 2149 In contrast, Camila's narration in Spanish showed more fluidity. Rather than sticking to a single point of view, she moved between third person and first person to tell the story. For example, on page 8 of The Girl and the Bicycle, Camila said “No tiene más money, no tiene más monedas,” meaning “She doesn’t have any more money, she doesn’t have any more coins,”. But later, on page 13, she exclaimed, “Ven con yo! No! ¡No quiero, no gracias!” meaning “Come with me! No! I don’t want to, no thank you!”, steppi ng into the character’s voice and embodying what the character would excitedly say in the story. Camila exercised narrative autonomy, shaping the story in deeper ways that felt meaningful to her in the moment. Her inventive dialogue and expressive stance reflect how learners construct meaning by using their voice and lived experience. Instead of simply retelling the events, Camila authored a story that reflected her understanding, feelings, and agency. Concluding remarks One of the most powerful lessons learned from observing students engage with wordless books is how quickly they are able to see themselves as competent readers. Even at a young age, children can step into stories with confidence and agency before they’ve mastered decoding text. They also don’t need to rely on others to access these books. This accessibility gives them the opportunity to take ownership of their reading. As a dual language teacher, this was powerful for students because it encouraged them to take risks and play with language. It was wonderful to see young children feel empowered with their reading, as if they could grab a book and tell a story all on their own. As a result of this work, a parent thanked Arlen for our work with wordless books because her son had a hard time feeling confident while decoding text. However, she mentioned that with wordless books, he was never discouraged and always saw himself as a storyteller and reader. Recently, Arlen saw this parent on campus again, and she shared that her son now reads books and loves being a reader. She attributed his journey and growth as a reader to wordless books because they made him feel like a competent reader as he learned to decode text. As a dual language teacher, A rlen also learned that wordless books encourage emerging dual language students to take risks. While there is clearly a story to tell, wordless books have no script; thus, there is no strict expectation of what students must say. Instead, students are able to freely use the words they already know or play with new and unfamiliar words in their storytelling. Through their experimentation with storytelling, they are able to stretch themselves in a low -stakes and playful way. This feeling of agency and creative freedom is what creates space for incredible growth. We also realized that wordless books served as a tool for equity because the stories welcome every child, no matter their background knowledge. Regardless of the child’s dominant or target language, wordless books provide everyone an opportunity for conversation, making literacy accessible across all learners. The books create a space of inclusivity and allow students to connect, share, and learn from each other. Thus, every child’s unique voice is honored through expression filled with emotion, because although children are reading the author’s art and images, they are ultimately telling their own stories. When children are able to bring aspects of themselves into the classroom, such as their home language or family stories, they naturally create a space f or cultural representation through wordless books. This affirms their identities as competent and agentic storytellers and makes them visible within the classroom setting. Wordless books become a universal resource for students. Institutionalized education often lacks opportunities for every child to be heard and valued. Wordless books remove these barriers, allowing every child to be seen. Throughout our research partnership, we came to realize how intertwined research, teaching, and learning are. Before becoming a teacher, Arlen studied with Fred Erickson, whose work with teachers showed Arlen the power in positioning educators as co-constructors of knowledge. In our work, we made decisions about how wordless books would be integrated into the curriculum and how to collect and analyze our data together. We respected and made space for our intellectual insights and curiosities in this work. Not only has this made our research stronger, but it has also given Arlen the confidence to speak to other educators to reform literacy programs, especially for elementary dual language classrooms. The collaborative participation in research gave Arlen the data and the tools to communicate and share the importance of wordless books in this paper, which invites other teachers to engage in this work as a way to transform and grow our teaching practices. papers.title: A “Co-Design Intervention” with AI analytics to Support the Academically Productive Talk of Title 1 School Math Tutors and their Students: A Comparative Interrupted Time Series Analysis
papers.authors: Amirpasha Zandieh, Jeffrey Bush Tayne, Chelsea Brown, Jennifer Jacobs, Sandra Sawaya
papers.design_stakeholders: Teachers; Educators & Practitioners; Youth & Adolescents; Educational Researchers & Designers
papers.abstract: This study examines whether a co- design-based professional learning intervention for tutors, supported by an AI feedback tool, influenced students’ Academically Productive Talk (APT) within a high-dosage algebra tutoring program in Title 1 schools in an urban U.S. school district. Using a comparative interrupted time series (CITS) design, we analyzed 9,037 tutoring sessions over the 42 weeks of one academic year, comparing tutors who participated in a nine - week co-design process with those who did not. Tuto rs in the intervention co -designed an AI interface called the “Talk Trees”, visualizing student talk patterns to guide student reflection on collaborative discourse. Results show short -term, positive shifts in students’ relating to academic ideas of their peers following the intervention, with modest, non- significant gains in instances of students making claims and providing reasoning. These findings highlight co- design’s potential to foster dialogic pedagogy in the context of boundary-crossing professional learning. They also demonstrate how CITS methods can evaluate AI-mediated interventions in authentic educational contexts.

papers.title: Learning through Partnerships: How Co-Design and Embodied Play Can Shape a Playful Learning Ecology
papers.authors: Melinda Renteria, Elsa Baumgartner, Haydee Renteria, Heidi Baumgartner, Akshay Nagarajan
papers.design_stakeholders: Middle School Teachers; Educators & Practitioners; Elementary Students & Children; Educational Researchers & Designers; Domain Experts & Technologists
papers.abstract: What happens when teachers and researchers partner to co- design a tangible, embodied game to foster computational thinking? Byte Beads is a game in which children compose and perform sequences of beads associated with actions to represent computational patterns. Initially conceived within computing education, the game evolved as teachers helped shape a design supporting pattern- based reasoning, collaborative embodied sequencing, and executive functioning skills, including attention and cognitive flexibility . Drawing on constructionist and embodied learning traditions, we examine how researcher -practitioner partnerships shaped the evolution of the game and the pedagogical practices surrounding it. Tracing these interactions across relational collaborations, p rofessional development, and classroom enactment, the paper illustrates how partnership itself becomes a site of learning where design, pedagogy and play co-develop. This work contributes to the ISLS 2026 theme of Partnerships with Purpose by conceptualizing partnership as an ongoing process of co-designing and sustaining environments supporting playful embodied learning.

papers.title: “A Makerspace is a Lousy Place to Do School In”: Studying Student-Driven Sociocultural Shifts in a Classroom Makerspace
papers.authors: John F. “Trey” Smith, Colin Hennessy Elliott
papers.design_stakeholders: Math Teachers; Higher Education Instructors / Faculty; Educators & Practitioners; Middle School Students; Educational Researchers & Designers; Community Members & Partners; Domain Experts & Technologists; School Administrators & Leaders
papers.abstract: This paper investigates longitudinal shifts in sociocultural activity in a K-8 classroom makerspace in the United States. Using cultural historical activity theory (CHAT) as a theoretical framework and practitioner reflections over three years as a primary data source, a school-based practitioner researcher and university -based researcher identify key shifts in activity and tensions that emerged when making was both enabled and constrained by school . Findings illustrate the central role that students’ acts of self-determination can have on shifting a classroom makerspace activity system, particularly when a teacher is attuned and receptive to those acts of self -determination. Key tensions emerged related to teacher as central node for facilitating activity, even as the system shifted with student-directed activity.
