papers.title: From Implementation to Innovation: Re-imagining the role of Practice in Research
papers.authors: Linette Victor
papers.design_stakeholders: Teachers; Educators & Practitioners; Students & Learners; Educational Researchers & Designers; Community Members & Partners
papers.abstract: Reverse Translation (RT) is a conceptual framework repositioning educational practice as a generative source of knowledge. Drawing from Design-Based Research (DBIR), Research-Practice Partnerships (RPPs), and Improvement Science (IS), RT challenges the conventional theory-to-practice pipeline by beginning with practitioner-identified tensions and insights. It offers a structured process for elevating practitioner insights into theoretical discourse, fostering reciprocal learning, and context-specific innovation. This model is especially relevant for knowledge mobilizers, such as instructional coaches and teacher leaders, who often support others ’growth without sustained opportunities to develop their own practice. RT contributes to the learning sciences by expanding methodologies for practice-initiated inquiry, deepening commitments to equity, and strengthening the relevance and adaptability of contextually grounded interventions. Using vignettes and applied examples, this paper identifies how RT can inform professional development and research design, bridging the research- practice divide in more effective ways.

papers.title: Teaching and Learning Mathematics with Artificial Intelligence
papers.authors: Victoria Delaney
papers.design_stakeholders: High School Teachers; Educators & Practitioners; Undergraduate / Graduate Students; Educational Researchers & Designers; Domain Experts & Technologists
papers.abstract: Novel technologies influence the curriculum, pedagogy, and learning in schools. My research explores the impacts of AI-based tools in mathematics education, attending to how these tools influence teaching practice and how students learn to think mathematically. My scholarly goal is to support mathematics and stochastics teachers in developing innovative and robust pedagogies that uphold cognitive demand in learning even as tools that automate humanistic thinking become endemic to schooling. Overview My research centers curriculum, pedagogy, cognition, and AI/LLM automation in mathematics. I am interested in how AI-based tools mediate students’ mathematical thinking and teachers’ development of expert teaching practices to support student thinking. My interests stem from my experience as a high school math teacher of seven years, where I learned that mathematics tools and curricular resources played a major role in lesson orchestration and what my students ultimately learned (Brown, 2011). I conceptualize teachers and learners as agentic, creative, and curious drivers of learning rather than recipients of societal changes influenced by developments in AI automation. I further envision teachers as lesson designers and orchestrators who, when faced with the latest technological disruptions, can design effective instruction based in part on multi-faceted forms of teacher knowledge, including knowledge of how students’ interactions with tools impact their learning. To support teacher learning with insights about AI-tools’ impacts on students’ mathematical thinking, I have recently begun to research students’ AI-mediated problem solving processes (Delaney et al., 2025b). This work is in its second year and involves both well-defined and ill-defined mathematics tasks. I conduct video- recorded task-based interviews and observe the problem solving processes that surround students’ decisions, evaluations, AI trust, and epistemic judgments of mathematics output produced by chatbots. I have initiated this work in both clinical and classroom settings with algebra, calculus, statistics, data science, and numerical reasoning tasks. The findings from these studies inform my own teaching practice and AI adaptations, and with this knowledge, I continuously work to help other teachers develop design skills for an AI-integrated future. Establishing this program requires proficiency with the latest technologies. Under some conditions, technologies can create dynamic, inquiry-driven learning experiences that raise the cognitive demand required to solve nonroutine tasks, such as appraising the quality of a dataset or designing a facial recognition classifier (Delaney & Lee, 2024; Delaney & Selbach-Allen, 2025). In other circumstances, technology can derail students (or teachers) from their learning goals. My research program explores how teachers and students use novel technologies, the affordances and challenges that arise from their technology use, transformations on student and teacher thinking that are mediated by technology, and implications for learning. Theoretical frameworks I draw from theoretical frameworks that foreground the complexity of teaching and learning. I have several lines of research that build from different lineages of theory. When I conceptualize relationships between math curriculum and teaching, I draw from Brown’s illustration of teaching as adaptative, improvisational design work, akin to orchestrating a jazz concert (Brown, 2011). His pedagogical design capacity framework formed the basis of my dissertation, where I studied how statistics teachers adapted and enacted a machine learning curriculum (Delaney, 2025). When I conceptualize teachers’ mathematical professional learning with AI, I draw from teacher knowledge (Shulman, 1986) and teacher noticing (van Es & Sherin, 2008). What teachers attend to, interpret, and how they respond to students is directly related to their knowledge. Yet while teachers are still in the early stages of developing their knowledge, they may not yet have the multimodal forms of expertise to evaluate LLMs’ output and/or claims about students’ mathematical thinking. I am therefore developing theories about when and how mathematics teachers may prompt LLMs as cognitive supports, and what additional (human) supports they need to grow their pedagogical content knowledge and noticing abilities. From the student perspective, I have recently explored knowledge building with AI-based tools (Scardamalia & Bereiter, 2020) and building expertise in mathematics with LLMs (Chi & Glaser 1985; Hiebert & Carpenter, 1992). Today’s LLMs can imitate humanistic mathematical reasoning, and can complete most of K- 12 mathematics tasks with minimal prompting specifications. It is therefore necessary for students and teachers to discern how to use LLMs to build knowledge and foster their own expertise rather than bypass the cognitive work involved in mathematics problem solving altogether. Recent work has begun to explore what human learning a nd epistemic agency may look like when LLMs are involved in mathematics tasks, proposing that students’ uses of LLMs are indicative of how much problem solving agency they retain versus offload to intelligent agents (Wu et al., 2025). I intend to extend this work and study how students’ LLM uses mediate their moment-by-moment thinking and what agency they preserve as they develop problem solving skills.

papers.title: Learning to Deconstruct AI/ML Systems: Scaffolds to Support Learners in Critically Evaluating
papers.authors: Luis Morales-Navarro, Yasmin B. Kafai, Olli Hilke, Nicolas Pope, Matti Tedre, Daniel J. Noh, Rotem Landesman, Jayne Everson, Jean Ryoo, Ole Sejer Iversen
papers.design_stakeholders: Science Teachers; High School Students; Educational Researchers & Designers; Domain Experts & Technologists
papers.abstract: Historically, the learning sciences have emphasized how computing construction activities can support learners in building relationships between old and new knowledge in interactions with others while creating artifacts of social relevance. With the ubiquity of socia l media and AI/ML, researchers have turned their attention to the social and ethical implications of computing, proposing that deconstruction—the process of critically examining and understanding how meaning and intentionality are encoded into computing systems and practices that impact people’s lives and the environment —is equally important. In this symposium we bring together researchers investigating how to design deconstruction learning activities in which young people critically evaluate AI/ML systems of social relevance. We present different perspectives on how to design activities and scaffold learners to examine the socio-ethical implications of AI/ML systems. We discuss the role of deconstruction in computing education and its relation to construction activities. Symposium overview The learning sciences have been concerned with how involving learners in the construction of socially relevant computing applications for and with other people can support knowledge construction (Kafai, 2006; Holbert et al., 2021). This interest in construction can be traced back to Papert’s work on constructionism (see Papert, 1991), which argued that knowledge structures are built through the creation of personal and socially relevant artifacts, centering on the connected nature of knowledge with its personal and social dimensions. Today, many tools and educational efforts have embraced constructionism, positioning young people as designers of applications, from commercial products such as Nintendo’s Game Builder Garage and Roblox to educational tools and curricula that have made designing applications a mainstay in most K-12 computing education initiatives (Kafai & Burke, 2014; Oleson et al., 2020; Waite & Sentance, 2021). 2203 Yet, with the ubiquity of social media and AI/ML and their ethical, environmental, and societal implications (Ko et al., 2020), coupled with the political or critical turn in the learning sciences (Politics of Learning Writing Collective, 2017), researchers have turned their attention to the equally important process of deconstruction. Iversen and colleagues (2018) define deconstruction as the process of “critically examining and understanding how meaning and intentionality are encoded into digital artifac ts and practices that impact upon our everyday lives.” Deconstruction involves describing, evaluating and reflecting on the values and intentions embedded in sociotechnical systems used in everyday life while considering their possible implications (Dindle r et al., 2020; Schaper et al., 2023). We argue that such practices can contribute to learners' development of both ethical and functional understandings of AI/ML systems. This involves assessing the properties of a system in terms of its inputs, outputs and materials (e.g., data); inquiring about the intended use and actual use of a system; foregrounding the values, worldviews, and assumptions embedded in the system; and investigating how the system impacts individuals, communities and the environment (Dindler et al., 2023). In this symposium, we bring together researchers taking different approaches to deconstruction to address the following research questions: How can we design activities that scaffold learners to deconstruct AI/ML systems? How does deconstruction support learners in developing their functional and ethical understanding of AI/ML systems? Contributions include presentations about tools and activities that foster deconstruction, participatory approaches that involve teachers in the design of deconstruction acti vities, and insights into learners' thinking processes when investigating socio- ethical issues. Furthermore, we discuss how deconstruction relates to construction and their role in computing education. This session is organized in three sections: (1) the chairs will introduce the topic and participants (~10 min); (2) participants will have seven minutes to share their work; (3) our discussants Jean Ryoo, a learning scientist and computing education researcher that has advocated for equity and inquiry-oriented computing, and Ole Sejer Iversen, a child-computer interaction and activity theory researcher that proposed the term deconstruction, will synthesize and reflect on findings (10 min), followed by a Q&A with the audience and presenters (~15 min). Presentation 1 — Deconstructing machine vision with breakable machine Olli Hilke, Nicolas Pope, Matti Tedre Many K–12 education initiatives use “Teachable Machine” -type tools to let students build simple models, but these activities face difficulties preparing students to interrogate or critique the complex commercial AI -driven systems they frequently use. The AI - and data-driven systems from major companies can often produce biased or misleading results, but when they fail, it often happens in subtle and unpredictable ways —and because they are proprietary black boxes, it is nearly impossible to see why they failed. Yet, understanding that AI systems are not neutral or infallible requires exposing their brittleness, hidden biases, and human design choices. Breakable Machine (Hilke et al., 2025) (spoof.gen- ai.fi) offers students an accessible entry point into scaffolded critical inquiry and analysis of construction, use, values, and consequences of AI systems. papers.title: DotQuest: Accessible STEM Games to Support Blind and Visually Impaired Learners
papers.authors: Ariel Han, Rajeev Joshi, Daniel Tsivkovski, Dylan Ravel, Maryam Etezadbrojerdi
papers.design_stakeholders: K-12 Teachers; Students & Learners; Educational Researchers & Designers
papers.abstract: Blind and low vision (BLV) students face persistent barriers to full participation in STEM learning, particularly due to the limited availability of accessible tools. This study introduces DotQuest, a technology probe that integrates haptic feedback, and a conversational agent to create narrative- driven, game -based STEM activities. To examine how such tools might support equitable participation, we conducted interviews with seven Teachers of Students with Visual Impairments (TVIs) across U.S. Analysis reve aled that teachers emphasize the importance of simultaneous tactile and auditory access, the need for classroom tools that foster both independence and inclusion, and the value of designing accessibility from the outset rather than as an accommodation. Fin dings show that multimodal game -based environments can enhance STEM engagement while revealing systemic barriers for BLV learners. This work contributes to the learning sciences by deepening understanding of how multimodal and inclusive design can guide the development of equitable STEM learning environments.

papers.title: Bodies, Participation, and Power: Learning as a Site of Inclusion, Exclusion, and Resistance
papers.authors: Morgan Vickery
papers.design_stakeholders: Middle School Students; Educational Researchers & Designers; Domain Experts & Technologists
papers.abstract: Youth bring diverse ways of knowing, communicating, and creating meaning to school, yet classrooms often privilege a narrow slice of these practices—treating difference as deficit and leaving many disabled, neurodivergent, queer, or trauma-impacted youth at the margins of participation. These exclusions affect belonging and access to civic, community, and disciplinary life. My research investigates how to design asset-oriented, participatory, and body- inclusive learning environments for young adolescents, where questions of identity and belonging are especially acute. Drawing on sociocultural and critical learning theories, participatory design-based research, and social models of ability and the body, I examine how multimodal repertoires can be recognized and leveraged as learning resources. This agenda advances three strands focused on designing multimodal learning environments that prioritize learner and educator dignity: (1) expanding conceptions of adolescent participation and literacy, (2) designing inclusive multimodal technologies, and (3) positioning youth as co-designers and co-theorists of their learning. Strand 1: Expanding conceptions of youth participation This strand is grounded in my experiences and those of current adolescents regarding secondary schools’ narrow conceptions of participation. Secondary schooling has privileged print and verbal literacies while devaluing embodied, affective, and multimodal avenues for meaning-making. These framings disproportionately exclude multiply-marginalized adolescents and reinforce deficit orientations and hegemonic norms. In my previous work, I employ a social model of disability to explore how schools ‘disable’ and ‘enable’ certain bodies, calling for researchers to shift responsibility for student performance away from the individual and onto the design of the system in which they operate (Vickery, 2023). In my dissertation, I introduce a five- dimensional inter-theoretical framework that conceptualizes the body as simultaneously thinking, feeling, observed, politicized, and autonomous. I also provide methodological guidance for conducting humanizing, dignity-affirming research with youth living in non-normative bodies (Vickery, 2025a) and employ critical resistance narrative analysis to examine how adolescents navigate and resist normative embodied expectations in schools (Vickery, 2025b). Moving forward, I expand normative notions of participation in youth civic education. I extend this work into civic and technical domains—motivated by the current sociopolitical climate. Such work demands multidisciplinary and multimodal competencies that cannot be siloed within individual subject areas. To these ends, I hope to support adolescents’ learning of media, data, digital, and scientific literacies through engagement with culturally relevant issues. Building from epistemic practices in science and engineering education (e.g., evidence evaluation, systems reasoning, modeling), I see opportunities to extend these into literacy/language education (rhetorical device usage, media & data literacy, interpretation of misinformation), social studies/history (complex sociopolitical systems, causal mechanisms), and computing education (engineering ethics, data privacy, transparency, ethical AI adoption). As political systems increasingly disenfranchise multiply-marginalized youth, these literacies become not abstract skills but conceptual and tangible tools for civic and social change. A society of care must acknowledge and design against these barriers. Strand 2: Designing inclusive multimodal technologies This strand is rooted in my experience as a UX designer and researcher, where access and inclusion were often addressed retroactively rather than prioritized from the start. In educational technologies, this reinforces deficit- oriented assumptions about learners whose practices do not align with normative expectations. This work centers on learners’ histories, needs, and desires in the edtech design process, ensuring technologies are proactive, responsive, and adaptive to learners’ needs. In my recent work (Vickery & Danish, 2025), I share my rapid design and iterative refinement of a mixed-reality embodied learning environment for a reverse-inclusion summer camp for youth with moderate-to- severe disabilities, aimed at identifying and addressing barriers to expression and participation. In my 2024 work o n the GEM-STEP project (Vickery et al., 2024; NSF Grants #1908632 & #1908791), I led my team in integrating trauma-informed pedagogies into the facilitation and evaluation of mixed-reality embodied activities (where students use motion-tracking technologies to collaboratively model complex scientific phenomena), demonstrating how centering comfort, choice, and agency can amplify students’ capacities for participation. In Zhou et al. (2025), we investigate how elementary learners' group-divergent embodied practices afford opportunities to learn about complex scientific phenomena. As a Visiting Research Scientist funded by the Engage AI Institute, I design and develop narrative-based, AI-scaffolded, gamified experiences for middle school students that are context-relevant and engage learners in critical thinking about food and environmental justice (Humburg et al., 2025). I build on my dual background in software engineering and UX design to critically engage with how ‘cutting-edge’ technologies such as AI, XR, and asynchronous learning tools are implemented at scale. My prior work has often relied on retrofitting inclusion into technologies – moving forward, I hope to (1) establish trusting partnerships with schools and communities, (2) conduct on-the-ground needs assessments, (3) co-design contextually grounded solutions with these needs prioritized at the onset, and (4) iteratively evaluate implementation. Access and inclusion are not endpoints but baselines; innovation must be defined by—and accountable to—those most impacted. Strand 3: Positioning youth as co-designers and co-theorists of their learning This strand addresses a tension across education and research alike – that too often, youth are positioned as passive users of and participants in designs they had no role in shaping. Thus, these designs (which here include pedagogies, activities, tools, communities, and theories) fail to provide the necessary scaffolding for youth to thrive and learn within them. My work takes an asset-oriented stance, treating adolescents’ perspectives and repertoires of practice as valuable resources for designing more sensitive, equitable, and emancipatory experiences for youth who would otherwise be forced to (at best) change themselves for the sake of compliance. In prior work, I’ve offered autoethnographic accounts of how my traditional notions of research-practice partnerships were challenged and remade in a collaboration with local paraprofessionals, special educators, and youth with disabilities (Vickery & Peabody, Under Review). In my dissertation Article 2 (Vickery, 2025c), I drew on Vygotskian notions of mediation and affect to understand what affective, sensory, and lived experiences are activated for youth with non-normative embodied experiences in the presence of various instructional design elements (i.e. various activity/task framings, technologies, proximity of embodiment, sensory demands, forms of movement, & participation structures). Further, Article 3 positions youth as co-theorists of a framework for dignity-affirming, body-inclusive embodied learning environments (Vickery, 2025d). This strand responds to a recurring theme across my projects—that “grown-ups just don’t get it.” This perceived ignorance strains opportunities for authentic educator–youth relationships and deepens youth distrust of educational systems. To address this, I aim to develop organized, protected “designer spaces”—digital and physical—for youth to co-design community-facing projects and professional development for educators and youth-service providers. papers.title: The Power of Scaling Slowly: Negotiation of Science Teaching in a Long Term Research- Practice Partnership
papers.authors: Scott McDonald, Jonathan McCausland
papers.design_stakeholders: Science Teachers; Higher Education Instructors / Faculty; Educators & Practitioners; Middle School Students; Educational Researchers & Designers; Community Members & Partners; Domain Experts & Technologists
papers.abstract: Moving innovations in education from small initial efforts to broader impacts has been a central challenge of supporting change in schools. This study is a part of a larger design- based research project where we worked in partnership to redesign the secondary science program at The Pennsylvania State University. We used the context as a test-bed for innovations and design-based research to develop “humble” theory and contest theory in teacher education. This study views teacher learning as the sociocultural practice of negotiation of professional vision within a community in broad temporal and physical scales . Professional vision is theorized not as a small scale, local negotiat ion of individual acts of practice , but as the on- going and dynamic collaborative negotiation of a learning community in response to the overlapping political economies of social organizations that occurs across different sites, places, or contexts, spanning decades. Subject/Problem Changing educational systems , and particularly the embedded cultural practices of teaching, requires in -depth, rich, extended engagement focused on building and sustaining trusting relationships. Characterizing this kind of change lies at the intersection of systems of community and individual learning, which are naturally intertwined. To address this complexity and support system change requires the cultivations of a learning environment for multiple role actors (e.g, preservice and in -service teachers, students, university faculty) and as a result involves bridging multiple cultural communities. While teacher learning occurs both in (and outside of) institutions of higher education and K -12 schools, the relationships between these two institutional contexts are often complicated. The culture and practices of K -12 institutional contexts often operate in tension with those of institutions of higher education, described as the two- worlds problem (Braaten, 2018). This tension complicates efforts at systemic change as do the multiple layers of practice involved in the culture of schools (Windschitl & Stroupe, 2017) - students engaged in science practices (as articulated by documents like the National Research Council’s Framework for K-12 Science Education or the Next Generation Science Standards); teachers engaged in designing and enacting learning environments to support students science practices (as articulated by documents/frameworks like Ambitious Science Teaching); and teacher educators engaged in designing and enacting learning environments for teachers (both in- service and preservice) to develop teachers’ practices (by extension, Ambitious Science Teacher Education). This multi -layer complex of interwoven practices contributes to the massive challenge facing attempts to change the culture of schooling, and of particular concern to us, science teaching as a cultural practice. Approaches to supporting these complex cultural shifts frequently involve attempts to “scale -up” changes, most often via curricular interventions in combination with distributed professional learning (e.g., Edelson, et al., 2021). While there has been success with change at scale, at least at the level of school districts attempts at large- scale change are mixed (e.g. Spillane, et al., 2018), generally have been shown to impact only smaller groups of “maverick” teachers more directly engaged with funded projects, or produce superficial changes in practice leaving the instructional core relatively stable (Cuban, 2013). Repeated efforts to change practice over time can also lead to a kind of change exhaustion, where teachers see all change efforts as transitory and choose to wait them out (Del Schalock, 2006). This manuscript describes an approach to school change that conceptualizes scaling in a long- term and organic way. The context is a 15+ year research-practice partnership built around a core community of secondary in-service science teachers, science teacher educators, preservice secondary science teachers, and middle school students. P articipants are in multiple overlapping professional learning experiences, but given our roles our narrative focuses on one activity of the community - an embedded, practice -based science teacher preparation program. The beginning of the partnership is retroactively marked by the meeting of members in 2006 and more officially and externally recognized with a more intentional and structured community of teacher learning that began to form five years later. Regardless, the consistent focus of the community has been on the negotiation and transformation of the cultural practices of science teaching and the intimately related transformation of the identities of the individuals of the community and their institutional contexts – their university, their schools, and more distal impacts on other schools, the state, and the field of science education. 774 Organizational structures are fundamentally dynamic, cultural, and porous. They are constantly being created and recreated by the interactions of the participants that make them up. As participants move between contexts they carry with them and create anew their identities as members of their multiple communities. They are constantly negotiating the work of those communities and how the present set of participants are constructing the meaning of that work. There is historicity to this process, which constrains and affords the possible work of participants and frames their on -going negotiation of meaning. To understand the nature of the organizational interactions (and change) that occur via more localized negotiations of meaning, there is a need to attend to interactions across scales. To see how small moments of interaction and negotiation construct patterns over time and (re)create the constituent communities. Much of the research on organizational change attends to macro scale, change is typically addressed via policies (including curricula and assessments) or other formalized components of organizations (e.g. Spillane, et al., 2018). Other approaches attempt to study change by focusing on micro-scale negotiation of meaning occurring between participants in classrooms or in professional learning contexts (e.g. Gomoll, Hmelo-Silver, & Šabanović, 2022). There is also a meso-scale, the stories and negotiated meanings that are created at the micro -scale and bridge to the creation and reification of macro -scale formalisms. As participants move through various contexts their pathways intertwine and separate creating a temporal fabric as imagined by Kurt Vonnegut’s Tralfamadorians, who see human lives as a kind of temporal skein of yarn. This fabric is woven of stories told between participants about themselves and each other across the contexts that make up their lives and their community participation. To successfully cultivate change in these tapestries of human interaction, we need to attend not just to the individual interactions, or the structure of the entire fabric; we need to think about the creation of learning environments as the creation of space to allow others to become new people, to create new selves that reflect new meanings they have negotiated with each other. To conceptualize this process we draw upon professional vision (Goodwin, 1994) to help us understand these social negotiations and how they continually recreate professional communities and their practices. Professional vision is not the particular lens an individual uses to view social interactions, it is a description of the stabilities and instabilities created by participants through the negotiation of meaning in a communities’ social practices over time. Conceptual/Theoretical framework “Knowing is inherent in the growth and transformation of identities and it is located in relations among practitioners, their practice, the artifacts of that practice, and the social organization and political economy of communities of practice” (Lave & Wenger, 1989, p. 122). Theoretical understandings of and research on teacher learning is often limited by its contextual focus (e.g., universities, schools, professional learning activities) or the conceptualization of teacher learning as individual/cognitive (e.g., knowledge framed as Pedagogical Content Knowledge, beliefs, or dispositions), which often carries with it a deficit framing ( Gray, McDonald, & Stroupe, 2022). In contrast, this study views teacher learning as a sociocultural practice of negotiation of professional vision (Goodwin, 1994) within a teacher community of practice at broad temporal and physical scales. We focus not only on a group of teachers in a single context negotiating a current set of dilemmas regarding changing practice (e.g., McCausland et al., 2023), but as a defining characteristic of an on-going, historical, and dynamic learning community that occurs across different sites, places, or contexts, as well as spanning years of collaborative negotiation, all of which is in response to the overlapping political economies of relevant social organizations. Communities of Practice (Lave & Wenger, 1991) is a well-established framing of how people learn focused on social practice as not just the mechanism of learning, but the definition of the outcome of learning. Learning is viewed as a change in practice, both of the individuals in the community, but also, in interaction with the changes in the norms and practices of the community. Similarly, individuals’ learning can be thought of as changes in identity within the community that are negotiated and manifest through practice with other participants in the community. One of the core pieces of this process identified by Wenger, is the negotiation of meaning. The term negotiation tends to evoke a discourse or even an argument, in the argumentation sense of that concept, between members of a community about the meaning of their practice; however, negotiation is more subtle and implicit in communities of practice. It entails subtle shifts in what is acceptable practice and talk that happen as groups of individuals determine what it is that defines the collective work of their profession. In short, it is a negotiation of professional vision. Over the past ten or more years, Goodwin’s (1994) original notion has often been taken up as a more individually cognitive focused notion (e.g., vanEs & Sherin, 2021), characterizing professional vision as a sort of 775 individual lens for viewing teaching and guiding individual’s decision making. We take a broader and more practice focused conception directly grounded in Goodwin’s original notion: “Discursive practices are used by members of a profession to shape events in the domains subject to their professional scrutiny. The shaping process creates the objects of knowledge that become the insignia of a profession's craft: the theories, artifacts, and bodies of expertise that distinguish it from other professions. Analysis of the methods used by members of a community to build and contest the events that structure their lifeworld contributes to the development of a practice-based theory of knowledge and action." (italics added, 1994, p. 606) It is this building and contesting that we consider to be a characterization of the negotiation of meaning that occurs in communities of practice. This kind of social negotiation is not only seen in the minute -to-minute discourse between members of a professional community ( McCausland et al., 2023), but also in how those members draw on other external communities they participate in, for example, to play with policies cutting across organizational levels of a system (Bateman & McDonald , 2023). Professional vision’s social negotiation focuses on how community norms and understandings shift over longer periods of time and are reflected in the reified and tacit activities of those communities. This can be seen in how teachers change the focus of their own profe ssional learning, the problems of practice they identify, and ideally how those problems without ceilings (Thompson, 2015) are continually renegotiated as the community deepens their understanding of their own goals and practices. Our work uses this more community negotiation focused framing of professional vision as a key construct of analysis to determine the dynamically negotiated objects of knowledge that form the core of a learning community. For the research community to move beyond less productive and deficit framings of professional learning that proliferate in the field such as short term (e.g. one week) sessions or narrowly focused session (e.g. targeting particular curriculum or content topics), we need to have ways of investigating teacher learning at different grain-sizes and scales which conceptualize teacher learning as the complex and embedded social practice that it is. This manuscript is an attempt to tell a richer story of the organic origin, development, and eventu al design-based evolution of a community of teacher learning thorough the negotiation of meaning done to establish the objects of knowledge that make up professional vision. Specifically, we address the research questions: 1) What are the patterns of growt h and development of the objects of knowledge for a teacher learning community that intentionally interweaves university and school contexts? 2) What attributes seem to support the long- term engagement, growth, and learning of such a teacher learning community? Design/Procedure The research-practice partnership in this study developed over the course of 15+ years. In that time, numerous funded and unfunded research projects took place, hundreds of pre -service science teachers were educated, thousands of K-12 science students were impacted, and generations of science education researchers were a part of participating in and investigating teacher learning within the partnership. We say this to indicate the context we are describing is complex both temporally and socially. To attempt to capture this complexity, to describe how the partnership negotiated science teaching and learning over time (Goodwin, 1994), we recognized that traditional qualitative coding of interactions would not suffice, so we turned to narrative methods. By using narrative methods, we can navigate temporal, social, and contextual boundaries to communicate and transmit complex knowledge (Huber et al., 2016) about a dynamic social system of learning. Narrative methods allow us to show how educational contexts might be transformed and render visible “things heretofore unnoticed” (Lewis, 2011, p 504) by telling “real stories” (Gallagher, 2011) that can help shift practices and pedagogies. In fact, narrative methods make it possible to capture the people, places, and events that occur over time in relation to learning. By telling stories it is possible to weave together learning and the context in which learning happens because as Clandinin and Connelly (2000) state, “People are individuals and need to be understood as such, but they cannot be understood only as individuals. They are always in relation, always in a social context” (p. 2). So, while narrative methods are used to delve into an individual’s experience, they can also be used as “an exploration of the social, cultural and institutional narratives within which individual’s experiences are constituted, shaped, expressed and enacted - but in a way that begins and ends that inquiry in the storied lives of the people involved” (Clandinin & Rosiek, 2007, p 42). To gather the narratives, we generated stories based on our memory and we contacted preservice teachers, mentor teachers, and others involved in the community over time to describe “your experience and what you feel are key takeaways about how students learn science and how teachers learn to teach.” Part of this process included revisiting data, that included video, audio, and documents, from previous funded and unfunded projects 776 and articles written that focused on actors in the partnership to help create a timeline of events, confirm particular stories, and support our narration of how the partnership grew over time. Once we gathered the data, we constructed narratives through a process of mutual storytelling to explain the learning in context rather than produce a cause -and-effect relationship (Connelly & Clandinin, 1990). Our process took the form of writing and rewriting narratives based on moments in the larger data corpus that stood out as important (Maclure, 2013). The stories demonstrated the tensions, successes, and serendipitous moments involved in the development of the partnership to help demonstrate the negotiations (i.e. learning) that occurred within it (Rodriguez & Morrison, 2019). Finally, we took the narrative(s) and embedded theory to help us make “connections” between learning and the “individual lives” of the participants and discern the “order and pattern” (Maclure, 2013, p. 229) necessary to produce “humble” theory (Cobb et al., 2003) that goes beyond a report of “what happened.” Below is an abridged narrative intended to provide insight into the data, findings, and analysis. papers.title: How Simulation Design Shapes Academically Productive Talk: An Epistemic Network Analysis of Teacher Discourse in Middle-School Physics
papers.authors: Wei Jia, Kexin Li, Gaowei Chen
papers.design_stakeholders: Science Teachers; Students & Learners; Educational Researchers & Designers
papers.abstract: Dialogic teaching, through Academically Productive Talk (APT), enhances student learning. While digital simulations are common in science education, their specific impact on teacher discourse patterns remains underexplored. This study examines how simulation design, Multiple Representations (MR) versus Single Representation (SR), shapes whole -class discourse structure and teachers’ use of APT moves. One teacher and 99 eighth-grade students from two classes in Western China participated. Using Epistemic Network Analysis (ENA) and discourse analysis of 147 teacher talk turns, we compared APT patterns between two conditions. ENA revealed distinct strategic repertoires: the MR condition showed an integrated, collaborative network centered on reasoning and building on ideas, involving more students in shorter, focused turns. The SR condition exhibited a linear, teacher- guided pattern dominated by elicitation and challenge, with longer explanations from fewer students. Overall, simulation design relates to teacher facilitation and student participation, suggesting that multiple representational tools may afford more collaborative-dialogic classrooms.

Participants were 110 PSTs in a semester - long instructional design course. We implemented a design that combined collaborative inquiry, delayed GenAI use, and reflective analytics, positioning GenAI as a design partner. Data from a DT scale and instructional design artifacts were analyzed. Results showed gains in problem discovery and definition and a shift toward more iterative design practices. The study offers a learning sciences account of integrating GenAI and ASRA to support DT in teacher education.

papers.title: Teachers’ Co-Evolving Insights on E-Learning Design and Design-Aware Learning Analytics
papers.authors: Pakon Ko, Linyuan Wang, Nancy Law
papers.design_stakeholders: K-12 Teachers; Students & Learners; Educational Researchers & Designers
papers.abstract: Learning analytics (LA) can provide teachers with timely insights into student learning, helping them adjust learning design (LD) and optimizing educational outcomes. However, the concept of LA is relatively new, and the use of LA integrated with e- learning platforms remains uncommon, particularly among K –12 teachers. This paper reports on a Research Practice Partnership ( RPP) project involving primary and secondary schools to develop a system and workflow that supports the integration of LA into teachers’ everyday professional practice, beginning at the LD stage. A qualitative case study of a teacher team over two years reveals how their professional learning evolved, from identifying meaningful learning analytics questions (LAQs) relevant to their LD context to recognizing the importance of selecting appropriate e- learning tools as a prerequisite for meaningful LA, and finally to incorporating targeted LAQs into their LD decision making process , thereby consciously closing the LD-LA loop in their professional practice.

papers.title: From Solo to Collaborative: Design Affordances in Multi-User Immersive VR Simulations for Transforming Science Learning
papers.authors: Michelle Lui, Sunnie Gong, Chloe Lok
papers.design_stakeholders: Undergraduate / Graduate Students; Educational Researchers & Designers
papers.abstract: Immersive virtual reality (IVR) shows promise for science learning by enabling visualization of microscopic phenomena and dynamic processes. However, research has focused predominantly on individual learning experiences, overlooking the social nature of learning. This study investigates the collaborative affordances of multi -user IVR for science education through participatory design, involving six teams of undergraduate students and educators who co- created IVR learning simulations. Findings revealed seven science learning affordances: microscopic visualization, spatial relationships, scale traversal, representational connections, perspective-taking, temporal phenomena, and procedural skills—which multi-user IVR amplified through embodied communication, role -taking that grounds collaborative discourse, and distributed perspectives that require coordination. Analysis of designs highlights how narrative structures establish group- worthy joint tasks, fostering six collaborative activity types. Variations in structuring collaborative processes emerged from play- level scripts with undifferentiated roles, and scene -level scripts with defined roles enhanc ing interdependence. Results provide design insights for leveraging IVR ’s spatial and embodied features in collaborative science learning.

papers.title: Co-designing and Implementing Reflective Tools and Routines with Children in Cooperative Inquiry
papers.authors: Elana Blinder
papers.design_stakeholders: Higher Education Instructors / Faculty; Educators & Practitioners; Elementary Students & Children; Educational Researchers & Designers
papers.abstract: Reflection is a valuable component of learning and design processes, yet motivating children to reflect in informal learning contexts can be challenging. My dissertation examines this issue in a university-based Cooperative Inquiry co-design team where children and adults collaborate as equal design partners. Leveraging a DBR approach, I conduct two studies. The first investigates how children co-design reflection tools and processes that align with their values and mental models. The second explores how they use these systems over time and how this shapes their developing self-concept as designers. Through this research, I will contribute an adaptable infrastructure for authentically integrating reflection into child co-design, insights into how DBR can meaningfully include children as co-design stakeholders, and a deeper understanding of how children think, learn, and develop their identities through co-design. Motivation and background The learning sciences have long documented the importance of reflection for a range of learning processes (Dewey, 1986; Moon, 2004; Schön, 2017), with classrooms traditionally serving as important spaces for developing children’s reflective learning. Though less structured and systematic, informal learning contexts can also offer rich environments for reflection and identity development, but it can be challenging to motivate children to pause and reflect in the absence of standard classroom norms and enforcing structures (Gardner et al., 2006). As a doctoral student at the University of Maryland with an interest in how children learn and develop their identities through co-design, I have experienced some of these challenges firsthand through my participation in UMD KidsTeam—an intergenerational co-design team where university faculty and students collaborate with children between the ages of 7 and 12 to design new child-facing technologies. Guided by the Cooperative Inquiry (CI) co-design framework (Druin, 1999; Guha et al., 2013), which aims to involve children as equal collaborators with adults across the entire design cycle, our team employs a variety of established CI ‘design techniques’ aimed at making co-design accessible, engaging, equitable, and empowering for children. One such technique that has been mentioned in the literature, but which has received considerably less attention, is ‘journaling’, which has been described as a tool for “design partners to reflect on their experiences by writing or drawing” (Guha et al., 2013). Despite this directive, CI scholars and practitioners have observed child design partners’ lack of intrinsic motivation to engage in reflective journaling and have reported challenges in communicating the goals and value of this technique in a manner that resonates with children’s personal interests and values (Blinder et al., 2025). Issues with implementing reflective journaling in CI are further complicated by logistical challenges (e.g., time constraints, the need for adult writing support), ideological challenges (e.g., adult discomfort with the solitary school-like nature of written reflection) and adult and child design partners’ conflicting conceptualizations of journaling (with children prioritizing documenting and remembering design ideas and adults prioritizing process- and identity-oriented reflection) (Blinder et al., 2025). These challenges indicate an opportunity to explore additional approaches toward fostering purposeful sustained reflection within CI and other child co-design contexts. In my dissertation, I capitalize on this opportunity by engaging UMD KidsTeam children in contemplating the role reflection can play in their lives and identities as designers through co-designing new developmentally accessible and personally meaningful reflection tools and routines to be used in our co-design context. I then examine how children’s engagement with these reflection approaches and their self-perceptions as designers evolve over time.

papers.title: Stories, Futures and Histories: Co-design Routines to Center Community Knowledge for Environmental Education in India
papers.authors: Gautam Bisht, Vishesh Kumar, Pankaj Dev, Jyoti Tiwari, Ankit Bhatt, Lata Upreti, Kiran Pant
papers.design_stakeholders: Teachers; Educators & Practitioners; Elementary Students & Children; Educational Researchers & Designers; Community Members & Partners; Domain Experts & Technologists
papers.abstract: Centering co-design as a site of social justice, we analyze a collaboration between learning scientists and local teachers from a non-profit organization in the Himalayan region of Uttarakhand, India. We ask, what design routines support the emergence of c ommunity-driven ideas for ecological education, and how do they build on each other to deepen cultural, imaginative, and historical engagement? Data for this paper comes from the initial phase of collaboration, which consisted of six online meetings, each two hour long. We conducted thematic analysis along to identify three interconnected routines: (i) autecology narratives surfaced ecological connections grounded in community and personal rituals, (ii) speculative futuring opened imaginative engagement with communication, technology, and markets; and (iii) interactions with community elders supported the development of critical historicity. Together, these routines illustrate a co -design approach which fosters collective sense -making integrating cultural, imaginative, and historical dimensions of community life .

papers.title: Integrating the Learning Sciences into Technical Infrastructure for the Future of AI in Education
papers.authors: Jeremy Roschelle, John Whitmer, Rene Kizilcec, Xin Wei

papers.abstract: As artificial intelligence becomes increasingly influential in education, attention must extend beyond AI applications to the technical infrastructure on which those applications depend. Datasets, models, benchmarks, and governance mechanisms are already shaping the future of educational AI, yet these foundational resources are often developed without sufficient engagement with the learning sciences. This workshop explores how learning scientists can contribute to the design of such infrastructural public goods in ways that better reflect what is known about learning, while also addressing concerns related to safety, privacy, ethics, and equity. By bringing together researchers working at the intersection of AI and learning, the workshop seeks to identify promising lines of work, articulate key tensions, and stimulate future collaboration on learning-science-informed AI infrastructure. Overview The learning sciences offer strong conceptual foundations for the design of educational AI, drawing on longstanding research on scaffolding, feedback, self-regulation, and collaboration (Quintana et al., 2004; Hattie & Timperley, 2007; Järvelä et al., 2016; Sawyer, 2022). Yet these principles still only lightly shape the datasets, benchmarks, and model documentation on which AI systems depend. Training data rarely reflect what is known about productive learning interactions; benchmarks tend to measure task completion or factual accuracy rather than the quality of scaffolding or the depth of learner understanding; and model documentation seldom describes how a system's design relates to evidence on how people learn. Recent work by major AI developers signals growing interest in grounding educational AI in learning sciences principles (Jurenka et al., 2024; LearnLM Team, Google, 2025), but without more intentional integration into underlying infrastructure, educational AI risks prioritizing efficiency or engagement over meaningful support for learning. As past waves of "personalized learning" have shown, technology that optimizes for engagement without attending to how learning works can reproduce rather than address longstanding inequities in educational opportunity. This challenge is particularly pressing as new efforts seek to build openly shared educational AI resources as public goods. The K–12 AI Infrastructure Initiative, a five-year, $26 million effort led by Digital Promise and a coalition of partners, is funding the development of tutoring interaction corpora, learning-aligned benchmarks, and model documentation frameworks that embed pedagogical principles by design (Digital Promise, 2025; Roschelle et al., 2025). For such resources to genuinely advance learning, learning scientists must be actively involved in their co-design alongside AI engineers, education practitioners, and policymakers — contributing not only domain knowledge but also the critical perspectives needed to navigate questions of safety, privacy, ethics, and equity. This workshop therefore explores how the learning sciences can be systematically integrated into these infrastructural public goods. It brings together learning scientists, AI developers, education practitioners, and funders to examine where and how learning sciences expertise is most needed in the development of technical infrastructure for educational AI. Its goals are to inform participants about emerging infrastructure efforts and the role learning sciences can play in shaping them, create space for participants to share current work and articulate concerns, identify promising directions for future research and investment, and stimulate the formation of cross- sector collaborations. Building on recent ISLS programming on AI and education (International Society of the Learning Sciences, 2022, 2024), the workshop positions the learning sciences not only as a field that evaluates AI applications after they are built, but as one that can help shape the foundations on which educational AI is constructed. Cambridge University Press. https://doi.org/10.1017/9781108776462 GoGoData Participatory Sensing: Students, Educators and Researchers Building Collaborative Data Networks Charles Pimentel charlespimentel@ufrj.br Federal University of Rio de Janeiro (UFRJ) Vithoria Cabreira vithoriacabreira@gmail.com Federal Technological University of Paraná (UTFPR) Walter Akio Goya, Paulo Blikstein, Renato Russo aag2197@tc.columbia.edu, paulob@tc.columbia.edu, renrusso@gmail.com Teachers College, Columbia University Arnan Sipitakiat arnan.s@cmu.ac.th Chiang Mai University Abstract: In this half-day workshop, participants will engage with GoGoData, an open learning plugin that connects the GoGo Board microcontroller, sensors, Internet of Things (IoT) communication, and the Common Online Data Analysis Platform (CODAP) to support participatory sensing and collaborative exploration of real-time data. Beyond experimenting with the plugin’s features for data collection, transmission, and interpretation, participants will analyze GoGoData as a design case that integrates constructionist principles with learning sciences perspectives on data literacy. Participants will, in turn, extend these theoretical and design lenses to examine how collaborative data networks can foster critical engagement with data in their own educational and research contexts. Proposers/Organizers Charles Pimentel Charles Pimentel is a Research Fellow at the Transformative Learning Technologies Lab, supporting the documentation of the GoGo Board and the development of data-focused learning activities. He holds a Master’s degree in Informatics from UFRJ and works in K-12 education with Programming, Artificial Intelligence, and Educational Robotics. Charles is a doctoral student at the Institute of Computing at the Federal University of Rio de Janeiro, researching Data Literacy, and a member of the FabLearn Fellows Cohort 3. He also teaches Design & Tech at Graded in São Paulo, developing tech-for-good projects connected to sustainability. Vithoria Cabreira Vithoria Cabreira is an undergraduate student in Computer Engineering at the Federal Technological University of Paraná (UTFPR). She supports the development of digital tools and web technologies for educational and research projects. Her interests include software development, web platforms, and the creation of digital solutions that improve user experience. Vithoria is currently strengthening her technical skills through practical projects and experimentation with new technologies. Akio Goya Akio is an Educational Technology Designer for the Transformative Learning Technologies Lab, coordinating the design, implementation, and documentation of GoGo Boards in Brazil, as well as the implementation of makerspaces in public schools. Akio holds a Master’s degree in Instructional Technology and Media from Teachers College, Columbia University (USA) and a Master’s and a Bachelor’s degree in Computer Engineering from University of Sao Paulo (Brazil), and a Teacher Licensure in Mathematics (Middle and High School) from FIAR (Brazil). Paulo Blikstein P aulo Blikstein is an Associate Professor at Teachers College and an Affiliate Associate Professor of Computer Science at Columbia University, where he directs the Transformative Learning Technologies Lab and the Lemann Center for Brazilian Studies. His research focuses on how new technologies can transform the learning of science, engineering and computation. Paulo is the co-inventor of the GoGo Board, co-leading its research and development since 2001. Paulo has a Ph.D. from Northwestern University, a MSc. from the MIT Media Lab and an M.Eng. and B.Eng. from the University of São Paulo, Brazil. Renato Russo Renato is a doctoral candidate at the Technology, Media, and Learning program at Teachers College, Columbia University and a researcher at Transformative Learning Technologies Lab. In his research, Renato explores how learning technologies can promote critical and emancipatory knowledge construction practices. Renato earned a MA degree in Learning, Design and Technology from Stanford University Graduate School of Education. Arnan (Roger) Sipitakiat Arnan (Roger) directs the Teaching and Learning Innovation Center (TLIC) at Chiang Mai University in Thailand. As a faculty and researcher at the Computer Engineering Department, he also directs the Learning Inventions Laboratory (LIL). Arnan is the co-inventor of the GoGo Board, co-leading research and development on the toolkit since 2001. Arnan focuses on designing technologically-rich learning tools, such as the GoGo Board, that have allowed students to explore areas including robotics, interactive art, games, agriculture, and community development. Arnan earned his MSc. and Ph.D. from the Massachusetts Institute of Technology and B.Eng. from Chiang Mai University. Intended audience This workshop is intended for graduate students, educators, and researchers interested in exploring participatory sensing, critical data literacy, and learning technology design through hands-on experimentation. It particularly welcomes those studying or developing tools that connect physical computing, IoT, and real-time data exploration to promote collaborative inquiry and learning. More broadly, the session is open to all participants interested in integrating constructionist and learning sciences perspectives into the design of educational technologies. (Note that GoGoData, the GoGo Board, and CODAP are open-source platforms.) Duration of the event Half-day (3-4 hours, flexible depending on conference scheduling demands). Description of the event The GoGo Board was invented in 2001 as a low-cost and learner-friendly robotics and scientific sensing platform. In the years since, the project has undergone several design iterations, each affording new possibilities for students across diverse ages and backgrounds to explore powerful ideas in computing and STEM. In this workshop, participants will also engage with GoGoData (2025), a new open-source plugin that connects the GoGo Board to the Common Online Data Analysis Platform (CODAP) for real-time data communication and visualization. CODAP, developed by the Concord Consortium, has a long-standing history as an open-source environment for data analysis and modeling that supports inquiry-based learning. Together, GoGoData, the GoGo Board Kit version 7, and CODAP create a participatory sensing ecosystem that enables students to collect, share, and interpret live data while examining the learning sciences principles underlying the design of these tools [1-3]. Workshop Format The workshop will be organized into five main activities. I - Historical framing. Participants will begin with a brief discussion on the evolution of tangible interfaces within the Learning Sciences and basic education contexts. This discussion will be situated alongside the rise of big data practices and participatory or crowd sensing, showing how learner-generated, real-time data from distributed sensors can reshape inquiry, evidence making, and classroom discourse. The framing will surface design lessons on openness, transparency, and agency, linking data practices to issues of provenance, privacy, and ethics, and highlighting how collaborative data networks can support critical engagement and community action. II - Exploring the GoGo Board 7 / GoGoData / CODAP. Participants will explore the core features of the GoGo Board version 7 and the GoGoData plugin, examining how each component emerged from research data and i terative design decisions. Using onboard controls, they will visualize sensor values, directly before connecting to a computer to interact with GoGoData and its integration with the Common Online Data Analysis Platform (CODAP). Through this connection, participants will experience how real-time sensor data can be collected, transmitted, analyzed, and explored within CODAP’s interactive environment. Facilitators will highlight how each feature embodies specific design principles that link tangible experimentation with data-driven inquiry. III - Participatory sensing exploration. Participants will collaboratively select a variable to measure, such as temperature, luminosity, pollution, or sound level, using a GoGo Board 7 kit sensor. Working in small groups, they will connect the GoGo Board to CODAP through the GoGoData plugin and deploy sensors in different internet-connected areas across the UCI campus. Each group will collect and share real-time data through the open-source plugin integrated with the data analysis platform, contributing to a collaborative network of distributed measurements. As data accumulate, participants will analyze emerging patterns across locations, drawing inferences about environmental or contextual factors. The activity will conclude with a collective discussion where groups interpret their findings, reflect on methodological decisions, and connect their insights to broader perspectives on participatory sensing, open data collaboration, and critical data literacy in education. IV - Conclusion and gallery walk. Participants will share and discuss the outcomes of their activities, reflecting on the lessons learned and insights gained throughout the workshop. The session will conclude with a collective show-and-tell, allowing groups to present their findings, highlight key observations from the participatory sensing exercise, and connect these experiences to broader questions about learning, design, and data literacy. V - Post-workshop interaction. Optional follow-up opportunities will be provided for participants who wish to continue collaborating after the session. These interactions may include online discussions, exchange of design ideas, and updates on future developments of the GoGoData platform. Participants will be invited to share reflections, resources, and potential research connections that extend the learning and collaboration initiated during the workshop. Throughout the workshop, facilitators will guide discussions connecting the design of GoGoData, the GoGo Board, and CODAP to learning sciences and constructionist frameworks, emphasizing how participatory sensing and data exploration are enhanced by open-source ecosystems. The session will highlight how openness, transparency, and accessibility in these tools empower learners and researchers to collaboratively collect, analyze, and interpret real-time data. Rather than serving as a technical training, the workshop offers a hands-on exploration of how open, theory-informed technologies developed through over twenty years of design-based research can foster agency, collaboration, and critical engagement with data. Participation requirements No requirements. We invite to join all participants interested in tangible interface design, educational robotics, and data science, irrespective of skill or experience levels. Relationship to similar events conducted in the past The author team conducted an NSF-funded project at the New York Hall of Science in collaboration with Teachers College, Columbia University, using the GoGo Board in data science camps for middle school students under the AISL program. We also did a physical computing workshop at ISLS 2024. Facilities and equipment required Facilities: ● Projector / screen for workshop facilitators ● Wifi connectivity Equipment: ● Gogo Boards Kits (board and sensors - we will provide them) ● Participants will be asked to bring their laptops with an available USB-C port. Minimal and maximal number of participants expected 8 - 15 participants Draft call for participation C alling all researchers, designers, and educators interested in exploring the power of participatory sensing to connect learning, data, and design. In this half-day workshop, you will engage with GoGoData (2025), a new open-source plugin that links the GoGo Board microcontroller, sensors, and Internet of Things (IoT) communication to the Common Online Data Analysis Platform (CODAP) for real-time data exploration. Together, these tools create a participatory sensing ecosystem where learners and researchers can collaboratively collect, share, and interpret live data (Figer 1). Beyond experimenting with the platform’s features, you will analyze GoGoData as a design case informed by constructionist and learning sciences perspectives, building on over two decades of iterative design research with the GoGo Board. This workshop offers a unique opportunity to experience how open-source technologies can empower communities to transform local data into meaningful insights and to apply these theoretical and design perspectives to your own educational research and development projects. Figure 1 Participatory Sensing Ecossystem : GoGo Code - GoGo Data on CODAP - GoGo Board GoGo Code and GoGoData CODAP plugin displaying sensor data from a GoGo Board. Workshop format The workshop is planned for in-person delivery, with the option of hybrid participation if necessary. The program will include interactive, hands-on activities supported by remote contributions from members of the international workshop team, ensuring collaboration and engagement across locations. papers.title: Participatory Design for AI in Teacher Education: From Top-Down Directives to Teacher Empowerment
papers.authors: Ekta Shokeen, Ane Vielandt Jensen, Ole Sejer Iversen, Christian Dindler, Marianne Graves Petersen
papers.design_stakeholders: Teachers; Educators & Practitioners; Students & Learners
papers.abstract: Empowering teacher educators to lead technology integration is essential for creating context-sensitive educational futures. This study examines how participatory design workshops can support educators in collaboratively developing sustainable capacity for integrating AI into teacher education. Drawing on a series of three participatory design workshops, the analysis focuses on the collaborative learning processes involved and the professional outcomes they produce. Structured around exploration, co- creation, and reflection, these workshops enabled educators to critically engage with the pedagogical, ethical, and institutional dimensions of AI, fostering both ownership and transformative agency. The findings demonstrate how participatory design can function not only as a design methodology but also as a framework for professional learning. A key contribution of this paper is the demonstration that participatory design supports sustainable AI integration by building e ducators’ capacity for change through the design process.

papers.title: Exploring Learner Engagement in an LLM-Supported Simulation Environment for Complex Systems Understanding
papers.authors: Amit Nair, Man Su, Tomohiro Nagashima
papers.design_stakeholders: Science Teachers; Undergraduate / Graduate Students; Domain Experts & Technologists
papers.abstract: Understanding complex systems is challenging, as learners often rely on linear reasoning and struggle to recognize decentralized and emergent processes. Large language models (LLMs) offer new opportunities to support inquiry in simulation- based learning, yet how learners engage with these tools and how such engagement relates to learning outcomes remains underexplored. In this study, we investigate learner engagement within a theory- informed, LLM -supported simulation environment, based on an exper iment with 69 postsecondary students that varied parameter control and questioning agency. Focusing on questioning agency, we examine how interactions with an LLM -based tutor and engagement with exploratory instructional regions relate to posttest performa nce. Results show that greater engagement with the tutor, particularly through content-focused interactions, is associated with higher learning gains. Time spent in exploratory regions also significantly predicts performance. These findings highlight the i mportance of fostering meaningful engagement with both conversational tutors and interactive features in LLM-supported environments.

papers.title: Co-design as a Catalyst for Becoming: Identity, Practice, and Learning Trajectories in Undergraduate Science
papers.authors: Sunnie Gong, Michelle Lui, Aidyn Intykbekov
papers.design_stakeholders: Teachers; Higher Education Instructors / Faculty; Undergraduate / Graduate Students; Educational Researchers & Designers; Domain Experts & Technologists
papers.abstract: Co-design is a collaborative methodology for creating educational innovations involving researchers, educators, and developers. While research -practice partnerships in the Learning Sciences have historically co-designed with teachers, recent developments have begun involving students. However, research on students’ experiences of co- design remains limited. This study explores what students learn from engaging in co-design through a situated learning framework linking learning to identity formation. Using a multiple case study methodology, the relationships between the identities, learning, and participation of six undergraduate science students were examined in a co -design project for creating educational virtual reality simulations. Findings reveal that identity, practice, and learning exist in dynamic and reciprocal relationships within co -design contexts. Students’ existing identities informed their co- design engagement. Through practice, students developed collaboration skills and learned about themselves which led to diverse identity development trajectories. These findings suggest engaging students as co-design partners creates unique opportunities for integrated learning and identity development.

papers.title: Visualizing Justice: Arts-Based Inquiry in Community-Engaged Climate Education
papers.authors: Rachel Sherwin
papers.design_stakeholders: Higher Education Instructors / Faculty; Students & Learners; Educational Researchers & Designers
papers.abstract: Impactful learning technology innovation doesn’t happen in isolation; it grows through relationships, among researchers, educators, students, technologists, designers, and institutional leaders. While some collaborations are carefully structured, others take root more organically, evolving to meet shifting needs and opportunities. In this keynote, Dr. Alyssa Wise explores how purposeful partnerships drive innovation across the technological, social, conceptual, and practical dimensions of learning, tracing three kinds of partnerships that have unfolded over the past decade in her work. Flexible Coupling articulates how institutional partnerships can leverage complementary strengths without becoming over-structured. In a longstanding collaboration with a university learning analytics service unit, in vivo studies of instructors’ analytics use informed both theoretical models of sense-making and applied tool design. Constructive Responsiveness describes how partnerships with educators can evolve around a shared object of inquiry when goals are not yet fully defined. In work with dental educators implementing an online reflection tool, the collaboration advanced from examinations of reflection quality to generate domain-specific insights into failure attribution and professional identity formation. Finally, Generative Pluralism characterizes interdisciplinary partnerships among researchers or co-designers where the goal is not convergence but conceptual creation. These collaborations embraced multiplicity, surfacing productive tensions, methodological bridges, and new vocabularies for imagining learning technologies. Together, these patterns illustrate partnerships as adaptable forms of collaboration, each suited to different problems, people, and purposes. This talk highlights how designing, studying, and sustaining learning with the support of technology can be supported by purposeful partnerships that bridge disciplines, organizations, and stakeholder perspectives. Bio: Dr. Alyssa Wise is Professor of Technology and Education at Vanderbilt University’s Peabody College, with a courtesy appointment in Computer Science in the College of Connected Computing. She also serves as Director of the LIVE Learning Innovation Incubator, Vanderbilt’s interdisciplinary hub for impactful learning technology innovation. Her research productively integrates tools of computational data science, theories of learning sciences and collaborative learning, and practices of human-centered design to build and study analytic and artificial intelligence systems that promote powerful learning for individuals situated in social context. She also conducts mixed-method investigations into how educational practices are being reshaped by new sources of data and the growing availability of new generative artificial intelligence capabilities. Dr. Wise holds a Ph.D. in Learning Sciences and M.S. in Instructional Systems Technology from Indiana University, as well as a B.S. in Chemistry from Yale University, was previously a Professor of Learning Sciences and Educational Technology and Director of the Learning Analytics Research Network (LEARN) at New York University and has worked in industry, with non-profits, and in classrooms across the Americas. https://tinyurl.com/alyssawisescholar https://peabody.vanderbilt.edu/bio/?pid=alyssa-wise https://lab.vanderbilt.edu/live https://www.linkedin.com/in/alyssawise

papers.title: Teacher Agency in Learning Sciences Co-design: Dubious or Undocumented?
papers.authors: Abigail A. Williams, Sam H. Ross, R. Benjamin Shapiro
papers.design_stakeholders: Teachers; Educators & Practitioners; Educational Researchers & Designers; Domain Experts & Technologists
papers.abstract: Frequent mentions of co- design in the learning sciences (LS) reflect an increasing effort to create resources through partnerships where researchers and educators share agency. Whether these partnerships meaningfully lead to new, teacher -shaped innovations depends on the dynamics of cross-role collaborations, including who gets to make design choices. We use Bratteteig and Wagner’s (2016) conceptual framework for the types of decision- making in co- design to evaluate LS research that involves co -designing with teachers. Our review reveals substantial gaps in descriptions of teacher decision- making, indicating either insufficiently described or insufficiently empowering co-design practices. We advocate for more transparent and egalitarian approaches to co- design at all phases of the design process, to increase the equity, robustness, research contributions, and potential real-world impact of co-design.
