papers.title: Social Capital by Design: Community-University Partnerships and Pathways into Technology Education
papers.authors: Tamara N. Sobomehin, Adam Banks, Olatunde M. Sobomehin, Olatayo A. Sobomehin
papers.design_stakeholders: Teachers; Higher Education Instructors / Faculty; Elementary Students & Children; Educational Researchers & Designers; Community Members & Partners; Domain Experts & Technologists
papers.abstract: This practice -oriented paper describes the design of a partnership between StreetCode Academy and the Stanford Institute for Diversity in the Arts, created to connect community learners in a technology education program with university students and resources through a co llaborative learning model. In this endeavor, social capital was emphasized as a lever for engagement to create opportunities for relationship- building across community and institutional networks. These relationships functioned as pathways for reciprocal learning and network expansion, which supported students’ and instructors’ engagement with technical skills and their development as innovators. Preliminary findings indicate increased student interest in continued participation in technology education. Instructors and mentors also reported an increase in confidence, skill development, and sense of purpose. This paper presents design considerations for operationalizing social capital and it shows how community- university partnerships can serve as a two -way bridge for reciprocal learning and network-building to expand pathways into technology education. Objectives and theoretical grounding Despite the growth of opportunities in the innovation economy, participation in computing and technology education continues to be marked by inequity, particularly for students from communities historically excluded from access to institutional networks. While several factors influence engagement and persistence in this area, including inequitable access to digital resources and high -quality STEM learning experiences, another critical factor is how learning environments are designed to recognize and extend existing relationships and forms of support that enable participants to navigate and persist in technology pathways. S ocial capital refers to the relational supports people access and share through family, friends, teachers, and communities (Bourdieu, 1980; Coleman, 1988), and as a potential factor contributing to ongoing marginalization, should be examined more thoughtfully. In STEM research, social capital is often used as an explainer of disparities in tech participation. In this paper, however, social capital is discussed as an existing asset that can be leveraged and designed to activate new, mutually beneficial relationships across institutional networks that expand access and support participation in technology pathways. This paper presents an ongoing partnership between StreetCode Academy, a community- based technology education nonprofit, and Stanford University, a world-renowned institution of higher learning known for its culture of innovation. Founded in 2014, StreetCode Academy is committed to bridging the technology education gap by offering free coding, entrepreneurship, and design classes to youth and their families in communities with longstanding histories of creativity and technological ingenuity, where access to technology learning opportunities is not always equitably available . The Stanford Institute for Diversity in the Arts is a “student-facing and serving organization" committed to offering opportunities to practice leadership, creative expression, and social responsibility through the arts. This partnership extended StreetCode ’s community-based learning model for communities historically underrepresented in formal technology institutions onto Stanford’s campus, a university with a strong institutional emphasis on technology and innovation, intentionally repositioning who participates in and belongs within these spaces. This created opportunities for students and their families to build new connections and engage with university spaces that are not often available or accessible to the public. For many participants, this included taking classes on a university campus for the first time, which positively influenced their sense of belonging and possibility within technology and higher education pathways. It also created meaningful opportunities for 2171 university students pursuing fields adjacent to technology, education, design, and the arts to contribute as mentors and instructors while developing their own perspectives and skills. Through this initiative, they were able to apply their disciplinary knowledge in authentic, culturally grounded contexts, which helped them experience affirmation and support that reinforced their sense of belonging in fields where they may have otherwise experienced marginalization (McGee, 2020). Positioning the role of social capital in tech education is significant because it can serve as an existing and malleable design resource within educational systems. Students bring with them unique social and cultural resources that serve as valuable assets in supporting their learning trajectories (Yosso, 2005). V aluing and leveraging students' existing networks and intentionally curating expanded connections, educators can engage relational dimensions that can be critical to fostering greater participation in technology-related learning pathways and academic settings, particularly among historically underrepresented groups. These relations can positively impact learners’ feelings of inclusion and their self -esteem as they navigate technology-related fields , which positively influence learning and identity development. In this context, social capital was treated as a catalyst as well as an outcome, cultivated to foster social and academic growth among the students and educators participating in the program. In this process, relationships were mutually constituted through ongoing interaction, as participants both drew on and contributed to shared relational networks. These dynamics created opportunities for co -development, where learners and instructors built confidence and capacity through shared engagement. This has the potential to extend existing research on social networks and opportunity (Chetty et al., 2024) , demonstrating how social capital can be intentionally designed within learning environments to encourage reciprocal relationships that help shape participants’ engagement and aspirational trajectories. These theoretical perspectives informed the program’s design, guiding its intention to respect and position all participants as active contributors to the learning culture, and structure community engagement in a way that centered reciprocal identity development, where students, mentors, and instructors developed in distinct but interconnected ways through their engagement in teaching, learning, and collaboration. Design The StreetCode Academy and Stanford University Institute for Diversity in the Arts (IDA) partnership shared three intersecting goals: the first was to increase accessibility to top -tier learning opportunities. StreetCode Academy is committed to providing learning experiences that help participants gain foundational skills in a variety of coding, design, and media platforms. Stanford University is a global research institution of higher education, known for its contributions to the innovation economy. The Institute for Diversity in the Arts, founded 25 years ago, was established to educate, activate, and transform students at Stanford and extend that mission to the local community. The second goal was to advance the conversation around culture, arts, and technology, exploring how these intersect to inspire creativity, expression, and innovation. The third was to bridge perceived and actual divides across communities by fostering belonging and community across institutional boundaries between the university and the local community. Designing for access, belonging, and shared participation To support these goals, the partnership was designed for both entities to contribute in complementary ways. Regarding accessibility, the Institute for Diversity in the Arts provided financial resources so StreetCode could coordinate free transportation, provide free laptop rentals and usage for students, and even offer free meals for participants, removing many of the logistical barriers that can often prevent engagement. Framing access as a design principle helped to promote more equitable participation and expand participants’ connections to social networks through the structural organization of the learning environment. The program design prioritized a family- centered learning environment. This partnership offered intergenerational learning spaces where youth, elders, children, and parents could learn together. This is atypical for many K12 or university classrooms, which are traditionally designed for a specific age range. One participant, a 76-year-old Spanish-speaking StreetCode student, spoke at the final-quarter Demo Day, sharing that it had been her dream to take a course at Stanford, and that, through this program, it was finally achieved. This example illustrates how designing for intergenerational participation supported a spirit of lifelong learning and expanded who could belong in the space while also creating opportunities for individuals across generations to l earn alongside one another and reimagine themselves as technology innovators. 2172 Building on these design choices, this program aimed to operationalize social capital so that learners and instructors could interact as mutual recipients and co-producers of value. This was an intentional move away from traditional one-directional service-oriented models of technology education, toward a more connected and empowering model of shared learning. Grounded in the principle of “learning through participation,” the project centered an epistemology of development that recognized access to diverse people, experiences, and environments as integral to how participants form affirming mindsets and identities as technologists and innovators. Across the program, three design considerations for operationalizing social capital were prioritized: reducing barriers to participation, centering shared participation and belonging, and expanding opportunities for purposeful network- building to support sustained engagement. Implementation A fourteen-week program was developed, encompassing a variety of courses. Courses were thematically designed around the topic of “culture and tech” and introduced participants to cutting-edge and emerging technology. Each course included opportunities to engage in practical, technical use of technology and in theoretical and philosophical discussions about how each person could use these tools to preserve and positively advance their cultural traditions and personal goals. This approach reaffirmed education as a force of personal liberation and advancement for each student as well as their local and global communities. Courses were offered in two seven -week rotations, with sessions held once a week for 2.5 hours each. Offerings included courses like “Storytelling & Tech,” “Music & Tech,” “Design & Tech,” “Jr. Design & Tech,” “Intro to Code,” and “STEMLabs Mechanical Engi neering.” Classes were hosted on Stanford’s campus at the IDA “house” and the Black Community Services Center, where the community room and lobby became classrooms that “felt like home” for students, filled with art, music, and warmth that reflected the students’ community aesthetics and values. Enacting bonding through shared rituals Classes began with a 30-minute ritual called “Huddle-up,” intended to inspire students for the upcoming courses and connect them with one another over food, engaging activities, and presentations by featured students or special guests. Huddle -ups began wit h a shared dinner, during which announcements highlighted past student accomplishments and upcoming events. Activities were designed to have students interact with one another so they could learn about each other. Discussing a topic around a table or acting out a scenario would bring people together. Huddle-ups also featured guest speakers or showcased the work and talents of community members, which often led students to follow up with each other or with a guest speaker about an opportunity they might not otherwise have known about. Following Huddle-Up, students would break into their courses, which were facilitated by several lead instructors and taught by StreetCode alumni, industry experts, and Stanford students. Each class had one or two lead instructors and was supported by three to four mentors. While 66% of classes were taught by Stanford students, every course had a lead teacher or mentor who represented the geographical or cultural background of the StreetCode students. StreetCode community members, industry representatives, a nd the Stanford affiliates were all treated as co -designers who collaborated on curriculum design, logistics, and pedagogy throughout the quarters. Enacting network expansion across community, university, and industry To deepen the connection to industry, each quarter had a day committed to exploring the field. Experiences included a trip to the Stanford innovation program, hosted by the director of publications and co- director of the K-12 Lab, and a visit to OpenAI, where a workshop was led by a former StreetCode instructor and Stanford alumnus and colleague. These trips were designed to strengthen the relationship between these organizations and the StreetCode community, empowering the social capital participants could access through more formal network development. Quarterly courses ended with a Demo Day, a community- wide public celebration that invited members of the broader community to experience a showcase of what students had learned and accomplished. Nearly 20 employees from Amazon and 15 members of Links, a professional organization of African American women, attended one of the Demo Days, along with numerous Stanford students, StreetCode community members, family, and friends. Students presented their work and exchanged information with visiting guests. One student who 2173 created a movie using an AI platform even raised $250 from attendees who wanted to support his continued subscription to the platform beyond the course. Through outside speaking engagements, field trips, and Demo Days, these relationships were nurtured beyond what was gained in the classroom, with enrolled participants expanding their personal and professional networks of opportunities and support. The implementation of each activity and the program overall was thoughtfully curated to expand the realization and potential of social capital across residential, academic, and industry communities, connecting StreetCode students with professors and students at S tanford University; also connecting Stanford University and industry partners and affiliates with genuine opportunities to engage with local community members around relevant and resonant partnerships. In doing so, the program strengthened individual trajectories and cultivated an ecosystem of shared learning and mutual investment. Practice-based learnings There are many context -specific factors that may have affected the efficacy of these efforts. However, early findings are encouraging. Participant feedback collected through post-class surveys indicated that 94% of students expressed a desire to continue learning about technology; and 70% reported an increase in their sense of identity as innovators. These data suggest positive implications for this approach, providing a generative introduction to technology for community participants. In addition, instructor feedback indicated that assuming the role of mentor or teacher supported the development of confidence and skills as they, too, navigated exploratory conversations and reflected on their growth as emerging professionals in computing and education. They also gained valuable first -hand experience designing learning environments aligned with principles they apply in their STEM courses (e.g., design thinking, Universal Design for Learning, Understanding by Design), reinforcing their technical skill development. Teachers also discussed how this experience acted as a space for personal mindset renewal. It provided opportunities to reflect on their relationships with technology and to reconnect with their motivating hopes and aims, empowering their journeys as developing professionals and technologists. In this way, teaching became a creative means of sustaining motivation and recharging their sense of purpose. Meaning- making is recognized as a dimension of well-being (Seligman, 2011). Connecting their academic work to an authentic teaching experience, student - teachers were able to deepen the connection between their learning and real -world practice. This contributed to their positive identity development and overall personal wellness. Outcomes experienced by all participants, students and instructors, point to a reinforcing developmental experience which was supported by shared participation, strengthened relationships, and expanded network connections. Instructors’ growing confidence in their skills and renewed sense of purpose were nurtured by their experiences teaching and supporting students, who affirmed their developing expert ise. Similarly, students’ increased confidence and emerging innovator identities developed through their engagement with near-peer instructors, whose mentorship and presence as accessible role models helped shape their identities as technologists. Relevance Preliminary learnings from this project implicate the need for more research to better understand the degree to which social capital, and in what forms, influences levels of student engagement and sustained participation in computing pathways. Future research might also inquire how a model like this could help to address gaps between student needs and available school offerings, particularly in expanding opportunities to develop technical skills and strengthen psychological supports. Implications for future practice-based initiatives include identifying community assets and opportunities to triangulate practice, bringing together resources that connect community organizations and academic institutions, with opportunities to connect to industry to spur individual and communal development through designed pathways across locally situated learning ecologies. This partnership’s preliminary outcomes suggest the potential for more strategic programming to expand equitable participation , positioning social capital as a designable mechanism for reciprocal learning and network-building across community and university contexts. papers.title: Designing AI Partner-Embedded Learning Environments to Support AI Literacies
papers.authors: Mon-Lin Monica Ko, Marcelo Worsley, Michael Alan Chang, Chelsea Chandler, Sierra Rose
papers.design_stakeholders: Teachers; Youth & Adolescents; Educational Researchers & Designers; Community Members & Partners
papers.abstract: As AI technologies become increasingly integrated into schools, questions arise about what students should learn about AI and how AI-powered tools can support collaborative learning. This symposium reports on the Institute of Student-AI Teaming (iSAT), which designs AI partners and curricular activity systems to promote AI literacy and collaboration. Unlike most classroom AI tools designed for 1:1 interactions, iSAT develops AI partners as social collaborators that both facilitate group learning and serve as objects of inquiry —helping students “look under the hood” of AI systems. Our multi -year co-design process across three U.S. states engages teachers, students, and parents to build integrated systems of curriculum, technology, and professional learning. The symposium’s six posters span AI design, infrastructure, curriculum, and teacher learning, illustrating how AI can be productively embedded within classroom collaboration. Together, they advance understanding of how AI systems can meaningfully support and transform collaborative learning. Objective of the session As AI technologies become increasingly embedded in education (Reich & Dukes, 2024), so do questions about what students should learn about AI systems (AI literacy) and how AI -powered tools may support (or hinder) student learning. While there is growing excitement about AI’s potential to transform education, decades of research highlight repeated failures of earlier innovations to do so. Scholars argue these failures often stem from underappreciating the infrastructural nature of technology and overestimating its power to drive change in classroom practice (Roschelle et al., 2010). First, technology is infrastructural in that its value lies not in its particular content but in its ability to generate new representations of disciplinary ideas and create opportunities for students to engage more deeply in those ideas (Hegedus & Kaput, 2003). Second, like previous technologies, today’s AI tools will not transform education on their own. Their success depends on how curriculum activity systems—teacher professional learning (PL), instructional materials, and technology —work together to reshape learning environments (Vahey et al., 2013). Their success also depends on how teachers and students work together within the system to support learning. This symposium reports on work from the Institute of Student-AI Teaming (iSAT), an institute that aims to design AI -powered tools and curricular activity systems that promote collaborative knowledge building and student learning around AI -literacy specifically (D’Mello et al., 2024, OECD, 2025). Our project intentionally combines both AI -literacy and AI as a tool for collaborative learning in ways that will enable the AI -partner to serve simultaneously as a collaboration support and an object of inquiry as students think critically about how the AI works. That is, our AI partners play a dual role of supporting student collaboration and as a tool for “looking under the hood” at how AI systems work. Supporting collaborative learning is a longstanding goal of both the ISLS and CSCL community, and is crucial because we know that learning is inherently a social process. Yet, the dominant approach to incorporating AI inside K-12 classrooms focuses on 1:1 interactions between students and AI systems. iSAT’s approach is radically different: we aim to develop AI as a social, collaborative partner that works alongside students and teachers to deepen their engagement with one another. This goal has required that our team engage in multi -year co-design processes to better understand the needs and desires of multiple users 556 and stakeholders (e.g. teachers, students, parents) as we work to develop and refine AI partners, curriculum materials, and professional development to support the development of AI literacies. Over the past five years, our work has involved working with stakeholders in districts across three U.S. states to conceptualize, develop, enact, and refine our curricular activity system. This session will focus on the design of iSAT’s curricular activity system to deepen the field’s conversation about the role of AI -systems in supporting collaborative learning. Across the posters, we will describe how our co- design practices, back -end models, classroom pilot studies, professional learning, and curricular routines and designs worked toward our emerging understanding of the utility of these tools for supporting collaborative learning. Overview of the symposium The 6 posters that constitute the symposium represent our collective efforts to take seriously what it means for AI systems to partner within the curricular activity systems of secondary schools. Poster 1 will detail the trajectory of co-design for our first AI partner, the Community Builder (CoBi) and how the ongoing design, implementation and analysis of the co- design space informed the values of our institute. Poster 2 will present on the design, development, and pilot studies of our second Jigsaw Interactive Agent (JIA) in secondary classrooms and how productive uncertainty was leveraged to design the AI partner interventions to suppo rt small group jigsaws. In Poster 3, we will report on the architecture and analytic pipeline that underlies our two existing AI partners, documenting how the pipeline infrastructure, state detection and dialogue policies inform the AI- partner outputs and interventions. Posters 4-6 address how we built both curriculum materials and teachers’ capacities to leverage them so that the AI partners could be meaningfully integrated into everyday classroom activities. In Poster 4, we examine how curricular routines can support students' sensemaking of their own collaborative practices. In Poster 5, we show how our PL design supported teachers’ learning about AI, our AI literacy curriculum and pedagogical approaches that center student sensemaking. Finally, Poster 6 describes the design and refinement of our curriculum materials that focus on AI literacy, a process guided by co- design, adaptation and refinement with teachers in their classrooms. Scholarly significance This session is both timely and essential. First, AI tools are becoming increasingly embedded in schools and in our world. At the same time, few teachers are currently prepared to teach about AI, use AI -enabled tools, and adopt student-centered, collaborative pedagogies—what we call a triple innovation challenge . We also know that external forces (e.g. social and news media) shape students’ understanding of AI, and that schools/educators play a less significant role (OECD, 2025) This session highlights a new approach to supporting AI literacy through the design of curricular activity systems where AI Partners are meaningfully embedded to support AI literacies through collaborative learning. Structure of the session The symposium will be organized as a structured poster session. The chair of the session will first provide a brief overview of the session (4 mins). Each presenter will give a one -minute elevator pitch to introduce their project (6 mins). Presenters will then move to their respective posters; participants can view posters, demos (if applicable) and engage in discussion. We will invite participants to engage in two “rounds” of poster-viewing (30 mins each), so that co-presenters have a chance to view other s’ posters . Our discussant will synthesize the posters and pose questions for the audience to discuss, focusing on the challenges and affordances of AI -powered systems in supporting collaborative learning in schools (20 minutes). CoBi Origins: Co-design narratives as boundary objects to translate Co-design findings into interdisciplinary implementation Michael Alan Chang Objectives Collaborative and participatory design is increasingly used to inform the design and implementation of AI -Ed tools that are responsive to the needs and lived experiences of interest holders (Ravi et al., 2025). An AI -Ed research team hosts a co -design context, completes an analysis of it, and then responds to the co- design efforts through implementation. While this sequential and linear process simplifies the already complex and interdisciplinary process of building AI-Ed tools, it can constrain both the types of analysis that can be conducted within the co-design context and the ways in which stakeholders can engage in the ongoing design of AI-Ed tools 557 (Chang, under review). Here, I share our efforts in iSAT, where there were parallel, longitudinal efforts to (a) develop and analyze a three- year co-design study with high school youth to surface their hopes and concerns around the use of AI in schools and (b) respond to the findings of those co- design studies to develop AI partners and curricular activity systems that surround the use of the technology. Here, I ask: how does the ongoing design, implementation, and analysis of co- design spaces shape the des ign activities of an interdisciplinary research institute? Perspectives Here, I view stories about co-design activities as an evolving boundary object that guides how large-scale AI-Ed implementation teams take on co-design findings (Star & Griesemer, 1989). Boundary objects are conceptualized as “how artifacts can fulfill a specific function in bridging intersecting practices” (pg. 134, Akkerman & Bakker, 2011). As Star (2010) clarifies, a boundary object is characterized by interpretive flexibility across different contexts, allowing each context to tailor the object to its own needs locally. Finally, boundary objects follow particular trajectories within organizational contexts; once created, boundary objects evolve through local tailoring, standardize over time, and, finally, fade away as the standardization practices begin to constrain possible local adaptations. In turn, new boundary objects are then created.

papers.title: Designing with Care: Exploring the Embodied and Affective Dimensions of Collaborative Noticing
papers.authors: Shivani Davé, Lindsay Lindberg, Ananda Marin
papers.design_stakeholders: Math Teachers; Students & Learners; Educational Researchers & Designers
papers.abstract: This paper brings together three cases to examine the question, what happens when we approach the design of research contexts to explore professional noticing with care? Through video-based interaction analysis, a pattern emerged within the researcher -participant interactions. When researchers engaged with care, research contexts became sites of collaborative sense- making that supported participants to come to new insights about their practices. Essential to the development of these research contexts was the emic nature of the researchers’ connections to the partnerships–each researcher had a personal connection to the professional practice. Together, these insights point to possibilities for the study of a researchers’ noticing practices, which we argue is integral to the analysis and design of future research partnerships and contribute to meaningful and care-full learning and research.

papers.title: Curricular Co-Design as Professional Development: Transformations in History Teachers’ Learning and Practice
papers.authors: Rachel S. Phillips, Shelton Daal, Angela Hardy, Abby Reisman, Emi Iwatani, Tiffany Leones
papers.design_stakeholders: Teachers; Students & Learners; Educational Researchers & Designers
papers.abstract: This paper reports on findings from a research-practice partnership that co-designed, piloted, and iterated on discussion -based world history lessons. Drawing on survey responses from design teachers (n=11) across two years, we identify that participation shaped three interconnected areas of teacher learning: (1) sustained shifts in instructional practices towards integrating clas sroom discussion, (2) growth in expertise and confidence as discussion facilitators, and (3) expanded professional identity and agency as mentors and leaders. In addition, the importance of collaboration and relationships w as strongly emphasized by all participants across both years, and analysis suggests that this was the key factor anchoring the co-design process.

papers.title: Connecting Teacher Sensemaking to Instructional Practice
papers.authors: Christina Kimmerling, Patricia Fuentes Acevedo, Rossella Santagata
papers.design_stakeholders: K-12 Teachers; Elementary Students & Children; Educational Researchers & Designers; School Administrators & Leaders
papers.abstract: A large body of research has identified core features of effective professional development (PD). Recently, scholars called for moving beyond core features to understand the mechanisms that support teacher learning. This study contributes to this aim by tracing teachers’ sensemaking of PD to their classroom implementation. In the context of a two-year PD initiative in mathematics, this study investigates the relationship between seven teachers’ perceptions of the PD and their instructional practice. Emergin g findings suggest three profiles of teachers’ conceptualizations of the PD approach to teaching and learning. How teachers conceptualized the PD was tightly aligned with what was observed in their practice. These findings have implications for theories of action to support teacher learning during PD. Objectives A substantial body of research has identified core features of effective professional development (PD) (e.g., Desimone, 2009; Darling- Hammond et al., 2017), recognizing the need for high -quality teacher learning experiences that change teachers’ practices and, in turn, improve student outcomes. Recently, this scholarship has been critiqued for overlooking the theories of action and mechanisms that support teacher learning and the highly contextualized nature of PD programs (Asterhan & Lefstein, 2024). Yet, h ow teachers take up PD learning is informed by their individual and collective sensemaking processes, and situational factors they face (Warner et al., 2022). Moreover, impactful professional learning often requires building teachers’ situation-specific decision- making skills, which is more complex than asking teachers to implement a set of procedures with fidelity (Kennedy, 2019). This suggests that the field needs more fine -grained analyses of how teachers make sense of PD focused on developing their decision-making skills and how that sensemaking is reflected in their instructional practices. This paper aims to serve that purpose. In our context, elementary school teachers participated in PD around Cognitively Guided Instruction (CGI; Carpenter et al., 2015), which aims to increase teacher knowledge of research on children’s mathematical thinking to inform their instructional decision- making. In this study, we ask: How do teachers conceptualize the PD’s approach to teaching and learning? How are teachers’ conceptualizations connected to their instructional practice? Implications from our findings can contribute to refining theorizations of how teachers learn and inform future PD designs that move beyond core features . Theoretical framework We draw on sensemaking theory (Weick et al., 2005), which recognizes sensemaking as an individual cognitive process and as socially situated. Teachers make sense of PD through an iterative, interpretive process of both talk and action; they begin to conceptualize PD learning within their existing understandings and practice, enact these new understandings in their teaching, which then leads to new conceptualizations of PD learning. At the same time, their sensemaking is influenced by the broader context in which they work, including their interactions with colleagues (Spillane et al., 2018) and the guidance they receive from school leaders (Coburn, 2005). Recent research on teacher sensemaking has highlighted its culturally situated (Liang et al., 2025) and socially constructed (Daniel et al., 2023) nature, suggesting that teachers make sense of PD through mental frameworks shaped by not only their district infrastructure but also broader cultural narratives surrounding mathematics teaching and learning. In this paper, participating teachers engaged in PD aimed at improving their knowledge-based reasoning and situation -specific decision -making skills. This type of PD recognizes that teachers must learn to enact particular practices contingent upon what their students understand and aims to develop teachers’ strategies and insights (Kennedy, 2019). In this study, we extend limited research that has investigated the link between teachers’ sensemaking of PD and their classroom decisions (Knapp & Peterson, 1995; Rimbey & Kucan, 2018; Warner et al., 2022), particularly around responsive mathematics teaching that builds on students’ emerging understandings.

papers.title: Productive Entanglements: Patterns of Partnership for Learning Technology Innovation
papers.authors: Alyssa Friend Wise
papers.design_stakeholders: Higher Education Instructors / Faculty; Students & Learners; Educational Researchers & Designers
papers.abstract: Impactful learning technology innovation doesn’t happen in isolation; it grows through relationships, among researchers, educators, students, technologists, designers, and institutional leaders. While some collaborations are carefully structured, others take root more organically, evolving to meet shifting needs and opportunities. In this keynote, Dr. Alyssa Wise explores how purposeful partnerships drive innovation across the technological, social, conceptual, and practical dimensions of learning, tracing three kinds of partnerships that have unfolded over the past decade in her work. Flexible Coupling articulates how institutional partnerships can leverage complementary strengths without becoming over-structured. In a longstanding collaboration with a university learning analytics service unit, in vivo studies of instructors’ analytics use informed both theoretical models of sense-making and applied tool design. Constructive Responsiveness describes how partnerships with educators can evolve around a shared object of inquiry when goals are not yet fully defined. In work with dental educators implementing an online reflection tool, the collaboration advanced from examinations of reflection quality to generate domain-specific insights into failure attribution and professional identity formation. Finally, Generative Pluralism characterizes interdisciplinary partnerships among researchers or co-designers where the goal is not convergence but conceptual creation. These collaborations embraced multiplicity, surfacing productive tensions, methodological bridges, and new vocabularies for imagining learning technologies. Together, these patterns illustrate partnerships as adaptable forms of collaboration, each suited to different problems, people, and purposes. This talk highlights how designing, studying, and sustaining learning with the support of technology can be supported by purposeful partnerships that bridge disciplines, organizations, and stakeholder perspectives. Bio: Dr. Alyssa Wise is Professor of Technology and Education at Vanderbilt University’s Peabody College, with a courtesy appointment in Computer Science in the College of Connected Computing. She also serves as Director of the LIVE Learning Innovation Incubator, Vanderbilt’s interdisciplinary hub for impactful learning technology innovation. Her research productively integrates tools of computational data science, theories of learning sciences and collaborative learning, and practices of human-centered design to build and study analytic and artificial intelligence systems that promote powerful learning for individuals situated in social context. She also conducts mixed-method investigations into how educational practices are being reshaped by new sources of data and the growing availability of new generative artificial intelligence capabilities. papers.abstract: In this talk, Dr. Ananda Marin traces her own history with the methodologies of community-based design research and co-design, linking what she has learned to key organizing constructs in this domain — matters of purpose, place, scale, impact, power, and equity. She shares axioms that were surfaced and re-membered while partnering alongside Indigenous families and most recently with improvisational jazz artists to design generative contexts that move toward collective thriving. From here, Dr. Marin reflects on how partnering can extend the field’s conceptualizations of learning in consequential ways. Sociocultural theories in the learning sciences have conceptualized learning as both the acquisition of practices as well as shifts in the use of cultural and cognitive resources for the purposes of meaning making. She suggests that these theories, which have played a pivotal role in her scholarly trajectory, can be expanded when we theorize alongside scholarship in Indigenous Studies and the work of Black and Indigenous learning scientists who have foregrounded the importance of kinship, relationality, respect, responsibility, reciprocity, and reverence. Turning to questions of human maturation, the talk will invite the learning sciences community to consider the field-wide consequences of theorizing from human centrism. Building with the work of scholars who have reminded us that sociality is organized through the interconnectedness of talk and interaction, as well as four years of conversations and art making with creative musicians, Dr. Marin proposes that wondering about and with sound making can expand our understandings of human learning in ways that are necessary for meeting the challenges we face as a society. Bio: Ananda Marin is associate professor in the Department of Education and faculty in American Indian Studies at the University of California, Los Angeles (Tongva territory). papers.title: “You Can Actually Do Something”: Shifts in High School Computer Science Teachers’ Conceptions of AI/ML Systems and Algorithmic Justice
papers.authors: Daniel J. Noh, Deborah A. Fields, Yasmin B. Kafai, Danaé Metaxa
papers.design_stakeholders: Science Teachers; Higher Education Instructors / Faculty; High School Students; Educational Researchers & Designers
papers.abstract: The recent proliferation of artificial intelligence and machine learning (AI/ML) systems highlights the need for all people to develop effective competencies to interact with and examine AI/ML systems. We study shifts in five experienced high school CS tea chers’ understanding of AI/ML systems after one year of participatory design, where they co- developed lessons on AI auditing, a systematic method to query AI/ML systems. Drawing on individual and group interviews, we found that teachers’ perspectives becam e more situated, grounding their understanding in everyday contexts; more critical, reflecting growing awareness of harms; and more agentic, highlighting possibilities for action. Further, across all three perspectives, teachers consistently framed algorit hmic justice through their role as educators, situating their concerns within their school communities. In the discussion, we consider the ways teachers’ perspectives shifted, how AI auditing can shape these shifts, and the implications of these findings on AI literacy for both teachers and students.

papers.title: Extending CSCL Affordances for Multilingual Classrooms: Teacher Perspectives on AI -Supported Collaboration
papers.authors: Pragati Maheshwary, Alina Guha, Shamya Karumbaiah
papers.design_stakeholders: Teachers; Students & Learners; Educational Researchers & Designers
papers.abstract: Multilingual classrooms add layers of complexity to collaboration: teachers rarely share every student’s home language, peers struggle to build common ground, and AI translation can miss linguistics nuance. We report findings from focus groups conducted with teachers of multilingual students to gauge their view on AI-supported collaboration across three collaboration pathways: student -student, teacher-student, and student-AI. Teachers welcomed real-time subtitling/translation to support comprehension and questioning, and lightweight tools that surface peers’ ideas via transcripts and highlights for clarifications. They were skeptical of in-class 1:1 student-AI partnering, citing risks to social connection, teacher workload, and scope creep. Using Jeong & Hmelo -Silver’s seven affordances as our lens, we identify where affordances blend within pathways, and where they need rethinking for multilingual equity. We translate teacher concerns into CSCL -aligned design adaptations and contribute extended versions of affordances to guide AI-integrated CSCL that is equitable for linguistically diverse classrooms.

papers.abstract: This study examines how Generative Artificial Intelligence (GenAI) can enhance learning design (LD) by exploring stakeholders’ preferences for five conceptual GenAI -based conversational agent functions —Authoring Assistant, Inspiration Hub, Design Feedback, Possibility Engine, and Ethics Guardian—adapted from the GenAI Speculative Functions Framework for LD. Proposed for the TRAILS teacher professional development platform, these functions target underexplored early phases of LD. Using a convergent mixed-methods design, 56 participants evaluated these functions, their support needs across design phases, and related opportunities and concerns. Findings reveal a two- pillar demand: creative inspiration, prioritized in the Investigation phase through the Inspiration Hub, and drafting efficiency, prioritized in the Authoring phase through the Authoring Assistant. The analysis revealed role- dependent value: experienced practitioners favored generative and creativity -oriented functions, while prospective teachers emp hasized diagnostic and feedback support. The Ethics Guardian emerged as an essential ambient safeguard. The study offers practical guidance for integrating human- centered GenAI into teacher professional development platforms and human-AI collaboration in LD.

papers.title: Prolepsis ’Till Infinity : Designing STEM Futures Through Play, Media, and Imagination
papers.authors: Kareem Edouard
papers.design_stakeholders: Higher Education Instructors / Faculty; Elementary Students & Children; Educational Researchers & Designers
papers.abstract: Prolepsis ’Till Infinity calls for an education that recognizes imagination as infrastructure. Dr. Kareem Edouard invites us to rethink how we build STEM spaces that honor culture, creativity, and care as the foundation of learning. His research at the ILLEST Lab challenges systems that reward compliance over curiosity, asking what becomes possible when play, storytelling, and design are treated as serious forms of knowledge, particularly for those most marginalized in STEAM, Black boys. Drawing from his design practices across learning, children’s media, and informal STEAM environments, Dr. Edouard examines how learners develop identity, agency, and understanding through participatory, culturally responsive experiences, highlighting key insights from the learning sciences. For example, in co-design projects with educators and youth, students engage in creative problem-solving and media production, positioning them as knowledge-makers whose ideas actively shape the learning environment. These collaborative partnerships demonstrate how purposeful engagement between educators, researchers, and communities fosters equitable and imaginative learning outcomes. Dr. Edouard envisions an educational future where play, imagination, and community are essential for liberation. This keynote invites us to build toward proleptic, possible, and connected futures already in motion, where creativity and meaning-making shape how we learn, teach, and thrive together. By treating play, imagination, and community as foundational, Dr. Edouard shows how learning and partnership are inseparable in designing educational spaces that cultivate curiosity, empowerment, and cultural relevance. Bio: Dr. Kareem Edouard is an Assistant Professor of Learning Technologies at Drexel University’s School of Education and Co-Director of the Informal Learning Linking Engineering, Science and Technology (ILLEST) Lab. His work explores how design, as a cultural, creative, and communal practice, intersects informal STEM education and children’s media to promote meaningful knowledge transfer across learning spaces. He examines how storytelling and co-creation cultivate belonging, purpose, and imagination in environments shaped by inequity. Through initiatives like the Black Male Animation Lab, Dr. Edouard redefines STEM as a space for cultural creation and collective care, empowering Black boys as designers, storytellers, and innovators. He focuses on Black boys because their experiences sharpen the stakes of equity work in STEM: to support those most marginalized by systemic exclusion is to test whether design can truly be liberatory. His liberatory co-design framework examines how collaborative creation transforms educational systems and expands equity and representation. In the Sneaker Lab, design, material science, and cultural expression are explored for their impact on identity and innovation. The GRIND initiative further investigates how sports, data, and technology can foster community-driven STEM engagement. Dr. Edouard integrates his co-liberty design framing vision into children’s STEM media. This approach combines his experience as a former music video and commercial director with his academic research. As Executive Producer of MayNERD’s Wild World of Science (YouTube Kids), Built From Scratch, and Creative Producer of Work It Out Wombats! papers.authors: Assyria A. Chambers, Carrie D. Allen
papers.design_stakeholders: Science Teachers; Educators & Practitioners; Elementary Students & Children; Educational Researchers & Designers; Community Members & Partners
papers.abstract: This short paper examines how two high school science teachers responded to invitations to position themselves as learners within an intergenerational program focused on environmental justice and data literacy, called E MPWER. Drawing on Holland et al.’s (1998) notion of figured worlds and Goodwin’s (1997) concept of interactional expertise, we traced how teachers negotiated identity and expertise within EMPWER as science educators, learners, and community members. A comparative case analysis showed that both teachers struggled with and resisted learner identities in different ways throughout the year-long project; however, one teacher was able to author a learn er identity more consistently, while the other resisted learner positioning. Our findings speak to how teacher learning identities are shaped by prior figured worlds of school science and social expectations associated with expertise. We argue that intergenerational designs should support teacher vulnerability, share authority, and create conditions for purposeful partnership that build collective agency across generations.

Symposium overview: Goal, structure, and highlights Teacher noticing, a core construct of teaching (König et al., 2022; Weston & Amador, 2023), broadly refers to teachers’ attention, interpretation, and decision-making of classroom interactions (Jacobs et al., 2010; Sherin et al., 2011). With the growing recognition of noticing as a core practice of teaching, there is an expanding line of research that seeks to understand how to support teachers’ learning to notice (Gaudin & Chaliès, 2015; Santagata et al., 2021). Prior research shows that well -designed professional learning opportunities can foster teachers’ learning to notice students’ thinking and teaching in interaction with student learning (e.g., Tekkumru-Kisa et al., 2018; Warshauer et al., 2023). As this knowledge has grown, it has prompted scholars to investigate what constitutes learning of noticing. In this symposium, we pause and ask: How do we think about what constitutes learning to notice? While efforts to support teachers’ learning to notice is evolving, less is understood about the mechanisms of teacher learning to notice (Walkoe & Luna, 2020). Some research investigates how video tagging tools focus teachers’ attention on particular features for further analysis (e.g., Walkoe et al., 2020). Others have considered how different kinds of video clips are selected and situated in professional learning and how collaborative analysis of particular types of clips can shape teachers’ learning (e.g ., Sherin & Dyer, 2017). Recent work has pointed to the role of discourse as a mechanism of teachers’ learning to notice (van Es et al., 2024). However, there is more to be understood about how teachers come to notice complexities of teaching and learning, and designs to better 2318 support that. Going beyond the descriptive account of noticing, in this symposium, our work collectively explores: What drives teachers’ learning to notice? All in all, the goal of our session is to examine different ways “learning to notice” has been conceptualized, and unpack the "mechanisms" that drive teachers’ learning to notice. Using multiple methods such as participatory design research approach and typological analysis of artifacts of teaching , these studies document shifts in teachers’ learning to notice, factors that contribute to teachers’ learning of noticing, and the design choices in facilitating teachers’ learning this complex practice. T he studies identify mechanisms of teachers’ learning to notice such as coding schemes that serve as epistemic mechanisms and collective sensemaking of the complexity of teaching through analysis of classroom videos in professional learning contexts. While some papers zoom in on noticing subprocesses that different video processes afford, others seek to understand teachers’ learning to notice when teachers worked on making links to socio-ecological issues relevant to their lives. Together, these papers advance theory on teachers’ learning to notice, while also considering the situated and relational features of teacher learning. At the same time, they offer methodological tools and frameworks to advance research on learning to notice across math and science. This 90-minute structured poster session will consist of a brief introduction to the session by the session co-chairs (5 min), followed by the interactive discussion of 10 posters (60 min), 10-minutes of commentary from a discussant, Adam Lefstein from the Hebrew University of Jerusalem, who brings expertise on teachers’ learning in professional development. We will conclude with 15-minutes of questions and discussion. The discussant will consider commonalities and differences across these studies, surfacing the considerations and tensions for supporting teachers’ learning to notice and mechanisms that drive learning of noticing among math and science teachers across the trajectory of teaching careers. Poster 1: Grounding prospective mathematics teacher noticing in socio- ecological issues: learning to notice in turbulent times Alf Coles, Sigal-Hava Rotem This study addresses the gap between current turbulent times and the seeming ‘objectivity’ of mathematics. We explore what constitutes prospective teachers (PTs) of mathematics learning to notice, during a time of war, the links they make to socio- ecological (Coles et al., 2024) issues of relevance to their lives, and the role of the mathematics teacher educator. Following van Es and Sherin (2002), we conceptualize teacher noticing as attending to and interpreting students' mathematical thinking. Following Mason (2002), we emphasize attention to event details for in -depth interpretation. We focus on “critical events” - moments when teachers notice students' mathematical thinking has potential for deepening. We also bring a notion of “authenticity”, which relates to teachers’ task design choices, and the extent to which tasks include social or ecological issues of relevance to their lives and the extent to which the mathematics includes opportunities for generalization. The study was conducted during wartime, heightening turbulence and data significance. We employed a case study methodology, to research a year- long problem-solving course in a B.Ed. mathematics program. The course focused on a reform in mathematics educati on emphasizing "mathematics in everyday life" and incorporated two design-teach-reflect cycles where participants: 1) photographed and discussed socio- ecological concerns (photovoice method); 2) designed mathematical tasks; and 3) taught and reflected on critical events they identified. Among 23 participants, we focus on Nadin (Bedouin community member) as an illustrative case. Our analysis examines shifts in her articulation of event details, interpretations, the social- ecological issue's authenticity and the role of the teacher educator. The analysis revealed three key findings. First, Nadin was able to bring a highly relevant socio-ecological issue to her classroom, surfacing deeply held beliefs and engaging with students about their beliefs. Secondly, Nadin wrote in great detail and we observed subtle and shifting relationships between detail and interpretation in her accounts, which is of significance to how noticing might be supported. Thirdly, in examining the role of the teacher educator, we uncover the significance of the way space w as offered on the course for PTs to discuss and work on socio-ecological issues of relevance to their lives. Through examining the particulars of one case, our findings offer an example of how teacher preparation, during a time of war, can still support the noticing of prospective teachers, in connecting mathematics to relevant socio-ecological issues. We tentati vely point to a role for prospective teachers’ sharing stories from their lives, and to the power of engaging in design-teach-reflect cycles, in supporting their noticing. 2319 Poster 2: Learning to notice students’ strengths: Coding schemes as epistemic mechanisms in design-based teacher education Thorsten Scheiner This investigation addresses a critical challenge in teacher education: developing teachers’ capacity to recognize and build upon students’ strengths rather than defaulting to deficit -based orientations. While research demonstrates that strength -based noticing practices foster more equitable learning environments (Louie et al., 2021), significant gaps remain in understanding the mechanisms through which teachers develop these sophisticated ways of seeing. This study examines how structured coding schemes function as epistemic tools that bridge cognitive and socio- cultural dimensions of professional learning, offering insights into design -based approaches for transforming teacher noticing practices. The study advances an integrated framework synthesizing professional noticing theory, transformative learning mechanisms, and frame analysis. Professional noticing encompasses attending to critical aspects of student reasoning, interpreting student thinking, and deciding how to respond instructionally (Jacobs et al., 2010). Frame analysis illuminates how interpretive schemas shape what teachers notice and value in student work (Sherin & Russ, 2014). Transformative learning theory provides mechanisms for frame shifting through critical reflection and conscious reorientation of perspective (Mezirow, 2000). The framework positions coding schemes as mediating artifacts that operationalize frame orientations while scaffolding transformative professional development through the dynamic interplay of cognitive restructuring and socio-cultural meaning-making. This exploratory study used a participatory design research approach within an intensive professional learning context. Prospective teachers engaged in three iterative cycles of analysis using a structured coding scheme distinguishing deficit-based, strength-based, and uncommitted orientations across noticing practices. Each iteration incorporated fine -grained examination of transformative mechanisms through structured reflective prompts targeting frame awareness, conscious reframing, and progressive integr ation. Data collection utilized standardized noticing tasks, complemented by reflective journals documenting participants’ evolving interpretive frameworks. Analysis combined quantitative tracking of orientation patterns with qualitative mapping of transformative processes. Analysis revealed three primary mechanisms driving teachers’ learning to notice strengths. First, epistemic visibility emerged through the coding scheme’s dual function as analytical tool and pedagogical scaffold, rendering implicit interpretive frames explicit and actionable. Participants demonstrated systematic shifts from deficit- based toward strength- based noticing practices. Second, collaborative meaning -making facilitated frame shifting through structured protocols that created social spaces for negot iating alternative interpretations of student thinking. Third, reflective reframing supported progressive integration of strength-based orientations through systematic comparisons of deficit-based and asset-oriented perspectives. The iterative design revealed how these mechanisms operated synergistically, with cognitive restructuring mediated by socio-cultural practices of professional discourse and collective analysis. The findings illuminate coding schemes as powerful epistemic mechanisms that render interpretive frames both visible and actionable in teacher education. By functioning simultaneously as analytical tools and pedagogical scaffolds, structured coding schemes support the cognitive work of frame identification while creating social spaces for collaborative meaning -making. This dual functionality bridges individual cognitive transformation and collective professional development, revealing how participatory desi gn research can systematically develop teachers’ capacity for strength- based noticing. The study contributes methodological insights for designing equity- oriented professional learning experiences that leverage the sophisticated interplay between cognitive and socio-cultural dimensions of transformative practice. Poster 3: From noticing to navigating: Pre-service teachers' expansive sensemaking in science instruction Heather Johnson, Tara Barnhart Teacher noticing—especially of student thinking—has become central in teacher education research (Weston & Amador, 2023). Noticing can be cultivated during teacher education (van Es, 2011), but connecting it to student - centered instruction requires space to reflect on the interplay between interpretations, decisions, and institutional contexts (Schwartz et al., 2021). In this study, we explore what pre -service teachers apply from their noticing of expansive sensemaking in videos of accomplished teachers to video analysis tasks in which PSTs design and enact student-centered science experiences. We ground this study in previous work that theorizes that noticing is a learnable skill (van Es, 2011) and that learning to notice is a social activity that takes place when individuals who 2320 share a common interest collaboratively engage with tools and tasks intrinsic to their professional context (Barnhart, 2021). We ground this study in previous work that theorizes that noticing is a learnable skill (van Es, 2011) and that learning to notice is a social activity that takes place when individuals who share a common interest collaboratively engage with tools and tasks intrinsic to their professional context (Barnhart, 2021). We conducted a typological analysis (Miles et al., 2014) of written coursework and fieldwork from PSTs enrolled in a secondary methods course prior to student teaching. Data included their planning documents, video analysis templates, and written reflections for four video tasks: one around an accomplished teacher’s classroom and three around their own teaching. Analysis of what teachers noticed in their own and others’ videos was guided by the Expansive Sensemaking framework (Bautista & Davis, 2024). By applying this framework, the study illuminates how PSTs bridge noticing of student thinking with enacting responsive science teaching. Accomplished teacher video When analyzing videos of accomplished teachers, PSTs attended to how classroom culture shaped student participation. They noticed who was given access to share ideas publicly, how ideas were taken up by the teacher and peers, and how norms and structure supported collaborative learning. PST Videos In their own lesson planning, PSTs designed inclusive tasks that positioned students as epistemic agents and included multimodal participation strategies. They also aimed to expand what "counts" as science and promote diverse ways of knowing. However, enac ting these plans surfaced asset -oriented, equity- oriented, and participation-oriented challenges. Though each PST intended to empower students, their enactments did not always lead to the anticipated engagement. These realizations revealed a gap between in tention and impact, especially in balancing student agency with institutional constraints such as pacing guides and test preparation. Equity-related challenges emerged as PSTs attempted to make lessons culturally relevant. Some PSTs reflected on how their examples did not resonate as expected. PSTs also identified challenges in fostering student-to-student interactions. They reflected on classroom dynamics, noting the need for psychological safety and clearer norms. Importantly, they attributed participation issues to instructional design, not student deficits—demonstrating asset - oriented thinking. Prior work on noticing student thinking has presumed that teachers will apply what they learn to notice in coursework to their own practice. These results support this hypothesis while also highlighting the challenges of responsive instruction and affirming the importance of reflection and collaboration in preparing teachers to sustain asset-based noticing through opportunities to analyze their own artifacts of practice and contribute to the research base for preparing teachers to teach responsively in diverse, authentic contexts. Poster 4: Noticing in college mathematics: Development of noticing discourse in a video-based professional development Patricia Fuentes Acevedo, Christina Kimmerling, Rossella Santagata, Alessandra Pantano, Roberto Pelayo College mathematics classrooms can be marginalizing spaces, particularly for women and students of color (Riegle-Crumb & King, 2010). Persistent inequalities motivate the call for more responsive and equity- oriented college teaching. Teacher noticing is at the core of responsive teaching, with substantial research primarily conducted in K-12 settings (Santagata et al., 2021). Building on K-12 evidence, we developed and tested a video- based curriculum for instructors and graduate and undergraduate teaching a ssistants that fostered expansive noticing of students' mathematical thinking and participation (Santagata et al., 2025). Recent work has emerged suggesting that evidence of learning to notice includes uptaking a particular form of discourse (van Es et al. , 2024). We seek to unpack the relationship between participants' discourse during PD sessions and observed changes in the groups' noticing. We ask: What are the features of participants’ discourse around video- based noticing tasks? Except for a few characterizations of exemplary cases (e.g., Louie et al., 2021), little is known about how educators can learn to notice for equity. We adopt a situative perspective on teacher learning (Borko et al., 2000) and draw on van Es et al.’s (2024) work on learning to notice by engaging in discourse-rich spaces where educators collectively make sense of instruction. Their model characterizes discourse practices that enable participants to learn how to attend to and interpret student thinking. We extend this to student participation. The authors define features of generative noticing for the different purposes that the discourse practices serve. 2321 Participants include three college instructors, five graduate and four undergraduate assistants. They engaged in whole and small group discussions around video clips during four PD sessions. For this study, we selected all segments where small groups discussed noticing prompts after watching a video clip (20 in total) and subsequent whole-group discussions. We portioned the transcribed data into conversational turns and idea units and created analytical memos. Finally, two of us deductively coded the data using van Es et al.'s (2024) features of noticing discourse (Table 1), allowing for emergent codes as well. Table 1 Features of Noticing Discourse Feature of a Noticing Discourse Definition of Feature Negotiating noteworthy phenomena A collection of discursive practices that intend to support attending activity, defining what is and is not worthy of attention, and supports learning to decide what to call out and what to ignore. Problematizing and puzzling over objects of teaching and learning A collection of discursive practices that intend to support interpreting and sense-making activity, which is adopting an inquiry stance toward objects of focus, such as offering conflicting viewpoints of what is observed or grappling over intent and meaning. Creating moments for further inquiry of objects of attention A collection of discursive practices that intend to support shaping interactions to gather more information for further attending and interpreting. Being accountable to evidence A collection of discursive practices that intend to support attending and interpreting activity by supporting one’s claims with concrete observations, using artifacts of teaching and learning to advance an idea, and elaborating one’s ideas with more specific and precise explanations. Positioning students’ ideas and actions as resources in learning A collection of discursive practices that intend to support attending, interpreting, and shaping activity by requiring an openness to seeing what might appear as mundane, or correct/incorrect, as something important and meaningful that can be figured out and used toward understanding.
