Participants discussed aspects related to student thinking and participation, primarily focusing on problematizing objects of teaching observed in the clips, and less frequently engaging in negotiation of noteworthy phenomena. An emergent and predominant feature of their noticing discourse was making connections to their own experiences, which included extending the observed episode to past or potential future teaching scenarios. Additionally, although there is little evidence of positioning students' ideas as resources, participants maintained an asset-based perspective as required by the facilitators. The identified features in our data provide evidence that PD video prompts supported productive noticing discourse among participants and shed light on the processes through which their collective sensemaking contributed to their learning to notice. Our findings reflect the PD emphasis on noticing as multidimensional and are encouraging as they suggest tangible implications for participants' future instruction. This work contributes to the limited literature on how mechanisms for learning to notice take place at the college level. Poster 5: Attending, interpreting, and shaping: How varied ways of working with video connect with subprocesses of teacher noticing Jennifer Richards, Miriam Sherin, Sarah Larison 2322 Research has documented how video- based environments can provide rich opportunities for teachers’ learning, including learning to notice student thinking (e.g., Gaudin & Chaliès, 2015; Santagata et al., 2021). Further, advancements in video-related technology have expanded how teachers can engage with video — moving beyond watching and discussing videos to filming and editing their own clips. In this poster, we extend a prior exploration of how teachers noticed student thinking as they engaged in multiple video processes (Richards & Sherin, 2025) by specifying ways in which these video processes map onto posited subprocesses of teacher noticing, contributing to understandings of potential drivers for noticing. The framework we animate specifies several interrelated subprocesses of teacher noticing — attending, interpreting, and shaping (van Es & Sherin, 2021). “Attending” refers to what teachers focus on in classrooms, acknowledging that humans cannot pay attention to everything. “Interpreting” refers to how teachers reason about classroom events. “Shaping” refers to what teachers do in order to support their noticing during or after instruction. While these subprocesses dynamically interact with and influence one another, we think they also reflect important opportunities for learning in their own right. Data come from three iterations of an online, video- based course for early elementary teachers in the United States on mathematical argumentation (Lomax et al., 2017). Twenty -nine in-service teachers participated in the course, in which they engaged in four sequential video processes — recording video in their own classrooms, watching and reflecting on the video, editing clips to share in the course, and interacting with others around their clips. Data sources included interviews and think- alouds with teachers about these video processes and video annotations on clips. Our prior analysis explored the affordances and constraints of each video process for teachers’ noticing of student thinking (Richards & Sherin, 2025). Here, we build on this prior analysis to characterize the noticing subprocesses that different video processes seemed to afford. When teachers recorded video in their classrooms, all three noticing subprocesses seemed to be in play as teachers iteratively focused on student ideas that required attention, sought to make sense of them in real time, and shaped interactions to test working interpretations and gather more information. Watching and reflecting on the video tended to afford continued “interpreting” and “shaping,” as teachers primarily used the video as a tool to make sense of and gain more evidence about student ideas that had intrigued them. Editing clips , in contrast, afforded “attending” with some further “interpreting” as teachers selectively identified moments of student thinking to make visible to colleagues. Finally, when interacting with others around clips , all three subprocesses were again in play as teachers highlighted specific student ideas to consider, discussed varied interpretations, and at times reviewed the video to seek more information. These findings suggest potential implications for targeted video-based designs to facilitate specific noticing subprocesses (e.g., cultivating teachers’ attending by providing multiple opportunities to edit clips). Further research could deepen understandings of how engaging with varied sequences of video processes drives teachers’ learning to notice over time. Poster 6: Developing professional vision through negotiating understanding of videorecorded whole-class talks in mathematics Håvard Johnsrud Evang, Inga Staal Jenset Supporting teacher candidates’ development of ambitious and equitable mathematics teaching is a key challenge in teacher education (Louie, 2018) and requires that teachers adapt their instruction in response to students’ content-specific ideas and ways of participating in the talk (Jacobs & Empson, 2016). Prior research has studied this situation -specific competence through concepts such as ‘noticing of students strengths’ (Jilk, 2016) and ‘equitable noticing’ (Louie, 2018) demonstrating how video- anchored activities may support candidates developing this capacity (Jenset et al., 2024). Building on a recent socio- cultural turn in noticing research (Scheiner et al., 2026), the present study extends this work by investigating how teacher candidates’ professional vision develops as they engage in discussions of video-recorded mathematical classroom talk in Grade 8 settings. This study draws on Goodwin’s (1994) concept of professional vision, defined as the ability to construct relevant knowledge through socio-historically developed practices of highlighting and coding. This framework is used to examine how teacher candidates interpret students’ utterances and actions within recorded episodes of classroom discourse. Adopting a socio- cultural perspective, the study assumes that cultural frames —that is, culturally and historically shaped interpretive lenses regarding school mathe matics, mathematical teaching, and learning (Goffman, 1974; Scheiner, 2021) —function as mediational means that shape these practices. Consequently, the negotiation and adaptation of cultural frames to make sense of students’ mathematical contributions are understood as mechanisms that drive the development of teachers’ professional vision. The study investigates how video- anchored discussions contribute to the development of mathematics teacher candidates’ professional vision. Data consists of approximately 30 hours of video recordings from five 2323 seminars integrated into an existing mathematics-didactics course across one academic year (24 candidates). The seminars were structured to progressively broaden candidates’ highlighting and coding practices, with the goal of fostering increased attention to students’ diverse mathematical reasoning and forms of participation. Candidates’ discussions were scaffolded through an observation rubric and prompts encouraging them to focus on the qualities of students’ contributions, rather than on perceived defici encies or errors. Through reflective thematic and discourse analysis, the study examines how these practices evolved over time and how cultural frames informed candidates’ interpretations of students’ mathematical work. The study yielded three insights into candidates’ professional vision development: (i) a shift from “glossy” to complex understanding of students’ participation, (ii) an expanded understanding of students’ multiple mathematical competencies, and (iii) pers istent privileging of an authoritative view on valuable mathematical outcomes. Video-anchored discussions supported candidates develop richer framing of students as valuable resources in building mathematical knowledge. However, persistent cultural frames constrained candidates’ appreciation of student’s mathematical thinking (Louie, 2018) highlighting the need for teacher education to explicitly challenge these frames to support the development of professional vision for ambitious and equitable teaching. Poster 7: Teacher-designed cases as a tool to support pre-service teacher noticing Tracy E. Dobie, Liza Escobar Aquino, Bailey N. Ondricek, Raven Burton, Angela Warnock Extensive research illustrates the value of supporting teachers’ noticing of student thinking (e.g., Jacobs et al., 2010). We respond to the call for more research that investigates learning to notice from an equity frame (van Es et al., 2017) by examining cases (Shulman, 1992) as a tool to support pre-service teachers’ noticing for equity. Teacher noticing is commonly described as having three components – attending, interpreting, and responding (Jacobs et al., 2010). Research on noticing for equity explores various facets of this construct including noticing of individual student histories, anti-deficit discourses, and status and positioning (Louie et al., 2021; van Es et al., 2017). Challenges include supporting pre -service teachers (PSTs) to attend to individual students’ participation (Wager, 2014) and notice more critical dimensions of equity (Graham & Roth McDuffie, 2023). Cases are written narratives describing authentic and complex teaching situations (Shulman, 1992) that can be intentionally designed to investigate certain themes (Dobie et al., 2024). We use cases to help PSTs grapple with the challenges of enacting equitable mathematics and science instruction —or leveraging students’ multiple strengths, honoring students’ diverse lived experiences, dismantling classroom power and status hierarchies, and challenging dominant perspectives (e.g., Aguirre et al., 2013). We partnered with local U.S. teachers, who designed cases exploring themes such as assumptions about multilingual students, inequitable group dynamics, and school structures that disadvantage minoritized students (Dobie et al., 2024). Data include PSTs’ written responses (N=1,036; 224 PSTs) to prompts for six cases that were implemented 2 -4 times each in an elementary math or science methods course. Our team deductively and inductively developed a coding scheme (Miles et al., 2014) capturing a) case details (what PSTs attended to), b) equity-oriented interpretations (PSTs’ reasoning), and c) solutions (ideas about how to respond). Two coders coded every response, and discrepancies were resolved. We highlight three findings: 1) Cases support PSTs to attend to details about students and their actions, 2) Cases and prompts can be designed to support PSTs to make wide-ranging equity-oriented interpretations, and 3) Case prompts elicit solutions that include in-the-moment actions, changes for future instruction, and advocacy- based actions including gathering data and research. We offer frequency counts across the dataset, PST quotes, and case comparisons. As an example, we explore how a subtle difference in prompts influenced PSTs’ breadth of interpretations in two similar cases focused on group dynamics: In one case, 83% of responses offering equity- oriented interpretations focused on a general imbalance in group dynamics; in the other, PSTs reasoned about a general imbalance in group dynamics (39%), as well as the roles of friendship (46%), language (43%), prior school experiences (24%), and gender (15%). Cases have significant potential for supporting PSTs’ noticing for equity including details of specific students’ participation (Wager, 2014) and more critical dimensions of equity (Graham & Roth McDuffie, 2023). Questions remain about trajectories of noticing over time and the impact of noticing in cases on noticing in classrooms. 2324 Poster 8: Accounting for teacher learning in a video club: Learning a noticing discourse Miray Tekkumru-Kisa, Elizabeth van Es, Melissa Luna Video-based professional development has been shown to support mathematics and science teachers’ learning to notice for responsive and equitable instruction (Santagata et al., 2021). This vision of teaching calls on teachers to attend to the substantive contributions students make toward the learning goals and adopt an inquiry stance to validate and interpret student thinking to position students’ ideas as resources for their own and others’ learning. What is less understood is how and why these settings support teacher learning. Thus, we ask what might be mechanisms of teacher learning to notice in the context of video- based professional development centered on noticing student thinking? We conceptualize video-based professional development as complex activity systems in which the video clips, the norms for participation, and the cultural and historical practices of professional development all coordinate to influence teachers’ opportunities to learn in these settings (Barnhart, 2021). Our research is informed by an often overlooked feature of complex activity systems of professional development that may be supporting teachers’ learning to notice: the nature of talk that takes place in video- based professional learning contexts. Professional discourse plays a central role in teacher learning (Lefstein et al., 2020), yet less is known about the character of talk that results in teachers’ learning to notice. Data include video recordings and transcripts from two video clubs to support teachers to learn to notice the complexity of teacher -student learning interactions. Video club facilitators prompted teachers to explore the details of student thinking, potential interpretations of their ideas, in relation to teaching. One video club included nine 4th and 5th grade mathematics teachers that met ten times for about one hour over the academic year, approximately once a month. The second video club focused on supporting six middle school science teachers’ learning to notice student thinking and teaching in seven hour -long sessions throughout an academic year. We analyzed an early and late video club meeting for both groups to identify features of a noticing discourse that were present in each meeting (van Es et al., 2024; Table 1). To account for teachers’ learning a noticing discourse, we coded the video club data and wrote analytic memos for evidence and disconfirming evidence of the noticing discourse features, also noting who enacted the talk moves that represented the noticing discourse features. Findings show that both groups shifted in their enactment of a noticing discourse over time. Both groups shifting their talk to highlight more ideas represented in the clips as worthwhile for noticing (i.e., negotiating noteworthy phenomena), pursue these ideas as objects of inquiry for the group to analyze (i.e., creating moments for further inquiry), anchor their analyses of student thinking in classroom evidence (i.e., being accountable to evidence), and demonstrate an openness to explore students’ ideas as resources for learning. Moreover, teachers demonstrated an accountability to the learning community by enacting talk that balanced respecting and honoring teachers' practice represented in the video, while also pressing on what was going on to further understand student thinking and teaching. This finding offers additional insights into features of talk that are enacted to support teachers’ learning to notice, which we argue represents the importance of collective sensemaking as a critical component of noticing discourse in professional learning. Looking across both video-clubs, this study provides evidence for a noticing discourse as key to teachers’ learning to notice, and has implications for design features, such as creating moments for further inquiry, to make video club discourse generative for teacher learning. Poster 9: Science teachers’ learning to notice expansively Miray Tekkumru-Kisa, Jennifer Richards There is growing agreement in the field that teacher noticing is critical in ambitious forms of teaching that center students (König et al., 2022; Weston & Amador, 2023). Joining other scholars in exploring the complexities of noticing (e.g., van Es et al., 2022), our ongoing work considers the multidimensionality of teachers' noticing for facilitating students’ sensemaking in science classrooms (Tekkumru- Kisa & Richards, 2025). However, there is much to learn about what supports teachers to develop multidimensional noticing practices. In this study, we explored whether a group of science teachers shifted their noticing through engaging in a specific video- based professional learning (PL) design. Briefly, with multidimensional noticing, we bring together key threads from prior work on noticing, such as the importance of noticing student thinking (e.g., Jacobs et al., 2010) as well as pedagogy connected to student thinking (e.g., Tekkumru-Kisa & Stein, 2015), and working toward anti -deficit ways of noticing disciplines and 2325 students (e.g., Louie et al., 2021). Taking a situative perspective on teacher learning (Borko et al., 2000), which emphasizes learning through interaction in activity systems, we sought to embody these noticing practices in PL tools and routines (Greeno, 2006; Sandoval, 2014). This study was conducted within the context of an NSF -funded project, Implementing Practices of Ambitious Teaching for Complex Assessment Tasks (IMPACT). IMPACT PL is centered around the implementation of science performance assessments, providing a laboratory for teachers to work with students’ ideas. Five 8th -grade science teachers from different schools in a large urban district in the United States participated. Teachers engaged in collaborative analysis of performance assessment video clips intentional ly selected to highlight relations between student thinking and ambitious teaching principles (Windschitl et al., 2018) and were consistently asked to focus first on student thinking, then aspects of teaching that seemed to support student thinking. To explore changes in teachers’ noticing, we analyzed teachers’ baseline and exit interviews during which they were asked to share what they noticed and how they might respond to events in a ~7- minute video clip. We separated teachers’ interview transcripts into idea units and coded each idea unit with respect to teachers’ noticing, using the multidimensional noticing framework as an analytical lens (Tekkumru- Kisa & Richards, 2025). At the end of the IMPACT PL, there was growing attention to student thinking among all five teachers. When they noticed student thinking, they began to see what students were saying or appeared to be thinking as valuable, taking an asset-based frame. Moreover, in the exit interviews, teachers focused more on ways to work with students' ideas as opposed to only correcting those ideas. In short, the video- based PL tools and routines seemed to hold promise for supporting shifts in multiple dimensions of teache rs’ noticing in concert with each other. Future research can elaborate on the dynamics of teachers’ noticing practices throughout the PL, particularly how teachers iterated among noticing student thinking and pedagogy. Poster 10: A learning to notice for equity framework Jose Mendez, Elizabeth A. van Es Descriptive accounts of teachers’ noticing for equity contribute to theorizing the complexity of teachers’ in the moment attention and sensemaking to advance responsive and equitable instruction (e.g. Louie et al., 2021; van Es et al., 2022). What is less understood is how teachers learn to notice for equity. Teacher noticing for equity is characterized by teachers ’ attention to multiple dimensions of the classroom environment including linguistic resources, power dynamics, relational interactions, social i dentities, and sociopolitical narratives (van Es et al., 2022). We theorize that learning to attend to equity involves the ability to name these classroom dynamics and see them as interconnected (e.g., Rubin & van Es, 2025). The second dimension involves the development of an interpretive practice , which entails continuously engaging with evidence to better understand and support students’ needs (Sherin & Russ, 2017). The third dimension involves embodied engagement , drawing on recent noticing-as-embodied c onceptualizations that highlight the nuanced and multi -sensory aspects of noticing (Mason, 2002; Scheiner, 2021). Embodied engagement of one’s noticing includes both actions, such as shaping, to position oneself to notice more expansively, and choosing to ignore particular aspects of classroom interactions that are less generative for student learning (Louie et al., 2021; van Es et al., 2022). Embodied engagement that disrupts inequities is a reflection of developing one’s noticing for equity (Scheiner, 2021). We qualitatively analyzed data from a research practice partnership that explored whether and how co - designing and analyzing practical measurement data could provoke a mathematics teacher’s learning to notice for equity (Mendez & van Es, 2025). We adopt sociopolitical perspectives to theorize teachers’ learning to notice as tied to their personal histories and the power -laden environments they teach in (Louie et al., 2021). We also theorize learning as a progression that can support teachers and teacher educators formatively documenting changes in teachers’ noticing over time (e.g., van Es, 2011). Data included transcripts of co- design meetings to develop a survey as a form of practical measurement data and data discussions of iterative cycles of survey implementation. This poster will present a framework for learning to notice for equity that consists of four levels. Each level is characterized by shifts in noticing along the dimensions of attending to equity, interpretive practice, and embodied engagement. As the case study teacher shifted in his noticing for equity, he came to see noticing as multidimensional and integrated, shifting frames to interpret events from an asset- and evidence-based stance. He also made connections to his practice and considered how to disrupt persistent inequities to create a responsive classroom through shaping noticing interactions focused on students’ ideas and patterns of participation. This framework moves from descriptive accounts of teacher noticing for equity to characterize the prog ression of learning to noticing from an equity lens over time. In doing so, this tool offers a framework to study teachers’ 2326 learning to notice for equity, while also providing guidance for designing experiences to support teachers’ expansive noticing. papers.authors: Kimberly Erickson, Kyle Dunbar, Kelly Mills
papers.design_stakeholders: Science Teachers; Educators & Practitioners; Students & Learners; Educational Researchers & Designers; Community Members & Partners; Domain Experts & Technologists; School Administrators & Leaders
papers.abstract: We describe how nine classroom teachers designed and reflected on assessment practices for measuring critical thinking as part of a larger district Portrait of a Graduate program. Instead of developing a single assessment approach, teachers created a set of design principles that could be used flexibly by other classroom teachers seeking to assess students’ critical thinking. Our findings indicate the importance of grounding assessment of complex, transferable skills in classroom practices and student artifacts.

papers.title: How Teachers Learn by Designing AI-Ethics Scenarios Using an LLM-Supported Authoring Tool
papers.authors: Jeanhee Lee, Sieun Park, Yue Wang, Kyuwon Kim, Yeji Ko, Hyo-Jeong So
papers.design_stakeholders: Science Teachers; Students & Learners; Community Members & Partners
papers.abstract: This study investigates how teachers learn by designing AI ethics scenarios using a customized LLM-supported authoring tool. Seventeen pre - and in-service teachers engaged in dilemma-based scenario design within the Learning by Design framework through int eractive dialogue with the LLM. Data from prompt logs, think- aloud sessions, surveys, interviews, and reflections revealed diverse prompting patterns. Teachers alternated between seeking guidance and generating, evaluating, and refining ideas. Through this process, they developed a deeper understanding of AI ethics, greater confidence, and more student -centered perspectives, viewing AI as a collaborative design partner. The findings suggest that iterative prompting and scenario design provide an effective pathway for teacher learning and highlight the potential of LLM-supported environments for professional growth in AI-integrated education.

papers.title: Youth Climate Storytelling as Transformative Learning: A Scoping Review of Designs, Contexts, and Digital Practices
papers.authors: Asli Sezen-Barrie, Yuxi Huang
papers.design_stakeholders: Teachers; Youth & Adolescents; Educational Researchers & Designers; Community Members & Partners
papers.abstract: This scoping review synthesizes 30 peer -reviewed studies (2014– 2024) on youth storytelling in climate change education, illuminating how storytelling approaches foster transformative climate change learning. Findings reveal that storytelling functions as relational infrastructure while relating climate complexity into lived experience, cultivating eco - emotional awareness and agency, and sustaining Indigenous and community knowledge. Across formal and informal settings, educators and youth partnered to co- create stories that merged data, emotion, and cultural meaning. Digital tools such as participatory video, multimedia, and augmented reality expanded access and impact but also raised questions of equity and authorship. By mapping designs, scaffolds, and digital practices, the review offers design implications for research -practice partnerships that nurture belonging, imagination, and civic participation through climate storytelling. The need and the goal As the climate crisis intensifies, educators face an urgent challenge: how to cultivate young people’s capacity to understand, feel, and act in relation to a rapidly changing world. Traditional climate change education often privileges scientific facts, da ta, and predictive models but rarely engages the emotional, cultural, and ethical dimensions necessary for sustained transformation (Walsh, 2022 ). Transformative climate change education reframes learning as an ethical, relational, and action -oriented process that centers justice, hope, and collective capacity (Leite, 2024; Sezen -Barrie et al., 2025). Within this reframing, storytelling emerges as a powerful pedagogical and epistemological approach that binds scientific sense-making with identity, emotion, culture, and community (Gottschall, 2012). Storytelling makes climate data meaningful, futures imaginable, and collective agency possible (Bentz & O’Brien, 2019; Bloomfield, 2024). It allows youth to relate abstract climate concepts into local experiences and shared narratives of resilience, repositioning them as authors of change rather than passive recipients of information. Yet, despite growing interest, the field lacks a compr ehensive synthesis of how storytelling is designed, scaffolded, and studied across learning contexts. Moreover, as digita l media and participatory technologies proliferate from personal storytelling platforms to augmented reality, the need for design frameworks that ensure equity, authenticity, and purpose becomes more pressing. This review addresses a central gap in the learning sciences: the absence of an integrated understanding of how storytelling, across diverse designs, pedagogical functions, and digital practices, shapes transformative climate learning. While storytelling is increasingly recognized as a catalyst for connection, agency, and inclusion, its implementation remains fragmented across specific areas of social science research. Drawing on 30 peer - reviewed studies (2014– 2024), this scoping review was guided by the following research questions: (1) What research designs and learning contexts characterize studies on youth storytelling in climate change education? (2) How do storytelling function and are scaffolded to support climate change education? (3) In what ways do digital tools and frameworks support engaging in storytelling related to climate change? Conceptual framework: Storytelling in climate change education “We are the authors of our lives. We compose our self -narratives and we are composed by them” (Gottschall, 2012, p. 147). In The Storytelling Animal: How Stories Make Us Human, Gottschall (2012) argues that stories are not only how we communicate experiences but also how we construct meaning, identity, and belonging. Storytelling, the structuring and sharing of lived or imagined experiences through narrative form, is thus foundational to human cognition, culture, and communication (Gottschall, 2012). Within education, storytelling functions as both an epistemological and pedagogical approach : a way of knowing the world and of teaching it. In climate change education, it extends beyond communication to become a transformative learning practice , weaving scientific understanding with emotional relations, ethical inquiry, and socio-cultural meaning. Mainstream climate change education often privileges technocratic and positivist paradigms, emphasizing data, models, and prediction (Krasny & Schneider, 2021). While such approaches are essential for understanding biophysical mechanisms, they rarely foste r the emotional, ethical, or civic engagement necessary 1877 for meaningful transformation. Storytelling intervenes by humanizing climate knowledge while translating complex systems into situated experiences and relationships. By embedding abstract concepts in personal or community narratives, it deepens comprehension and fosters empathy (Bloomfield , 2024). In this sense, stories “relocalize” climate learning, situating it within histories of place, culture, and justice rather than abstract global metrics. Storytelling aligns with transformative climate change education frameworks (Sezen-Barrie et al., 2025; Leite, 2024), which highlights attention to learning across epistemologies and improving emotional well -being. Climate stories , especially those from marginalized or Indigenous communities , which operates as counter- hegemonic discourses that challenge dominant narratives of progress and environmental relationships (Leite, 2024; Tuck, McKenzie, & McCoy, 2014). These narratives open epistemic space for lear ners to question assumptions about development, responsibility, and belonging in the Anthropocene. Through engagement with such stories, learners cultivate more pluralistic and justice -oriented understandings of socio- ecological systems. Indigenous storytelling traditions exemplify this transformative potential. In many Indigenous epistemologies, story is both method and ethic: a means of transmitting knowledge and sustaining reciprocal relationships among humans, nonhumans, and the land (Whyte, 2017). Integrating Indigenous storytelling into climate curricula enacts decolonial praxis, repositioning learners as participants in relational webs of care rather than as detached observers of climate data (Tuck et al., 2014). Empirical research reinforces the pedagogical value of storytelling. Pahl et al. (2019) found that climate messages conveyed through stories were significantly more effective at fostering emotional engagement and pro- environmental intentions than statistical presentations. Educational research further shows that storytelling supports identity work: when students create or analyze stories about climate change through oral narratives, filmmaking, or digital media, they articulate their roles, values, and hopes within broader ecological systems (Leite, 2024). In sum, storytelling is far more than a communication tool; it is a transformative framework for learning. It bridges the cognitive, affective, and ethical domains —helping learners think, feel, and act with relational awareness. By integrating storytelling into climate change education, educators can nurture imagination, agency, and care, cultivating learners who are not only informed about the planetary crisis but also empowered to participate in r eimagining its futures. Storytelling, in this sense, becomes both pedagogy and praxis —a way of composing more just and livable worlds.

papers.title: Entities Detonating Potentials: Interuniversity Design Workshop TiUD as an Exploratory Lab for Actants of the Futures
papers.authors: Inés Alvarez-Icaza, Claudia Garduño-García, Edrei Ibarra-Martínez, Reneé Harari Masri
papers.design_stakeholders: Higher Education Instructors / Faculty; Undergraduate / Graduate Students; Educational Researchers & Designers; Community Members & Partners
papers.abstract: The Interuniversity Design Workshop is an exploratory laboratory that promotes the study of design activism, sustainable design, and transition design. The seventh edition of the workshop aimed to visualize the organizations, institutions, or companies that must be created to enable Mexico City to reach its potential for social well-being. The object of this educational experience is to enable design students to discover new ways to promote social activation through design as a professional activity. A group of 60 undergraduate design students from five high education institutions (HEI,’s) analyzed their own contexts, emphasi zing the identification of potential sources of wellbeing; later, they were given the task to design interactions, including giving shape to the agents that would make them possible. Their projects revealed three key findings: (a) that students are able to identify potentials through contextual observation; (b) that the creation of new actors can potentially activate new realities; and (c) the proposed entities hint potential future roles of designers in Latin American contexts. This study contributes to the field of design, looking towards a fairer, more pluralistic and diverse future .

papers.abstract: As the impacts of climate change intensify, it is critical to support high school students in developing Critical Science Agency (CSA) and Systems Thinking (ST) to leverage science learning to address environmental concerns in their local communities and beyond. This study is part of a project involving a collaboration between university researchers, informal science educators, and high school students and teachers to codesign a place - and community- based environmental engineering curriculum. papers.title: Co-Designing Hybrid Intelligent Learning Environments: One Educator’s Journey Navigating Relationships with AI
papers.authors: Lili Yan, Jina Kang
papers.design_stakeholders: Science Teachers; Students & Learners; Educational Researchers & Designers
papers.abstract: Recent advancements in artificial intelligence (AI) have resulted in a “replacement framing” in education. Hybrid intelligence (HI) has been proposed to reframe the relationship between educators and AI as collaborative, positioning humans and AI as partners in learning. Empirically, however, little is known about the impact of the HI system on the complex ecologies of learning in K -12 classrooms. To foreground educators’ agency in shaping HI systems for learning, we partner with a group of secondary science teachers exploring the role of hybrid intelligent systems in science learning contexts. We present a case of one educator’s experience to illustrate how teachers navigated their relationship with AI during the process to co-design a hybrid learning environment based on the existing science learning simulation, HoloOrbits. Findings highlight teachers’ evolving trajectories and leadership in co- designing AI-augmented systems, which reveals how teachers negotiate forms of AI-teaming aligned with their pedagogical visions.

papers.title: Codesign and Translanguaging as Tools to Challenge Monoglossic Spaces in Teacher Preparation
papers.authors: Kira LeeKeenan, Gavin Tierney, Ferran/Fernando Rodriguez-Valls
papers.design_stakeholders: Pre-service Teachers; Higher Education Instructors / Faculty; Students & Learners; Educational Researchers & Designers
papers.abstract: In an era where knowledge and identities have been dismantled by reductionist views and voices, this paper examines how co-design, a process of shared power and equitable voices, and translanguaging, a framework for identity development and social and linguistic justice, draw from each other to reimagine a teacher credential program. Within the context of redesigning a teacher credential program, we study how co-design processes leverage past ‘pre- service teachers’ expertise as plurilingual individuals and examine hierarchical relationships to disrupt traditional instructor roles. We examine the reproduction of power, privilege, and inequity in educational domains, employing frameworks to affirm diverse identities and challenge monolingual epistemologies. Methods include constructivist grounded theory and critical discourse analysis to understand participants' language use. Co- design sessions with faculty and alumni aim to foster equitable classroom discourse, enhancing pedagogical repertoires and challenging traditional roles to support English Learner/ Emergent Plurilingual (EL/EP) students effectively. Purpose Research highlights the importance of creating spaces for pre- service teachers to evaluate their language and languaging practices and the subsequent impact on lesson design, implementation, and assessment for English Learner/Emergent Plurilingual (EL/EP) students (e.g., Yoon, 2008; España, Herrera & Garcia, 2019; Yilmaz, 2019; Cárdenas et al., 2024). Fostering linguistically inclusive and just classroom discourses ensures students: a) participate in experiences celebrating, embracing, and amplifying bilingualism (Dover & Rodriguez-Valls, 2018); b) achieve academically and socio -emotionally (López et al., 2015); and c) develop critical consciousness (Cannizzo, 2021). This proposal focuses on how two faculty members engage in a co- design process focused on linguistic inclusion and justice with students and alumni from our teacher preparation. The following research question guides this paper: What language and languaging practices guide, persist, and emerge from co -designing and redesigning university courses that focus on linguistic inclusion? This research is part of a larger grant -funded project that examines how pre -service teachers, clinical coaches, and in -service teachers redesign learning experiences to support EL/EP students by reaffirming their identities and including their language and languaging in the core of learning and teaching praxis. Spanning from October 2025 to September 2030, the larger project seeks to leverage past teachers’ expertise in a co -design and redesign course process. We aim to examine hierarchical relationships in learning sites, disrupt typical instructor/pre -service teacher roles, and amplify students’ perspectives through a co-design process. Theoretical perspectives Theories of critical literacy and translanguaging and linguistic justice provide the analytic lenses we use to understand the co- design space discourses and how they intersect with structural, cultural, disciplinary, and interpersonal domains (Collins & Bilge, 2016). Theories of critical literacy (e.g., Freire & Macedo, 1987; Janks, 2010) argue that language forms and shapes experience (Anderson & Irvine, p. 98); furthermore, languaging is always situated and contextualized (Zuñiga, 2019). Aligning with other critical literacy researchers, our research continues to work toward the goal of action, which challenges social inequality and is informed by the interrelationships between theories of domination and power, identity and social difference, equity and access, and multimodal design and redesign. Translanguaging as a concept/construct captures how many named language scholars conceptualize and operationalize and how language users create meaning with their linguistic and semiotic resources (García, 2011). García (2011) argues that when people translanguage, they are using knowledge of multiple named languages and varieties (their linguistic resources) in “a single language system that creates meaning and accomplishes goals” (p. 45). Translanguaging informs and frames our research to examine how language and languaging practices could contribute to or deny identity development, equity-centered practices, and social justice (Dover, Rodríguez- Valls, Ott & Bryant, 2025). Finally, the concept “linguistic justice” (Baker -Bell, 2020) is a useful analytic to ol 1642 because it helps us conceptualize when participants act in ways that disrupt monocultural and monoglossic spaces. Recognizing how systems oppress plurilingualism requires reconciling how society silences or enables language. Collectively, translanguaging emphasizes affirming the identities of culturally diverse students and disrupting processes that privilege White, monolingual epistemologies. Our goal is to identify how, why, when, and where white-gaze ideologies enacted by teachers interrupt and deny emergent plurilingual students’ opportunities to fully contribute to the learning and teaching occurring in their classrooms, in their schools, and in their communities (García-Mateus, Strong, Palmer, & Heiman, D., 2020)

papers.title: Designing the Next Generation of Computational Modeling and Learning with AI
papers.authors: Tamar Fuhrmann, Line Have Musaeus, Ole Sejer Iversen, Paulo Blikstein
papers.design_stakeholders: Teachers; Higher Education Instructors / Faculty; Educators & Practitioners; Elementary Students & Children; Educational Researchers & Designers
papers.abstract: As generative AI rapidly transforms how humans interact with computation, it challenges the foundations of many educational technologies designed to teach coding, modeling, and computational thinking. Systems that were once built around writing or arranging code—whether block-based or text-based—now coexist with tools that generate programs through natural language. This workshop invites the learning sciences and design research community to collectively explore how educational technologies that include coding must be re-envisioned in light of these shifts. What will it mean to “code,” “debug,” or “model” when AI becomes a co-author? How might our existing environments—like MoDa, a block-based modeling platform, or text-based NetLogo simulations—need to be rethought for an era where learners reason through prompts, outputs, and model interpretation rather than syntax and structure? Our goal is to identify key design principles, challenges, and opportunities to guide the next generation of AI-powered computational learning environments. Theoretical background and significance Integrating computational thinking (CT) into science education equips students with powerful tools to explore scientific phenomena, foster deeper conceptual understanding, and engage in authentic scientific practices. The interdisciplinary potential of this work empowers students and practitioners to engage meaningfully with emerging local and global challenges (Barr et al., 2011; Weintrop et al., 2016). Existing literature identifies several core CT practices: abstraction, generalization, decomposition, algorithmic thinking, and debugging (Caeli & Yadav, 2020). Computational modeling, including agent-based modeling (ABM), has long been recognized as a valuable tool that can simultaneously support students' science learning and CT (e.g., Wilkerson et al., 2015; Musaeus et al., 2023; Musaeus et al., 2022). Recently, however, developments in Artificial Intelligence (AI) have introduced new possibilities for how learners and educators may interact with computational models (Chen et al., 2023). In the future, it may no longer be necessary to write code to create scientific computer models, putting learners in the role of collaborators with generative AI. For decades, coding has served as both a tool for learning and a language for thinking (Papert, 1980; diSessa, 2000). Block-based and text-based environments embody constructionist ideals, empowering learners to express, test, and refine ideas through computation. Yet today, this paradigm is shifting. AI’s ability to generate executable code from natural language redefines what it means to “speak computation.” As we transition from programming languages to prompting, foundational concepts—such as loops, conditions, and agents—risk becoming invisible. At the same time, new epistemic practices emerge: prompt engineering, iterative interpretation of AI outputs, and ethical reasoning about algorithmic agency. This timely workshop for the field of learning sciences demands that we rethink not only curricula, but also what fundamental concepts in programming that we still need to teach and how to design the tools themselves; how they mediate learning, distribute agency, and scaffold understanding when code is no longer the learner’s sole artifact of construction. Organizing team Line Have Musaeus leads research at the Center for Computational Thinking & Design, focusing on computing education, computational modeling, and STEM learning. Her work explores how integrating computational thinking into school subjects supports both student learning and teacher development. She co-designed CoTinker and has extensive experience organizing workshops on computing and AI in education. Tamar Fuhrmann leads research at the Transformative Learning Technologies Lab at Teachers College, Columbia University. She is a founding leader of the MoDa project, focusing on computational modeling in science education. Her work integrates STEM, AI, and constructionist approaches, and she regularly leads professional development and international collaborations. Paulo Blikstein is an Associate Professor at Columbia University and director of the Transformative Learning Technologies Lab. His research focuses on using technology to t ransform learning in STEM and AI. He founded the FabLearn program and has received major awards, including the NSF CAREER and AERA Early Career Award. Ole Sejer Iversen is a professor at Aarhus University and director of the Center for Computational Thinking & Design. His research focuses on computational empowerment, helping young people become active creators of technology. He works at the intersection of participatory design, computing education, and policy, leading large-scale international projects. Workshop goals and intended audience This workshop is designed for researchers, designers, and educators in the learning sciences, computing education, and educational technology who are exploring the future of computational learning in the age of AI. It will particularly interest those developing or studying coding-based environments—such as block-based, text-based, or modeling tools—and those investigating how generative AI transforms students’ epistemic, creative, and design practices. Participants with backgrounds in design-based research, computational modeling, or AI in education will find opportunities to share perspectives, contribute to collaborative redesign activities, and help shape a research agenda for rethinking the role of coding and modeling in AI-mediated learning environments. Outline of planned activities and facility requirements The four-hour workshop (plus one hour for lunch and coffee) will begin with an opening and framing session (20 minutes) introducing key tensions in AI-integrated coding environments. This will be followed by case study provocations (40 minutes), during which participants engage with two computational modeling environments: MoDa, a block-based agent-based modeling tool, and CoTinker, a collaborative modeling environment. Participants will explore and design models while considering how these tools might evolve as learners use AI to generate, modify, and explain models. In the collaborative design challenge (60 minutes), small groups will reimagine an educational technology that includes coding, redesigning it to integrate AI while preserving learners’ epistemic and creative engagement. This will lead into a group synthesis and discussion (40 minutes), during which participants share insights, identify emerging principles, and surface tensions, producing a poster as the group outcome. The workshop will conclude with a closing reflection (20 minutes), focusing on articulating open research questions and opportunities for future collaboration. Participation requirements Participation is open to researchers, designers, educators, and graduate students interested in computational modeling, coding education, or AI-supported learning environments. No specific technical expertise or prior experience with educational learning environments is required. We would like to support a dynamic, collaborative environment in which multiple perspectives on the redesign of coding-based educational technologies can emerge. Relationship to similar events conducted in the past Over the past several years, ISLS conferences have hosted numerous workshops and symposia exploring computational modeling, data science education, and AI-supported learning, for example, Kafai et al., 2025; Wagh et al., 2024; Fuhrmann et al., 2022; Fuhrmann et al., 2024; and McElhaney et al., 2020. These events advanced theoretical and design frameworks for integrating computational practices into science and engineering education. However, few have directly addressed the implications of generative AI for redesigning the educational technologies that include coding, particularly how block-based and text-based modeling environments must evolve when learners can construct programs through natural language. This workshop builds on that lineage but reframes the central question: not how to teach coding, but how coding itself—and the tools built around it—should be reimagined for an AI-mediated future. By convening researchers working at the intersection of computational modeling, design-based research, and AI in education, the session extends ongoing ISLS dialogues toward a new design agenda: understanding how AI reshapes the epistemic and pedagogical foundations of computational learning tools. Expected outcome and outputs The workshop will strengthen a community of practice focused on designing tools that preserve human sense- making and agency alongside AI assistance. It will generate open-ended questions that help rethink computational educational technologies in an AI-mediated context, and build a shared vocabulary around emerging hybrid practices where coding, prompting, and modeling intersect. Rather than defining what the future of coding should be, the session aims to open a dialogue on how our tools—and our field—must evolve to meet it. papers.title: The Impact of Discourse in Knowledge Building Teacher Communities on Professional Agency in Interdisciplinary Instructional Design
papers.authors: Li-Ting Tseng, Mei-Ju Chen, Huang-Yao Hong, Chao-Yu Guo
papers.design_stakeholders: K-12 Teachers
papers.abstract: This stu dy examines how discourse within a Knowledge -Building (KB) teacher community shapes professional agency in interdisciplinary instructional design. Sixty- nine teachers participated in collaborative design tasks, and their discourse was categorized i nto sharing-oriented and knowledge -building-oriented groups. Mixed- method analyses revealed a shift from exploratory sharing to knowledge -building discourse, characterized by negotiation and i ntegration of teaching strategies. Teachers’ professional agency im proved across all dimensions, particularly in positive interdependence and collective efficacy. The findings underscore the critical role of knowledge -building discourse in fostering teacher agency and supporting interdisciplinary instructional innovation.

papers.title: Creating Artifacts for Expansive Science Teaching through Art-Based Collaboration
papers.authors: Deborah Dutta, Miwa A. Takeuchi
papers.design_stakeholders: Science Teachers; Educators & Practitioners; Elementary Students & Children; Educational Researchers & Designers; Community Members & Partners
papers.abstract: The need for newer ways to enact human- nature relationships calls for educational practices to expand their boundaries of learning. Several educational initiatives have engaged in integrating arts -based practices with science learning to broaden the scope and aims of learning. However, the creation of artifacts that mediate the processes by which science educators can expand their pedagogical repertoire to engage with the emergent possibilities of arts-based practices has received less attention. This study describes collaborative processes between an artist and a pre-service teacher, Becca, which inspired her attempts to reimagine her teaching aims and practices, as part of a summer camp research –design partnership on a community urban farm. The study highlights how the evolution of pedagogical artifacts through collaborations made space for emergent learning anchored in embodied experiences.

papers.title: Design-Based Approaches to Co-Analysis in Collaborative Research
papers.authors: Kylie Peppler, June Ahn, Maggie Dahn
papers.design_stakeholders: Teachers; Educators & Practitioners; High School Students; Educational Researchers & Designers; Community Members & Partners; Domain Experts & Technologists; School Administrators & Leaders
papers.abstract: Research-practice partnerships (RPPs) and design- based implementation research (DBIR) emphasize co-design with stakeholders, yet approaches for collaborative data analysis remain underdeveloped. This paper examines how design approaches can scaffold quali tative and quantitative inquiry for diverse partners in co-analysis processes. We present two working examples: the TRACE Project, which developed a community -driven taxonomy of arts program outcomes through collaborative classification with 26 community arts organizations, and the Whole Child Analytics Project (WCAP), which employed AI -assisted reflection tools to measure college and career readiness competencies through teacher and student co-design in a large, urban school district. Through these cases, we illustrate methods for creating spaces that afford meaningful engagement from all partners while honoring multiple perspectives, voices, and worldviews in the analysis process.

papers.title: Community Convergence Among Science Education Practitioners, Structural Biologists, and Biology Teacherspractitioners
papers.authors: Amber M. Cesare, Amy Voss Farris, Kathleen M. Hill
papers.design_stakeholders: High School Teachers; Educators & Practitioners; Undergraduate / Graduate Students; Educational Researchers & Designers; Domain Experts & Technologists
papers.abstract: We present the design of a partnership among science education practitioners, molecular biologists , and high school biology teachers. Using Lave and Wenger’s (1991) construct of legitimate peripheral participation, we demonstrate how the partnership created conditions for meaningful engagement in the specialized epistemic and cultural practices of structural molecular biology. The SHAPE MATTERS project facilitated an iterative professional learning program in which 24 teachers and their students engaged in increasingly sophisticated approximations of modeling practices ––from using physical and computational molecular models to presenting molecular stories. The team also developed a continuum of molecular modeling for high school biology. The structural biologists ensured disciplinary authenticity; science educators provided pedagogical knowledge. Our case presents a proof-of- concept for a practical approach that moves beyond generalized enactments of scientific practice by grounding teaching and learning in specific research contexts, supporting teachers and their students to develop experience in nuanced enactments of scientific modeling.

papers.title: Speculative Interaction Geography: Imagining How Embodied Interactions Take Shape Beyond AI Prediction
papers.authors: Ben Rydal Shapiro, Deborah Silvis
papers.design_stakeholders: Teachers; Educators & Practitioners; Elementary Students & Children; Educational Researchers & Designers; Community Members & Partners
papers.abstract: Recent advances in qualitative data visualization are expanding how researchers and educators analyze interactions among people and things across learning environments. Yet , these tools remain primarily retrospective , representing what has already occurred from data such as video. Bridging traditions of interaction analysis with research centering affect and speculative design, this paper explores how qualitative data visualization tools can also serve as speculative instrument s for creating data to imagine possible interactions in learning spaces. Specifically, we extend a method called interaction geography through two illustrative cases that demonstrate new technical capabilities. These capabilities enabl e researchers and practitioners to sketch imagined interactions and spatial configurations, reconfiguring interaction geography as both an analytic and speculative practice. We propose the notion of speculative interaction geography and show how speculative data visualization can serve as a human-centered counterpoint to AI-driven prediction in the learning sciences, with implications for areas like teacher education and participatory design.

papers.title: STEAM in the Learning Sciences: Foregrounding Heritage Algorithms in the Design of Learning Tools
papers.authors: Madison Allen Kuyenga
papers.design_stakeholders: Teachers; Educators & Practitioners; Youth & Adolescents; Educational Researchers & Designers; Community Members & Partners
papers.abstract: My research examines how cultural practices (e.g., barbering, cosmetology, fashion design) and epistemologies (i.e., ways of knowing) can be learned and sustained while acquiring computer science (CS) skills. I draw on ethnocomputing and leverage heritage algorithms— hybrids of computing and culture—to create simulations of cultural practices using algorithms. These simulations can be used to teach cultural ways of knowing and making as well as CS skills. Overall, my research focuses on sustaining cultural making practices and cultivating the creative aspects of CS education through community-based participatory design research. In this statement, I share my previous work in CS education and ethnocomputing and situate future strands of my work in STEAM and the learning sciences.

papers.title: Insights from International Partnerships on Infrastructuring for Maker Education
papers.authors: Yuval Segev, Yotam Hod, Shiri Kashi, Akshay Nagarajan, Alekh Velayudhan, Ann Berger Valente, Anna Santo
papers.design_stakeholders: Elementary / Early Childhood Teachers; Educators & Practitioners; Elementary Students & Children; Educational Researchers & Designers; Community Members & Partners; School Administrators & Leaders
papers.abstract: Maker education is a disruptive innovation spreading globally, fundamentally challenging schooling by shifting focus from abstract ideas to creating and sharing tangible artifacts. Often driven by grassroots enthusiasm rather than top- down mandates, this diffusion lacks corresponding supportive infrastructure from established systems, posing a timely question: What can be learned about the infrastructures and infrastructuring processes required to support the integration of maker learning? Maker education offers an opportunity to employ infrastructuring as a conceptual lens and strategy to analyze the inherent tensions between this movement and formal schooling. This structured poster symposia embodies the Annual Meeting's theme, Partnering with Purpose . It convenes international research groups who actively collaborate with local stakeholders to share diverse insights from their efforts to integrate maker learning into school systems. By illuminating these infrastructuring processes, we aim to inform a more robust theory of sustainable, systemic change within the Learning Sciences.

papers.title: Multimodal Interactions with AI: Human–AI Partnerships in Learning, Teaching, and Research
papers.authors: Hanall Sung
papers.design_stakeholders: Math Teachers; Higher Education Instructors / Faculty; Elementary Students & Children; Educational Researchers & Designers
papers.abstract: My research program examines how multimodal interactions with AI shape learning, teaching, and research. I investigate how learners build and express knowledge across verbal, embodied, and digital modalities, and how AI can meaningfully participate in these processes. My work spans three interconnected strands. First, I design AI-based systems that personalize learning by assessing cognitive processes through multimodal data triangulation. Second, I develop human–AI hybrid intelligence approaches for modeling complex, temporally layered learning processes, leveraging methods such as the interleaving approach, epistemic network analysis, and computer vision. Third, I design immersive XR learning environments in which AI agents scaffold embodied STEM learning through interactive multimodal guidance. Across these strands, my goal is to advance theoretically grounded and methodologically rigorous frameworks for understanding and designing human–AI partnerships that enhance multimodal sense-making and meaning-making in learning sciences and CSCL contexts.

papers.title: How Educational Practitioners Envision Employment-Focused Transition Services for Students with Disabilities: Insights from a Game-Based Activity
papers.authors: Indu Garg, LuEttaMae Lawrence, Stephen Kwiatek
papers.design_stakeholders: Educators & Practitioners; High School Students; Community Members & Partners; School Administrators & Leaders
papers.abstract: This paper explores how educational practitioners conceptualize employment‑focused transition services for students with disabilities through a collaborative, game‑based planning activity. Drawing on a fictional case study of a high school student, practitioners worked in cross‑role teams to design a four‑year plan to document how they can support the student’s transition from high school into adulthood. Analysis of 217 practitioner contributions, coded using Lee and Carter’s (2012) framework of high‑qualit y employment transition services, revealed that career development experiences and customized transition supports were most frequently emphasized, while family support, job‑related supports, and self‑determination appeared less consistently and often only in response to roadblocks. These findings align with established predictors of post‑school success but also highlight gaps in proactive family engagement, and employer and interagency collaboration. The study demonstrates how designed, game‑based environme nts can surface practitioner reasoning, mediate professional learning, and inform the design of more inclusive, employment‑focused transition services.

papers.title: Teacher Autonomy in Organized Informal Learning
papers.authors: Racheli Davies, Nadav Ehrenfeld
papers.design_stakeholders: Teachers; Students & Learners; Educational Researchers & Designers; Domain Experts & Technologists
papers.abstract: Researchers often refer to teacher autonomy in either how they learn in professional development or how they make choices about what and how to teach. These two areas of teacher autonomy are usually studied separately, which we argue is problematic, and thus bring them together. We focus on a 4- day summer workshop where teachers were given unusually high levels of freedom to set their own goals and learning. By looking at the choices teachers made we explore what it means for teachers to exercise different kinds of professional judgment. We draw on Boote’s (2006) idea of professional discretion, illustrating how some relied on existing materials and organized them for their classrooms, while others developed new materials that addressed local student needs. By examining these choices, we highlight potential opportunities for how teacher autonomy can be supported to foster more innovative professional practice. Objective Research on teacher autonomy is fragmented across two main bodies of research. The first stems from teacher education and professional development literature and deals with different forms of teacher autonomy or its absence in their learning (e.g., Horn & Garner, 2022; Kennedy, 2019; Lefstein et al., 2020), and the second stems from policy and curriculum investigations and deals with teachers’ freedom to make choices about what they teach and how (e.g., Hong & Youngs, 2016; Pearson & Moomaw, 2005). The gap between these two bodies of knowledge is problematic because autonomy cannot be “provided” without proper support to realize it (Hargreaves, 2016; Marco et al., 2025). For these reasons, we position this paper and investigation at this intersection, in line with scholars who bridge that gap (e.g., Boote, 2006; Severance et al., 2016). From this stance, we argue that teacher curricular autonomy is both necessary and requires support for teachers to exercise it. Our overarching goal, in both practice and research, echoes Boote’s (2006) argument that “developing innovative professional discretion should be the long- term goal of teacher development and curriculum policy” (p. 468). Towards this goal, in this exploratory paper we first define teacher curricular autonomy as teachers’ capacity to make curricular choices and to implement them (Hong & Youngs, 2016; Pearson & Moomaw, 2005). Then, we present Boote’s conceptualization of three levels of teacher professional discretion marked by increased competence: procedural, substantive, and innovative professional discretion. Finally, we illustrate teacher choices in a professional development setting we call organized informal learning, distinguished from more typical PD activities by the high level of autonomy teachers are provided with. Within the context of this 4-day-long summer workshop, we ask, What type of choices did participants make about the structure and content of the curricular materials they developed? What choices did participants make about their own activity within the PD? We explore these questions with an eye towards providing fertile ground for future research and professional development designed to develop teachers’ ability to exercise innovative professional discretion. Prior literature: Connecting two notions of teacher autonomy Teachers’ autonomy in PD activities The last quarter century of research on teacher professional development (PD) is rife with critiques of traditional top-down PD, sometimes referred to as “pull -out” (Cobb et al., 2018) or “commercially available” (Kazemi & Hubbard, 2008). Within such top-down PD activities, teachers are seen as passive consumers of knowledge, with little to no influence o ver what they will learn and how (Lefstein et al., 2020). In contrast, current notions of quality teacher PD emphasize collaborative reflection on problems of teaching raised by teachers and situated in their everyday practice (e.g., Darling-Hammond et al., 2017; Ehrenfeld, 2025). A prominent example of such PD designs are Professional Learning Communities (PLCs; Brodie, 2014; Grossman et al., 2001; Popp & Goldman, 2016; Vescio et al., 2008). papers.abstract: This dissertation examines how learning environments for K–12 teachers can be designed to foster radical imagination through speculative activities. Data were collected across four mathematics teacher education courses at a large U.S. university, and a core group of participants joined a collective inquiry group to explore how to create elements of their imagined futures in their present classrooms. Anticipated findings include design principles that promote radical imagination among teachers, the forms of collectivity that emerged within the inquiry group, and the focal points of teachers’ radical reimaginings of mathematics teaching and schooling. Goals and background The aim of the present study is to design and analyze various learning environments where K-12 mathematics teachers engage with radical imagination and collective futuring. Radical imagination is the act of crafting new possibilities for the future that are not constrained by systemic structures or the status-quo of the “possible.” Neoliberal logics typically locate the source and the solution of (educational) problems in the individual, and thus leave unexamined the structures and collective action needed to challenge systemic forces (Barker & Scheele, 2016). Radical imagination by collectives of teachers, and fostering that imagination through teacher education, intentionally endeavors to rewrite the dominant power structures that maintain the status quo of capitalist, white supremacist, and settler-colonial systems in education. This is of particular importance in mathematics teacher education, as the discipline of mathematics is viewed as politically neutral (Harouni, 2015), which ultimately serves to maintain hierarchies of power and underscores patriarchal ways of knowing (Hesse-Biber et al., 2004). Specifically, this research explores: (1) How can learning environments in mathematics education be designed to contribute to the development of teacher radical imagination, and (2) How can collectives of teachers act on their imagined future in the present? papers.title: Designing Equitable Partnerships for the Future of Play
papers.authors: Cristina Paul, Anna Terrazas, Christine Lee
papers.design_stakeholders: Elementary / Early Childhood Teachers; Educators & Practitioners; Elementary Students & Children; Educational Researchers & Designers; School Administrators & Leaders
papers.abstract: Educators and a university researcher co -designed play-based learning to support children to gain a deep and enduring understanding of scientific concepts, critical consciousness, and practicing joy. We present how reciprocity emerged through our equitabl e partnerships and how these partnerships make research, theory, praxis, and student learning more robust. Play Play is messy; while we wanted to include play in our classrooms as social justice advocates and practitioners, the structures, schedules, and everyday boundaries of typical classrooms make it a challenge. Play allows us to grasp important ideas from multiple angles with empathy and care, both as educators and students. This is a freedom we are slowly losing with the rise of standardized curricula, testing, and the prevalence of unfeeling screen-based learning. Standardized and for-profit curricula can also strip educators of autonomy. Play is learning. Play advocacy and research aren’t just about joy—they’re about justice too. We present four design components from our equitable partnership that made our participatory design- based research successful. Our poster shares how we practiced reciprocity in our researcher -educator partnership. Understanding how future educator - researcher collaborations can design their partnerships in equitable ways is critical for the future of design -based research. Co-designing play The goal of our partnership was to design an interdisciplinary environmental curriculum that empowered young students to learn through play. Throughout the school year, we designed play lessons to support students in learning about interdependent relationships between people, pollinators, and plants. Cristina and Anna are elementary teachers of mixed -age 1st and 2nd grade students at an elementary school in Los Angeles. Cristina teaches in a dual language bilingual education (DLBE) program with 90% instruction in Spanish and 10% instruction in English. Christine, a university researcher, has been interested in designing a curriculum for environmental education through play and has been collaborating with Cristina and Anna since the Spring of 2022. Throughout the academic school year, our team met weekly to co -plan play-based lessons. Our year -long play-based curriculum had three parts that wove together play and movement: first, we investigated plants and flowers; then, we investigated bees as pollinators; an d finally, we investigated how people impact and rely on plants and pollinators. Designing partnerships: Reciprocity While our participatory design-based research study (Bang & Vossoughi, 2016) aimed to integrate play into our curriculum, the goal of our poster is to reflect on the design of our equitable partnership that made it possible. The data in this poster are fro m our collective experiences and reflections on educator -researcher relationships in design-based work. Through reflection, we identify and present four components that made our work reciprocal. Our partnership was built on curiosity, trust, humility, and multiple competencies. Instead of focusing on the distinct tasks of rigid roles, we practiced reciprocity through equitable partnerships –sharing responsibilities and making decisions together about how to implement play. Component one: Play Play is a human need and everyone has the right to play (United Nations, 1989). Throughout our work, play was a goal and a means for children, teachers, and researchers. We intentionally designed our curriculum with embedded play, and to accomplish this, we also played with one another and alongside our students. Of course, we played with our lesson designs, with how to collect data on students’ learning, and even played with the design of our classroom spaces by moving furniture to make room for play. More importantly, we made and played with costumes, created art, and pretended to be creatures and plants alongside our students. Play helped us to reflect on and refine our thinking–not only with our own experiences to anticipate challenges, but to revise our lessons, and to make decisions about lesson sequences. This freed us from restrictive, static, and hierarchical ways of learning, designing, and researching. 2907 Component two: Autonomy for all While traditional research methodologies tend to uphold a sense of control in research settings, our participatory work is grounded in the context of our classrooms. We rejected the notion that we could have complete control over research and what happens in the classroom. Instead of controlling how teaching and learning should occur, we embraced unscripted, yet meaningful interactions, discoveries, questions, and misconceptions. For example, children unexpectedly sang during play lessons. When teachers asked children about word choice and how they mixed Spanish and English, the volume, and/or speed of their singing, the children’s responses demonstrated the intentionality of their decisions and their nuanced understanding of big ideas like pollination. If t eachers had simply asked children not to sing during a dance lesson or to follow the instructions with more fidelity and play quietly like a pollinator, these understandings may have never emerged and developed. Play offers opportunities for children to participate in expansive and joyful ways. It gives students space and agency to explore ideas, negotiate meaning, and co -create rules of engagement as they interact with peers. It is impossible to predict all the ways children may engage in a topic, and that should delight educators and researchers. Component three: Support for all Our classrooms have a diverse student population, which includes neurodiverse students, students with disabilities, and emergent multilingual learners. We wanted to design play for all, not just for the majority of our students. Throughout the school year, we noticed some neurodiverse students struggled with noise, lack of explicit directions, and more freedom in moving in classroom spaces. This led us to modify our lesson designs. Some of the design changes included frontloading ideas for where to play, roles to take on with which students might feel most comfortable, creating boundaries in our indoor and outdoor spaces, using noise -reducing headphones for certain children, and including children in decision- making about classroom set up for play. When desi gning classroom spaces or thinking about how to use available outdoor spaces, we ask ourselves if the physical, emotional, and academic environment we’ve created is autonomy -supportive (Amado et al., 2020). Are the materials, furniture, and structures for participation accessible to all children? Are relationships being tended to with care and curiosity? Are researchers and teachers modeling care and curiosity for students? Sometimes it’s not simply the chairs that must be moved; it’s our hearts and minds. Component four: Data sharing Our partnership was designed to share knowledge and resources, which often led us to teach one another new skills. Taking photos or videos for formal research analysis was new for Cristina and Anna. Video recordings allowed us to see and hear movement, con versation, negotiation, discussion, and problem- solving that led to the creation of each movement during play. We could see and hear students' reasoning and decision- making, which demonstrated a clear understanding of the function of each part of a flower. In a busy classroom of students, it is difficult to observe and gain a deep understanding of how each student is making sense of the information. As teachers, video recordings made it possible to follow children’s understanding; we could see how knowledge cross-pollinated between students so they could make deeper connections to the content and each other. More importantly, analyzing and re -watching the video alongside Christine changed how Anna viewed participation structures when students were playing. It changed how Anna listens, observes, and builds on students’ ideas in new ways. Concluding remarks The future we dream of is one of delight. Yet, education and academia are fraught with constraints and seeming barriers to joy -filled work. Educators are taught behavior management strategies. Administrators and other evaluators that walk through classrooms expect to see a level of control that demonstrates that children's behavior is being effectively "managed." Play is the antidote to control. The future is relational. To be in healthy relationships with each other as researchers, teachers, and students is to relate to each other in mutually respectful ways—ways of being that anticipate the beauty and logic of knowledge created in collaboration rather than in isolation. We cannot do reciprocal work without being in equitable partnerships. The future we hope for is one of reciprocity between students and teachers, teachers and researchers, and researchers and children. The democratization of knowledge and expertise in our classrooms and research wasn't accidental. It was dignity -affirming (Espinoza et al., 2020) and humanizing for children, educators, and researchers. 2908 References Amado, D., Molero, P., Del Villar, F., Tapia -Serrano, M.
