papers.title: Evaluating and Assessing Learning in AI-Embedded Environments: Perspectives Across Learning Scientists
papers.authors: Jeffrey Bush Tayne, Rafi Santo, Nga Hoang, Collette Heskett, Mon-Lin Monica Ko, Julia Eden, William
papers.design_stakeholders: Science Teachers; Students & Learners; Educational Researchers & Designers; Domain Experts & Technologists
papers.abstract: This hybrid poster symposium brings together eight studies that examine how evaluation can serve as a generative process for designing, enacting, and refining AI-supported learning environments. Moving beyond questions of technical accuracy or efficiency, these contributions frame evaluation as a relational and ethical practice that shapes how educators, learners, and technologies collaborate. Across diverse contexts —from middle school classrooms and tutoring programs to teacher coaching and high school psychology— researchers employ mixed methods, including discourse analytics, qualitative video analysis, and practical measures of student experience, to understand AI’s impact on collaboration, belonging, and cognition. A shared emphasis on human -centered des ign and co -creation underscores the importance of positioning teachers and students as partners in shaping AI systems that amplify rather than automate human intelligence. Together, the studies highlight how rigorous, equity- oriented evaluation can illumin ate both the affordances and risks of educational AI.

papers.title: Teacher Perceptions of AI-Generated Feedback on Student Scientific Models
papers.authors: Heewoo Lee, Ha Nguyen, Troy D. Sadler
papers.design_stakeholders: Science Teachers; Students & Learners; Educational Researchers & Designers
papers.abstract: Effective feedback is essential for supporting student learning in complex tasks such as scientific modeling, yet teachers often struggle to provide high -quality feedback. This study explored the utility of MLLM-generated feedback from teachers’ perspectives through a focus group with four middle school science teachers. Overall, participants regarded the feedback as promising. They valued the feedback’s degree of detail, supportive tone, and potential to deepen teachers’ knowledge and enrich classroom discussions . Participants also raised important concerns about the feedback’s alignment with instructional contexts, length, and readability.

papers.title: Reimagining Learning through Arts and Making: Creative Identity Work in Partnership
papers.authors: Kristina Stamatis, Joseph L. Polman, Jrène Rahm, Sanne Akkerman, Jeroen Vermeulen, Antero G. Garcia, Royston
papers.design_stakeholders: Pre-service Teachers; Middle School Students; Educational Researchers & Designers; Community Members & Partners; Domain Experts & Technologists
papers.abstract: This hybrid symposium brings together learning sciences research exploring intergenerational identity development in relation to the arts and making as a means of deepening partnership. We look across continents through projects that center art and making as identity work, particularly for people navigating historic oppression, to better understand the ways these creative acts can provide pathways of resistance and reimagination. We follow the conference theme to reimagine the ways that learning scientists interpret “impactful learning experiences” (Fishman et al., 2013) in partnerships that emphasize notions of joy and creation as meaningful forms of reimagining learning in our present global context. Each paper reimagines how intergenerational participants inscribe themselves into the world, positioning acts of identity building as a deeply rooted engagement in possibility. Through this session, we strive to build conversations across these nine projects and in collaboration with attendees toward more nuanced, critical, and culturally grounded notions of partnership. Overview This proposed hybrid symposium brings into conversation learning sciences research exploring how people develop identities across lifespans in relation to the arts —broadly conceived as making and tinkering, creating, writing, composing, and creatively engaging with others toward more transformative futures. Drawing from traditions of design- based research (e.g., Brown, 1992), participatory design research (e.g., Bang & Vossoughi, 2016), testimonio and pláticas (e.g., Delgado -Bernal, 2012), and decolonizing and indigenous methodologies (e.g., Bang, 2020; Patel, 2016), we examine the ways that partnerships resonate and grow alongside the identities of participants when grounded in notions of joy, play, creativity, and belonging (Mirra & Garcia, 2024). In this symposium, we collectively define learning as ontological, a process of becoming someone new (e.g., Lee, 2016), 2340 and view learning and associated identities as expansive, developing along pathways in relation to our histories, communities, partnerships, and collective ecologies (e.g., Bang, 2020; Gutiérrez et al., 2019; Nasir et al., 2020). We see identity as an ever -changing part of human experience, both related to and disruptive of structures of power that have continuously led to oppression and genocide based on race, ethnicity, culture, religion, language, gender, socioeconomic status, ability, and the growing number of traits deemed “illegal” by those in power in the U.S. and other nations. We follow theorists whose work has pushed boundaries of what it means to embody artistry, particularly for historically marginalized peoples whose collective efforts have alwa ys been the catalyst for movements toward more equitable futures (Bang & Vossoughi, 2016). Our aim with this collective conversation is to look across our projects, all of which center art and making as part of learning trajectories through which people build identities (Nasir et al., 2020), particularly for people navigating historic oppression, to better understand the ways creative acts can provide pathways of resistance, reimagination, and transformation in relationship with and to one another, our environments, and the more -than-human beings whose ecologies we share. This session will center on the questions: 1) How can projects focused on identity-building within creative contexts help to reimagine the ways partnerships operate toward more joyful, just, and transformative ends? 2) How can conversations across projects move the learning sciences to more deeply attend to the creativity essential for reinvention of systems and structures? In this symposium, we discuss papers in three 18- minute rounds, ending with collaborative discussion with Dr. McKinney de Royston, audience, and participants, to push back against restrictive notions of identification, instead taking up dialogical approaches to identity (e.g., Akkerman & Meijer, 2011). Across these papers, scholars examine the ways that making and the arts can extend toward more transformative notions of what it means to be and become a certain kind of person (Enyedy et al., 2014). We bring into conversation projects drawing from narrative (e.g., Delgado- Bernal, 2012), proleptic (Lee, 2016), and liberatory notions of identity development across generations (Nasir et al., 2020), and engage in conversations to push these silos toward more holistic and transformative ends. Framing identity building as an artistic process, rather than a solely scientific one, we reimagine how young people and their elders inscribe themselves into the world. We position every act of identification as a potential artistic act of defiance, imagination, and creation toward more transformative futures. In considering the call for this year’s conference, we use these pieces to speak together about the ways that partnership and design can act as levers to engage in joyful resistance and creative reimagining of structures of power (Hayes & Kaba, 2023). The scholars in this symposium draw from sociocultural, sociocritical, and constructionist theories of learning, as well as notions of criticality, embodiment, temporality, and design to reconsider the ways that our work can build knowledge and community collectively. Although the papers feature a variety of methods, all share perspectives that data can and should be representative of the multiple and complex ways learners navigate the world (Bridges, 2020). This complexity is part of our session structure, where we offer both traditional and creative opportunities for participants across modalities to engage and build knowledge collaboratively and in partnership. Despite differences in epistemology and analysis, each project suggests new ways of understanding identity development as a deeply cultural and artistic process of reimagining both oneself and the world. Paper abstracts are listed below alphabetically by first author and referred to here by number. While all papers engage in examining arts and identity development through design, partnership, and collaboration, the projects differ in stages of development and are situated across varying contexts, nations, and continents with an array of participants. Papers 1, 3, 5, and 6 examine the ways university students engage across settings to build identities artistically alongside diverse communities of learners. P apers 2, 3, 4, 6, 7, and 8 take up notions of intergenerational identification and learning to examine the ways that making and the arts can support attunement to new conceptions of self as activist and part of a “political-ethical becoming” (Vossoughi et al., 2021). Paper 9 acts as an overarching commentary across the papers, examining making and tinkering and proposing new ways of framing acts of artistry as supportive of learners’ critical consciousness (Freire, 1970). Each of the papers focuses on a diverse community of learners, where participants with historically marginalized identifications as well as other actors draw upon powerful identity resources (Nasir and Cooks, 2009) to support the reimagining of self and the world as a joyful and creative act, deeply rooted in cultural pathways of learning (Nasir et al., 2020). Together, these papers offer rich groundwork for conversations in the learning sciences, pushing on notions of partnership and learning as identity-making, while interrogating disparate yet deeply interconnected sociopolitical contexts. Paper 1: Identity work in a community and art based engaged university program Sanne Akkerman, Jeroen Vermeulen 2341 This paper reports on identity work taking place in a transdisciplinary community -engaged master’s track at Utrecht University. In this year-long program, students are invited into the everyday life of an urban public park, where they meet, talk with, and collaborate alongside local citizens representing a wide range of interest -based communities, including skaters, graffiti artists, rappers, youth care workers, and caretakers of trees, grass, and water. Through the track, students are asked to move beyond predefined disciplinary orientations and questions. They are challenged to explore the stories and practices of these communities, while inviting and bringing diverse community members and groups together to exchange perspectives and potentially build new relations around central communal themes. In this paper, we examine what it means for students to engage in what in this track is intended as a form of ontological synchronization with what happens and matters to local communities at a specific site and what it means for community members to become involved in prescenery science (Akkerman, Bakker, & Penuel, 2021). Our focus is on identity work that emerges in the process of synchronization and community engagement. Following Akkerman and Meijer (2011), we understand identity work from a dialogical perspective, where people come to explore and dynamically understand themselves through relations and collaborations with others. In the context of this track, we analyze how students and community members from various subcultures develop new understandings by relating to others with less familiar backgrounds and perspectives. We consider motivation letters, reports of interest, week ly meetings during the year and the communal creation of a light -art story and public event over time. Findings show the ways in which students and community members of the park take outside and inside perspectives of others but also develop new shared perspectives in the art works being produced functioning as an effective boundary object (Star, 1989) to materialize and structure the open, and at times discomfortable, educational process of mutual engagement. Paper 2: Joyful immigrant family storytelling during politically perilous times Antero G. Garcia, Alix Dick, Christián Thaniari This paper shares findings from a yearlong community- engaged storytelling project with immigrant parents and their children. In the final weeks before the 2025 U.S. presidential inauguration, immigrant families prepared for the worst, based on President -elect Trump’s ongoing vows to implement “the largest domestic deportation operation in American history” (Colvin, 2023). As the future for immigrant families remained uncertain even in “sanctuary” states like California, the narratives around immigrant life focused on hopeless narratives of struggle (Dick & Garcia, 2024). And yet, despite these dire contexts, immigrant families thrive. Amidst a climate of fear, immigrant families sustain joy not in spite of dire policy consequences but as ongoing, embodied pr actice. This paper shares how immigrant families manifested joyful identities through storytelling in perilous times. This paper builds on sociocultural literacies scholarship that centers immigrant and transnational identities (Bernal, 2001; Delgado- Gaitan, 2005; Villenas, 2005). Further, the emphasis on immigrant family artmaking practices also guides this work (e.g. Flores 2018; 2022). Finally, recognizing family storytelling as occurring with a community of practice (Lave & Wenger, 1991), this project extends understanding of identity and expertise within transnational informal learning environments. This qualitative case study (Dyson & Genishi, 2005; Yin, 2013) was conducted entirely online. Monthly, the community of families would convene online to share and reflect on the multimodal artifacts they created. These meetings concluded with a design prompt to take up for the following month. Methodologically, this project is situated within Chicana feminist plática methodology (e.g. Fierros & Delgado Bernal, 2016; Hannegan- Martinez, 2023). This approach centers participants’ lived experiences as forms of expertise. The ongoing conversation—plática —of each meeting guides how joy is named, measured, and shared in this group. In addition to recordings of community meetings, data for this project included the multimodal artifacts parents and children made together as well as individual interviews conducted with each family twice throughout the yearlong project. All data was inductively coded alongside a cadre of youth and parent community members. These community- created testimonies of hope ( testimonios de esperanza) acted as opportunities to explore political and structural contexts of joy. Participants’ artifacts centered communal expertise and joy tied to familial pride, cultural identity, and expressed hope for future generations. Notably, families centered “struggle” as a kind of superpower. This work, as demonstrated in poems, photo- based family trees, and family -created collages revealed ongoing narratives of solidarity that emerged through c ommunity-based artmaking. Participants’ proleptic vision of cultural identity interweaves multimodal storytelling of joy across varied timescales. In contrast to dominant, deficit narratives of immigrant experiences, findings from this study illuminate an alternative, speculative narrative of immigrant ingenuity. These findings illustrate sustained community joy through collected, family-made artifacts. The field of education does not yet utilize specific forms 2342 of joyful creation by marginalized families; the possibilities for leveraging these as assets for pedagogical application in various settings pose clear guidance for future research and design. Paper 3: Identity work in a community and art based engaged university program Teyona James-Harris, Shirin Vossoughi, Lulu Madise This paper examines educator learning and mutual becoming in a longstanding STEAM and storytelling program serving Black, Latinx/e and Asian/South Asian middle schoolers. We ask: What conditions support learning across an intergenerational collective of ed ucators of color? How do educators describe the identity shifts and forms of mutual becoming they experience over time? Here mutual becoming refers to moments when student and educator learning are dynamically interrelated and mutually generative. Research has identified key conditions that support teachers’ professional learning and efficacy (e.g., communities of practice, guidance around equitable pedagogies, instructional materials designed for teacher learning [Patton & Parker, 2017; Wei, et. al ., 2010]). Yet there is a need to better understand the paradigmatic identity shifts and forms of political- ethical becoming that can emerge for educators in settings that reimagine disciplinary domains and social relations, and practice expansive forms of arts and political education. Here we draw on Vossoughi et al.’s (2021) definition of political-ethical becoming as “not only reorganizing our thoughts but reshaping our relations,” and Rogoff’s (2023) fractals as attuning to mutually constituting processes at smaller and larger scales over time. Utilizing interpretive ethnography (Erickson, 1985) and participatory design research (Bang & Vossoughi, 2016) we report on a data set documenting student and educator learning within a 6- week summer STEAM/Storytelling program over eight years through audio -video recordings, field notes, student and educator interviews, and documentation of co- design processes. We share findings developed through qualitative coding and memoing of pre - and post-program educator interviews, analysis of one focal educators’ t rajectory across years, and field notes that capture mutual becoming through educators’ reflections on key interactions with students. Our analytic approach involves working closely with an intergenerational group of educators of color (ages 13-62) who blend the role of teachers, artists, and researchers. Our findings show how participants describe both structural and relational conditions of educator learning as consequential to the identity shifts they experience. Structural conditions include intergenerational apprenticeship, daily debriefs and educator reflections, opportunities to witness and try out others’ pedagogical moves, and fieldnote writing. Relational conditions include intentional community building and care among educators, encouragement to show up as their full selves, and a culture of playful communion that aligned with the forms of artistic creation supported among students. Patterns across field notes and educators’ pre- and post-interviews reveal the ways educator learning and political-ethical becoming involved embodying the artistic ways of being supported with students (e.g., taking our imaginations seriously, embracing the process of creation and learning, engaging in various forms of language work and conceptual revision) in ways that connected with educators’ own complex histories with schooling, learning, and life. One educator, for example, discussed the ways she was taught to avoid mistakes within a rigid schooling context, and how she needed to learn to soften this tendency within herself as she supported our middle school students to embrace process. Another example of language revision shows how the kinds of thinki ng we were supporting our students to engage around rethinking inherited terms was taken up by novice educators. One undergraduate educator referred to Red Winged Black Birds during an outdoor walk as “territorial” and then later revised his language to “protective,” sharing with students the “why” of his revision. Our paper also includes a deeper look at one teacher’s trajectory over time and the ways she took up storywork. Pedagogical storytelling was a routine practice within this setting and involved careful decision making on the part of educators around language and nourishing forms of political education and storytelling for middle school students. This teacher's journey reveals how guided feedback and revision of her story through intergenerational apprenticeship played a key role in expanding not only what she offered youth story listeners, but how she thought about and walked with her own story over time. We also found educators practiced these ways of being in relationships and contexts outside the learning environment, with family and friends. This included discussing the ways they noticed their language changing in conversations with others, and how they are enacting new forms of careful noticing and attunement to others and the world outside the educational settings. We found that all educator interviews narrated this type of “rippling out” of learning as a key indicator of the identity shifts supported by transformative projects. Such findings can support intentional design of the conditions that cultivate transformative educator learning, and ways of conceptualizing educator learning as a deep process of identity work and political -ethical 2343 becoming. Further, mutual becoming both troubles student -teacher binaries common within oppressive educational structures (Freire, 1970) and helps theorize identity shifts in ways that carefully attune to the centrality of relationality and creativity in human learning. Paper 4: “We are all becoming”: Exploring the design of improvisational activity within researcher-artist collaborations and zine making Lindsay Lindberg, Ananda Marin, Shivani Davé, Brenda Lopez, Trinity Collins Artistic identities develop across time, through conversation, and within creative practices. Throughout a co- design project with five improvisational jazz artists, including co -design conversations and performances, artists drew on identity-relevant experiences to reflect on their distinct and developing roles as individuals and ensemble members. We focus on how storywork (Archibald, 2008) shapes artists’ and researchers’ participation in improvised modes of creative activity including art making, music making, and analytic processes. We understand identity as one’s sense of self and the roles they embody in relation to others. From this perspective identities are always in a process of becoming, as individuals participate in and explore the roles that are available to them within communities of practice ( Nasir & Cooks, 2009) . Learning alongside collaborators, we also understand identity as connected to the creation of an expressive multi -modal language that is rooted in experiences and places. papers.title: Bridging Gaps: Participatory Design as a Tool for Social Justice in Education
papers.authors: Tugce Aldemir, Rogers Kaliisa, Rotem Israel-Fishelson, Nitzan Koren, Emily Oswald, Paulo Blikstein, Danielle P. Espino, Seung B. Lee, Eric R. Hamilton
papers.design_stakeholders: Science Teachers; Higher Education Instructors / Faculty; High School Students; Educational Researchers & Designers; Community Members & Partners
papers.abstract: This symposium explores how participatory design (PD) can disrupt the "one -size- fits-all" approach by fostering equitable, responsive, and contextually relevant practices in the learning sciences. Leveraging PD to address systemic inequities, the symposium showcases studies that empower immigrant teens as co -designers and learners in crafting experiences for informed civic participation, employ micro-genetic analyses to examine equitable partnerships among diverse stakeholders, explore curriculum co -design in resource-constrained settings to enhance teacher agency, utilise cooperative inquiry for designing inclusive schools for LGBTQIA+ students, and use of participatory design to advance inclusiveness in an international network of informal STEM clubs. This symposium illustrates how PD can change educational spaces and advance the Learning Sciences' commitment to social justice, ethical collaboration, and inclusive practices through case studies, methodological insights, and interactive discussions. Overview and significance Participatory design (PD) is increasingly recognised for its potential to advance equity and inclusion in education. Rooted in collaboration, PD engages learners, educators, researchers, and community members in co -designing learning environments, tools, a nd systems that address diverse experiences and needs. The Learning Sciences community has long emphasised the creation of ethical, inclusive practices that disrupt systemic inequities and foster equitable learning opportunities (e.g., Bang & Vossoughi, 2016; Gomez et al., 2021). However, despite the continued focus on inclusion within the learning sciences, empirical evidence and case studies that highlight how marginalised and underrepresented voices are included remain limited. This symposium aligns with the learning sciences’ commitment to social justice by showcasing how PD can challenge the "one -size-fits-all" approach to education. PD provides a pathway to address systemic challenges such as language barriers, identity affirmation, and power dynamics, creating equitable and contextually relevant educational practices (DiSalvo & DiSalvo, 2014; Hoadley, 2017; Vossoughi, 2020). PD fosters inclusive practices that support all stakeholders, particularly in diverse, resource-constrained settings, by including marginalised voices. The symposium presents five contributions that cover a wide range of educational contexts, including empowering immigrant teens as co-designers and learners in crafting civic engagement experiences, using micro- genetic analysis to explore teacher- stakeholder collaborations in curriculum co- design, designing inclusive schools for LGBTQIA+ youth through Cooperative Inquiry, and how participatory design can advance inclusiveness in an international network of informal STEM clubs. These cases illustrate how PD can adapt to real-world constraints, enhance agency, and create educational spaces aligning with the learning sciences' commitment to diversity, equity, and inclusion. Through interactive presentations, participants will engage with empirical, methodological, and theoretical insights, fostering discussions that bridge research and practice. This symposium not only advances the understanding of PD as a tool for social justice but also invites the learning 2365 sciences community to reimagine educational research and design for a more equitable future, echoing calls for ethical and inclusive practices (Gomez et al., 2021; Uttamchandani et al., 2020). Paper 1: Participatory design to promote teen civic engagement Nitzan Koren Abstract: This paper discusses the benefits of Participatory Design for empowering and engaging teens from immigrant backgrounds in informed politics. Two roles assumed by teens: co-designers, brainstorming and ideating learning activities for non- citizens to engage in informed politics, and learners, testing and participating in design activities to practice informed politics and improve political skills, knowledge, and self -efficacy. Techniques that led to meaningful civic learning and led to meaningful design recommendations are discussed.

papers.title: Belonging Infrastructure: A Designable Construct for Cultivating Teacher Agency in RPPs
papers.authors: Gregory Benedis-Grab, Alexandra Gendreau Chakarov
papers.design_stakeholders: Teachers; Elementary Students & Children; Educational Researchers & Designers; School Administrators & Leaders
papers.abstract: Research-Practice Partnerships (RPPs) often rely on boundary infrastructure to explain how collaboration is organized, but this lens overlooks how teacher agency is cultivated. We introduce belonging infrastructure, the designable features of collaboration that legitimize participant contributions and make belonging visible. papers.abstract: From Mapuche palikantun rhythms in Chile to Uruguayan rural futures, from WhatsApp organizing at the Mexico-US border to Brazilian constructionist reinterpretations— this symposium weaves together studies reimagining the Learning Sciences through Latin American epistemologies. We gather not to import theories from distant academies, but to honor knowledge systems flowering in our territories: mathematical wisdom in Mapuche weaving, learning that unfolds at the Tijuana -San Diego border, resistance enacted through digital practices. Our work traces how communities transform constraints into creativity, how intergenerational memory becomes a pedagogical method, how the periphery generates its own centers of gravity. Together, we offer distinctive interpretative lenses that expand the field by centering community knowledge and lived experiences situated in Latin America.

This exploratory study investigates the impact of educational game design workshops on promoting CRT, positioning teachers as serious game designers. papers.abstract: Undergraduate research methods education faces numerous challenges with respect to student affect, interest, and conceptual understanding. papers.abstract: Teachers play a crucial role in shaping learning opportunities within classrooms, and yet their voices are often missing from educational design efforts. Our work resists the normative roles ascribed to teachers in world-making efforts and partners with them to (re)design a justice-oriented high school computing program. We present findings from a collaborative video analysis of a co-design session (~40 minutes) where nine high school computing teachers, two researchers, and a senior designer engaged in a design activity uncovering what it means to center justice within computing classrooms and to support new teachers to teach justice-oriented computing. They emphasized ongoing professional and personal growth, relatable professional learning experiences, and opportunities for reflection as teachers become “co-conspirators” for social justice. We discuss findings in connection to STEM teacher preparation and solidarity.

papers.authors: Xinran Zhu, Bodong Chen
papers.design_stakeholders: Students & Learners; Educational Researchers & Designers
papers.abstract: In CSCL, productive collaborative discourse requires continual advancement of student ideas, often through the creation and modification of digital artifacts. To support this process, this study proposes a knowledge synthesis intervention, supported by technological and pedagogical designs, to facilitate the continual development of digital artifacts in a graduate class. To examine the enactment of this intervention, we asked: How did the knowledge synthesis artifacts facilitate the progression of collaborative discourse? How did they facilitate the development of shared group artifacts? Presenting six federally funded projects, the session showcases how co-design methodologies empower learners to shape tools and interventions that prioritize equity, access, and belonging. These initiatives leverage emerging technologies, including AI, AR, VR, and BCI, as well as museum- and place-based STEM activities, to address barriers to learning while fostering agency and identity development. Each project exemplifies how co-design not only creates more effective and responsive tools but also builds communities and promotes systemic change. Attendees will gain practical insights into recruiting and engaging co-designers, navigating challenges, and sustaining equitable collaborations, with a focus on scaling these practices for broader impact. Through these examples, the symposium illustrates how co-design can reimagine learning systems to better serve all learners and create more equitable educational experiences.

papers.title: Attending to Teacher Perspective on the Role of Network Visualizations in the Humanities
papers.authors: Kyle M. Dunbar, Jerika Miller, Jess Alanís, Merijke Coenraad, Kalani Craig, Joshua Danish, Mengxi Zhou
papers.design_stakeholders: Teachers; Students & Learners; Educational Researchers & Designers; Community Members & Partners
papers.abstract: To provide students with opportunities to develop data and network literacy in K-12 learning, we aim to understand how to support teachers in their design and implementation of network visualization lessons. This study examines teacher reflections on the enactment of network visualization lessons in middle school humanities classrooms, a relatively nascent field. Teacher adoption of new practices like network visualization requires changes in knowledge and attitudes that are influenced by and have influence on teachers’ implementation of these new strategies. We used Clarke and Hollingsworth’s Interconnected Model of Professional Growth (2002) to identify shifts in teachers’ knowledge and attitudes when implementing these lessons. We found student social and cognitive engagement salient for teachers, impacting their changes in beliefs about network visualizations in the humanities. Findings indicate professional development for network visualization in the humanities should be designed with a focus on student connections and interests as well as curricular alignment.

papers.abstract: This practice-oriented paper seeks to examine the role of Research-Practice Partnerships (RPPs) in promoting educational improvement in the digital era. The RPP co-development project described here aimed to bridge the gap between research and practice by providing school practitioners with research-informed knowledge while simultaneously offering researchers insights into practical development processes. The study focuses on a case school participating in the RPP co-development project to enhance its development initiatives through additional support in the form of knowledge and resources. The university partner played a pivotal role by supplying research-based knowledge, resources for data collection and analysis, and ongoing mentoring throughout the iterative co-development cycle. This two-year collaboration resulted in significant structural and pedagogical advancements within the school, as well as substantial professional growth for participating teachers. Key areas of development included enhancing home-school collaboration, effectively utilizing digital tools for internal communication, and fostering students’ well-being and sense of belonging.

papers.title: Meaningful Automated Feedback? Balancing Tensions in Participatory Learning Analytics Design
papers.authors: Susan Harrington, Sonja Klein, Alice Catherine Fratoni, Charlott Sellberg, Oskar Lindwall
papers.design_stakeholders: Teachers; Undergraduate / Graduate Students; Educational Researchers & Designers; Domain Experts & Technologists
papers.abstract: Simulators have become central in professional training, in this case maritime education, where they support the development and assessment of skills and competencies required of competent seafarers. This study aims to inform the design of a learning analytics dashboard utilizing multimodal learning analytics to deliver automated, adaptive feedback to maritime students. Feedback is critical in simulator-based training, yet the characteristics of meaningful automated feedback in professional training remain underexplored. Drawing on a participatory design workshop with maritime students, the study examines tensions arising from the conceptualization of automated feedback. Using cultural historical activity theory, we frame tensions as opportunities for innovation, highlighting the dynamic interplay between students, instructors, and technology. In doing so, we offer insights into designing meaningful automated feedback for simulation training, and the need to balance students’ dual roles as learners and future professionals, reconciling collaborative learning with personalized feedback, and prioritizing educational goals over technological innovation.

papers.title: Towards Decolonizing Agency in Addressing Racialization of Behaviors in Settler Colonial Schools
papers.authors: Dian Mawene, Aydin Bal, Dosun Ko, Linda Orie, Elizabeth Schrader, Jahyun Yoo

papers.abstract: This paper proposes a decolonizing agency framework, emphasizing how a diverse group of policy actors center Indigenous sovereignty, histories, lived experiences, and expertise to address racial disproportionality within a school community. Decolonizing agency builds upon existing frameworks on agency, in particular relational agency (Edwards, 2005; 2007) and expands the concepts in practice by incorporating decolonizing methodologies (Brayboy, 2005; Lomawaima, 2000; Smith, 2018; 2021) and cultural-historical activity theory (CHAT). We have developed the concept of decolonizing agency through a five-year-long transformative research partnership with an Anishanabee (Ojibwe) Nation to address the overrepresentation of Indigenous students in exclusionary school discipline and special education for “behavioral disturbance” at a rural high school. Six dimensions of decolonizing agency emerged based on our research-practice partnership to address the racialization of behavioral problems in a school serving Indigenous students.

papers.title: Fostering Sociopolitical Awareness in Genetic Education: Investigating Racial Health Disparities in Diabetes
papers.authors: Ravit Golan Duncan, Dalia Hassan, Na’ama Y. Av-Shalom, Rishi Krishnamoorthy
papers.design_stakeholders: Science Teachers; Elementary Students & Children; Educational Researchers & Designers; Community Members & Partners
papers.abstract: Schools are not neutral sites of learning, and (re)produce white supremacy through seemingly neutral teaching and learning interactions. Heeding the calls to incorporate the sociopolitical into science education, we developed a high school biology unit that critically engages genetics education. The unit highlights environments as not neutral and not benign, and that the inequities plaguing these environments were created through structures and forces of oppression. We analyzed post interviews to understand the extent to which students developed non-deterministic views of genes and sociopolitical awareness of the nature of the environments in gene-environment interactions. Our findings suggest that students understood trait variation as resulting from interactions between genes and the environment and were able to reason about the environment in these interactions as non-neutral and harmful for marginalized communities. However, they struggled to explain how gene-environment interactions work at the biological level and the intentionality of environmental inequities.

papers.title: Desiring Learning in a Hospital School Arts Education Program
papers.authors: Christian Ehret, Ji Yoon Chung
papers.design_stakeholders: K-12 Teachers; Elementary Students & Children; Educational Researchers & Designers; Domain Experts & Technologists
papers.abstract: This study analyzes desire as a dynamic force driving learning in a children’s hospital school arts education program. Data come from an ongoing, three-year co-design project addressing a challenge for hospital schools in designing learning opportunities that move students to participate through ongoing social and emotional disruption, and that maintain continuity in students’ sense of themselves as learners. Analysis shows how students’ affective revelations while working collaboratively on a map-based art project are inseparable from the ongoing production of desiring learning that is essential to their elective participation. This conceptualization of affective revelations contributes to learning sciences research theorizing how affect relates to learning and learning ecology design. Drawing on critical design-based research in the learning sciences, the project challenges infirming narratives of children undergoing hospitalization, and it illustrates how coming to feel differently is an essential dimension of coming to know differently while learning in the arts.

papers.abstract: Educators’ self-perception as individuals who could engineer influences their motivation and support they provide during engineering learning. This study examines ways to support engineering identity development of library professionals and position them as educators for children’s engineering learning. Drawing from the theory of identities-in-practice and the concept of boundary crossing, this study conducts a case study to investigate how rural library professionals developed traces of emerging engineering identity. By examining nine library professionals’ engagement over two years in a three-year project to co-design and facilitate an online engineering program for children and their parents, this study contributes to the understanding of how public library professionals perform boundary crossing practices to position themselves as engineering learners and educators. papers.title: High School Teachers’ Approaches for Integrating AI Literacy into Planned Instruction: Uniformity or Heterogeneity?
papers.authors: Ibrahim Oluwajoba Adisa, Christopher Mah, Victor R. Lee
papers.design_stakeholders: High School Teachers; Higher Education Instructors / Faculty; Undergraduate / Graduate Students; Educational Researchers & Designers
papers.abstract: While various frameworks exist to promote K-12 AI education, little is known about how teachers bring AI literacy into their classrooms. In this study, we examined how two teachers designed and implemented AI literacy in their individual classes. Using epistemic network analysis (ENA) to analyze co-design records and interviews, we found that both teachers shared a common goal of enhancing student learning with AI but diverged in how they emphasized foundational and technical understanding of AI versus responsible and practical use. These varied approaches highlight the complexity of AI literacy and illustrate that a one-size-fits-all model does not apply. By examining these multiple pathways, we offer insight into how educators can tailor AI literacy instruction to meet diverse student needs and instructional contexts.

papers.title: Equity-Logics for Designing New Activity Systems Toward Rightful Familial Presence in Middle School STEM
papers.authors: Angela Calabrese Barton, Edna Tan, Wisam Sedawi
papers.design_stakeholders: Science Teachers; Middle School Students; Educational Researchers & Designers; Community Members & Partners; School Administrators & Leaders
papers.abstract: Minoritized parents have historically been sidelined in parent-school engagement opportunities. Research-practice-partnerships (RPP) have been one way to bring together stakeholders across communities in collective sense-making. We explore the design and enactment of a new activity system where minoritized parents, their middle school children and science teacher and researchers, engaged in the FamJam RPP, to co-design and enact engineering curriculum that centers community and seeds rightful familial presence in middle school STEM. Guided by frameworks of rightful presence, RPPs for learning at the boundaries, and cultural historical activity theory, the findings highlight new possibilities for family engagement through considering the underlying logics of equity. These include spatial and temporal equity, solidarity for equitable collaboration, collective responsibility for justice-oriented STEM, and fostering STEM for thriving and democratic citizenry. The study explores how these equity-focused logics can disrupt and transform systemic injustices in educational practices through new modes of relationalities and role/boundary mediation.

papers.abstract: This study explores how a secondary science teacher enacted a justice-oriented data science module in a seventh-grade life science classroom. Co-designed by the teacher and a group of researchers, the module engaged students in investigating quality of life using real-world datasets about their own neighborhoods. Classroom observations and debrief interviews revealed that the teacher effectively connected data science to life science and students’ lived experiences, facilitating discussions that linked data practices with justice issues. papers.authors: Davinia Hernández-Leo, Emily Theophilou, Jun Oshima, Tsubasa Minematsu, Kana Matsueda, Shotaro Naganuma, Ulrike Cress, Bodong Chen, Xinran Zhu, Fernando Díaz del Castillo, Wenli Chen, Qianru Lyu, Xuanyu Chen, Lishan Zheng, Armin Weinberger

papers.abstract: Generative Artificial Intelligence (GenAI) tools, driven by large language models (LLMs), are increasingly explored for their potential in educational contexts. However, significant concerns remain regarding their efficacy, cognitive impacts, and ethical implications. The Computer Supported Collaborative Learning (CSCL) community faces critical questions regarding the broader implications of this technology for the field. While GenAI offers advanced opportunities for collaborative learning through conversational interactions and other functions, research in this area is still in its early stages. The goal is to provide evidence-based recommendations for practice and identify key research directions and challenges for the future of CSCL in the context of GenAI.

papers.authors: Bernice d’Anjou, Sophie Derman, Carol Gilligan

papers.abstract: This research explores how high-achieving middle school girls see themselves as learners and how academic performance shapes their sense of self. Aiming to provide a nuanced understanding of the stresses, pressures, and coping strategies these girls experience, the study uses the Listening Guide method, a feminist, qualitative, voice-centered approach to discovery through listening. Data include multiple interviews with 19 high-achieving middle school girls from a large city in the northeastern United States, highlighting four key narratives. papers.title: Non-Disruptive Teacher Evaluation: From Case Analysis to Key Implementation Processes
papers.authors: Yi Chen, Hanbing Yan
papers.design_stakeholders: K-12 Teachers; Students & Learners; Educational Researchers & Designers; Community Members & Partners
papers.abstract: Reforming teacher evaluation is essential for promoting educational innovation and advancing sustainable development goals. Non-disruptive assessment offers a promising direction by embedding evaluation into everyday teaching practices with minimal interference. Yet, its implementation remains conceptually and practically underdeveloped. This study investigates the theoretical foundations and design principles of non-disruptive teacher evaluation through six representative cases. It identifies three key challenges: (1) technological tools support seamless data capture, but struggle with diagnostic precision; (2) online representations of teaching are expanding, yet fail to reflect critical offline practices; and (3) indicator frameworks are advancing, but linking evidence to competencies remains difficult. In response, we propose a four-step process—unify concepts, clarify standards, establish mappings, and formulate guidelines—to guide system design and support teacher growth through embedded, adaptive evaluation. The framework aims to support professional growth while contributing to more equitable and sustainable education systems.

papers.authors: Ana Bañuelos, April Valdez Garcia, Perla Ramos Carranza, Alejandra Yep, Jasmine Nation
papers.design_stakeholders: Pre-service Teachers; Higher Education Instructors / Faculty; Educators & Practitioners; Elementary Students & Children; Educational Researchers & Designers; Community Members & Partners; Domain Experts & Technologists; School Administrators & Leaders
papers.abstract: Through university-community partnerships (UCPs), educators and practitioners identify practices that leverage students’ assets to enhance science learning. We study Nuestra Ciencia, a UCP where undergraduates teach microbiology in Spanish to elementary students in bilingual schools in the United States. We describe how the program’s design transformations impacted elementary and undergraduate students’ perceptions of science, scientists, and their heritage language. Design-based framing enabled ongoing programmatic adjustments while identifying best practices for asset-based science learning. From analyzing 200 pre-post questionnaires, we found elementary students learned microbiology content and felt more like scientists after activities. We also analyzed focus groups with 34 Spanish-speaking undergraduates, revealing three themes related to science identity: using Spanish as a tool, reframing science as relevant, and healing their younger self. We describe how participants’ perceptions of science and science education helped us understand the impact of the program and ways to improve it.

papers.title: Fostering Familial Presence in STEM Education through an Identities-in-Practice Perspective
papers.authors: Wisam Sedawi, Angela Calabrese Barton, Edna Tan
papers.design_stakeholders: K-12 Teachers; Educators & Practitioners; Elementary Students & Children; Educational Researchers & Designers; Community Members & Partners
papers.abstract: Supporting parental/familial presence in STEM education requires forging new parent-teacher relationships and epistemologies to bridge home and school. Through the FamJam project, using participatory critical design ethnographic methods, we collaborated with an urban public-school teacher, immigrant students, and their mothers to foster familial rightful presence in a STEM unit focused on engineering for sustainable communities. Our study employs the “Identities-in-Practice” framework to investigate how relationships among mothers, teachers, and students cultivate emerging epistemologies and new social learning practices. Findings reveal how teachers and mothers acted as allies, developing new relations that yielded three powerful practices: 1) fostering porous boundaries in STEM; 2) incubating new epistemologies into STEM; and 3) authoring new identities/positions among teachers, mothers, and students, while disrupting normative perspectives in STEM learning. We argue for recognizing, supporting, and leveraging new relationships among identities-in-practice to expand opportunities for parent engagement and advance justice in STEM learning.

papers.design_stakeholders: Elementary / Early Childhood Teachers; Elementary Students & Children; Educational Researchers & Designers; Domain Experts & Technologists; School Administrators & Leaders
papers.abstract: As computer science (CS) is integrated in elementary science curricula, it is important to consider teachers’ perceptions in how they access CS and support students to engage in CS skills and standards through NGSS-aligned activities. This single case study utilizes the Interconnected Model of Professional Growth (IMPG) to examine teacher change and explore the perspectives of a teacher, through semi-structured interviews, as he implements an NGSS-aligned, project-based CS unit over the course of four years. Findings indicate that the teacher perceived that changes in his practice helped inform changes in student outcomes and the curriculum and, in turn, these changes in outcomes further informed his teaching practice in the next iteration of the unit. Results highlight the importance of reflection and feedback as a way to impact the teaching practice of integrating CS in elementary science education.

papers.title: The Making of Competent Outsiders: Using Epistemic Practices of Science to Enhance Student’s Critical Evaluation of Misleading Scientific Explanations in Classrooms
papers.authors: Noora F. Noushad, Susan A. Yoon, Clark A. Chinn, Zhitong Yang, Claire LeBodvidge, Huma Hussain-Abidi, Kyle Hunkar
papers.design_stakeholders: Science Teachers; High School Students; Educational Researchers & Designers; Community Members & Partners; Domain Experts & Technologists
papers.abstract: Eroding public trust in science has become a critical challenge due to the proliferation of misleading scientific explanations in the media. Scholars recommend integrating scientific epistemic practices into classrooms to help students become competent outsiders—citizens who can critically evaluate misleading scientific explanations without being subject matter experts. However, limited empirical evidence exists on how teaching these practices influences students’ evaluation of misleading scientific claims. This study examines the performance of four high school students during a two-week inquiry unit where they used scientific epistemic practices to construct explanations for containing an epidemic similar to COVID-19. Students then evaluated misleading scientific explanations on three newspaper articles. Analysis of their pre- and post-responses revealed that students improved in identifying and critiquing erroneous representation of science in these articles. We discuss the implications of using epistemic practices to develop competent outsiders in classrooms.

papers.title: Teachers Grappling with Representing Historical and Political Contexts in Science Curriculum Materials
papers.authors: Katarzyna Pomian Bogdanov
papers.design_stakeholders: Science Teachers; High School Students; Educational Researchers & Designers; Domain Experts & Technologists
papers.abstract: Science learning environments have been primarily shaped by Eurocentric ideologies that center science as a set of culturally neutral and color-blind systems which science teachers are often reluctant to acknowledge. However, current reforms in the U.S. ask science teachers to connect science to real world environmental and societal problems, which create opportunities to teach in more justice-oriented ways. This requires challenging shifts in teachers’ approaches. Co-design environments can be helpful learning spaces for teachers because they support deliberations around dilemmas through which teachers can deepen their content knowledge or practices. Dilemmas during design revolve around curricular values teachers bring into the design process. I use a curricular values framework to examine deliberations between values – specifically the intersections of ones related to historical and political contexts in science – to understand how teachers negotiate and redefine science to be represented in justice-oriented ways.

papers.title: A World-Making Lens Towards Relational Understandings of Data
papers.authors: Heather Killen, Samuel T. Arnold, Vien Nguyen, Ashley Quiterio, Trang C. Tran, Ashieda McKoy, RaeSheena Kennedy, Iris Tabak

papers.abstract: World-making has not been commonly considered in data science education. We were inspired to explore how a lens of world-making might deepen and expand our relational understandings of data. We are scholars working in diverse contexts united by a broad interpretation of what data is and can be. By entering a collaborative, sustained dialog, grounded within and across our research projects, we recognized that adopting a world-making lens supported us to envision the now and future more pluralistically and agentically by recognizing the multidimensional, multifaceted world(s) present in our research. Exploring world-making prompted explication and clarification of obscured relations, pointed to bridges across worlds, and surfaced assumptions about worlds. We convene this symposium to share how world-making operated in our work and to invite symposium attendees to take up these approaches in positioning data and data science education in service of greater societal and global goals.

papers.authors: Daniel Wendel, Aditi Wagh, Jennifer Elisabeth Mesiner
papers.design_stakeholders: Teachers; Students & Learners; Educational Researchers & Designers
papers.abstract: There is consensus that computational modeling can support integration of science with computing for student learning. However, it can be challenging for teachers to gain comfort with this relatively new practice, reconcile how it relates to science, and recognize its pedagogical value. In this paper, we illustrate how teachers working with a (serendipitous) analogy between a familiar process and a topic covered in chemistry class–frogs catching flies and reaction rates–enabled them to take up computational modeling in their science teaching. Drawing on notes from co-design sessions, teacher interviews and student worksheets, we illustrate how a focal teacher shifted from initial reluctance to taking ownership of designing and teaching a computational modeling lesson sequence. We also briefly show how her students took up this work. Finally, we reflect on the importance of leveraging teachers’ existing domain and pedagogical expertise as we bring these new practices into their classrooms.

papers.authors: April Luehmann, Elizabeth A. van Es, Adma Gama-Krummel, Alison Munzer, Elizabeth Wilson

papers.abstract: Research practice partnerships (RPPs) are a promising approach to transforming educational practice by amplifying the voices of teachers. This approach is especially powerful for disrupting educational inequities by positioning local actors as experts to generate solutions and take action. This cross-case study examines how engaging mathematics and science teachers in collaborative inquiry gave voice to teachers’ experiences as they sought to transform their instruction for equity and justice. papers.title: Embodied Transfer of Mathematical Ideas Through Gestural Replay
papers.authors: Fangli Xia, Chaeyeon Kim, Joel P. Beier, Michael I. Swart, Kelsey E. Schenck, Mitchell J. Nathan
papers.design_stakeholders: Teachers; High School Students; Educational Researchers & Designers
papers.abstract: This study examines how students embodied their ideas about geometric relationships and how those ideas transfer between groups. High school students used The Hidden Village – Online, a motion capture video game that allows them to create new content through movements and perform these movements while evaluating the veracity of geometric conjectures. Each group (1) co-designed directed actions—a sequence of movements representing a body-based interpretation of the structure and transformation of mathematical objects—for other groups and (2) played the game with conjectures and directed actions created by their peers. Qualitative analyses of multiple cases demonstrated that students used gestures to develop directed actions that simulated the generalized geometric properties. When directed actions were spontaneously replayed by other groups, these gestural replays facilitated a form of distributed transfer. This study offers new insights into redesigning mathematics curricula that emphasize embodied interactions to support generalization and transfer.

papers.abstract: K-12 students need to understand technical and ethical knowledge about Artificial Intelligence to utilize ubiquitous AI-powered technologies responsibly. Recent studies have explored ways to teach AI to K-12 students effectively, but little is known about ways to assess their learning. In this study, we describe how five computer science teachers from urban and rural Georgia school districts designed, adapted, and implemented assessments in their classrooms while teaching a middle school elective course aligned with the Five Big Ideas of AI. papers.abstract: Learning for complex world-making practices cannot be understood without embracing theoretical perspectives that acknowledge the complexity and dynamics of the interconnected and distributed among people and their environments nature of such practices. This symposium aims to advance the conceptual foundations for studying learning as an ecological phenomenon. It builds upon the recent special issue of Journal of the Learning Sciences, “Beyond disciplinary engagement: Researching the ecologies of interdisciplinary learning” (Markauskaite et al., 2024). The papers in this special issue adopted diverse ecological perspectives to study interdisciplinary learning, offering unique insights into how personal resourcefulness, teamwork dynamics, institutional processes, and disciplinary cultures intertwine in this context. However, the underpinning conceptual issues of theorizing and empirically studying learning as an ecological phenomenon were not specifically examined. In this symposium, we extend this work to unpack different ecological conceptualizations of learning and discuss critical directions for further development.

papers.abstract: Professional development is crucial for teachers to build their skills and adopt three-dimensional science. Effective professional development should be ongoing, collaborative, and spread over time to ensure lasting changes in teaching practices. Rural teachers often face isolation and less training compared to their urban counterparts, limiting their opportunities for collaboration. This research explored how technology-mediated lesson study (TMLS) helped rural teachers improve their teaching abilities and three-dimensional science skills. TMLS adapts lesson study using technology, allowing teachers to collaborate remotely. Based on four years of evidence, this research developed and refined the steps of TMLS with rural science teachers. This work also aimed to improve their three-dimensional science teaching abilities by forming small, collaborative groups that co-design, implement, and evaluate lesson plans together. Overall, TMLS offers rural teachers a valuable platform to enhance their teaching skills, collaborate meaningfully, and overcome the challenges of isolation.

papers.abstract: This study explores how an experienced mathematics teacher organized and disciplined a student’s perception during a lesson that incorporated data science practices. As data science gains national attention, this research addresses the complexities teachers face in integrating data practices into mathematics curricula. Drawing from a multiyear design-based study, the analysis focuses on classroom interactions during a “Barbie Bungee” lesson, highlighting competing disciplinary goals of mathematics and data science. Using an interactionist perspective and the construct of disciplined perception, this paper illuminates the breakdowns and interactional work involved in aligning student understanding with mathematical concepts like slope while grappling with noisy, real-world data. This case underscores the need to address competing disciplinary practices in classroom contexts, offering insights into fostering interdisciplinary engagement and reshaping data science integration in mathematics education.

We examine the transformation of a middle school geography teacher’s perspective as the teacher incorporates CS content into their teaching through a co-design process. Utilizing the Interconnected Model of Teacher Professional Growth, we analyze interviews and classroom observations to describe shifts in the teacher’s practices, beliefs, and understanding of CS integration. Our findings suggest that the teacher redefined CS from a set of technical skills to a human-centered discipline, making geography learning more engaging. Additionally, the co-design allowed the teacher to view students as active creators of digital artifacts and to embrace their own role as a creator able to modify existing technologies to better suit their educational context. Our findings indicate promising ways to engage teachers from non-STEM backgrounds in effectively connecting their subjects with CS.

papers.authors: Eve Manz, Annabel Stoler
papers.design_stakeholders: Teachers; Elementary Students & Children; Educational Researchers & Designers; Community Members & Partners
papers.abstract: As youth and teachers engage in modeling conversations, they are simultaneously negotiating how knowledge is generated and how people are accountable to each other in a community. Typically, design and analysis have privileged the epistemic focus, including within a recent emphasis on sensemaking and collective knowledge development. In this paper, we examine epistemic and relational work during science classroom modeling conversations. We share a close analysis of a typical conversation structure, where individuals present models and other students evaluate and build from their ideas. We show how classroom members experienced relational challenges and opportunities in these conversations. We also examine how alternative structures taken up by teachers and students presented different opportunities and constraints. This work contributes to the field’s understanding of science practices and suggests implications for work on evaluation and care in science classrooms.

papers.abstract: Centering students’ Funds of Identity (FOI) in the classroom is important for moving towards asset-based frameworks for learning. However, it can be challenging to identify the FOI of an entire class and use those FOI to design instruction. Motivated by this challenge, we explore how network visualizations in which students create a network that displays connections between themselves and classroom content can simultaneously elicit and connect students’ FOI to instruction. papers.abstract: To broaden and improve machine learning (ML) education, researchers must partner with teachers and study the affordances and challenges of ML instruction. Yet, most teachers are not ML experts and may need curricula that align ML concepts with their disciplinary expertise. This study explores three cases of classroom enactments of Mathematics of Facial Recognition (FaceID): five co-designed ML lessons aligned to high school statistics standards. As with any perceived contradiction in human experience, paradoxes may urgently demand resolution, thereby motivating and orienting learning and changemaking through design. However, resolving a paradox involves grappling with an apparent antinomy between equally sound, justified or valued perspectives, processes or solutions. This may drive very rational, inclusive and well-structured co-design processes towards activities and outcomes that may seem irrational, ironically counterproductive and even absurd. papers.authors: Sadhana Puntambekar, Dana Gnesdilow, Rebecca Passonneau, Chanmin Kim
papers.design_stakeholders: Teachers; Students & Learners; Educational Researchers & Designers
papers.abstract: In this paper, we present a case study of designing AI-human partnerships in a real-world context of science classrooms. We designed a classroom environment where AI technologies, teachers and peers worked synergistically to support students’ writing in science. In addition to an NLP algorithm to automatically assess students’ essays, we also designed (i) feedback that was easier for students to understand; (ii) participatory structures in the classroom focusing on reflection, peer review and discussion, and (iii) scaffolding by teachers to help students understand the feedback. Our results showed that students improved their written explanations, after receiving feedback and engaging in reflection activities. Our case study illustrates that Augmented Intelligence (USDoE, 2023), in which the strengths of AI complement the strengths of teachers and peers, while also overcoming the limitations of each, can provide multiple forms of support to foster learning and teaching.

We draw on participatory design research to emphasize the value of theorizing with teachers, as methodologies that center practitioner expertise provide insight into the unique character of noticing and how it unfolds in local contexts. papers.authors: Bertrand Schneider, Richard Davis, Roberto Martinez-Maldonado, Gautam Biswas, Marcelo Worsley, Nikol Rummel

papers.abstract: The field of Multimodal Learning Analytics (MMLA) is expanding, allowing researchers to capture rich, fine-grained data on learning processes in a variety of learning environments. High-quality process data can open the door for new insights on how people learn, creative interventions to support them, and build the foundation for personalized learning platforms. There is, however, a growing recognition that there is a lack of ecological implementations in MMLA (Cukurova, Giannakos & Martinez-Maldonado, 2020): the vast majority of projects are lab-based, which limit the generalizability and impact of multimodal sensing in education. This symposium brings together researchers who have used MMLA methods in the wild. The panel will discuss obstacles to the use of multimodal data in real-world settings, share lessons learned from current projects, and propose productive next steps for the field to become more ecologically relevant.

papers.authors: Chelsea Brown, Jeffrey B. Bush

papers.abstract: TalkMoves is an AI assistive tool that provides automated feedback to educators to support their daily teaching practices. papers.abstract: The Next Generation Science Standards promote students’ engagement in authentic science practices, including theory-building practices such as modeling and explanation. The role of teachers in NGSS-aligned classrooms includes devising strategies for identifying, understanding, and connecting students’ ideas. In other words, teachers are required to respond to student ideas. Yet, the demands of responsive teaching pose challenges for teachers. To address challenges and support teachers in implementing responsive teaching, we co-design classroom lessons and strategies with teachers. This paper presents our co-design approach to supporting teachers in developing responsive teaching strategies. We analyze classroom video of one teacher’s classroom from two consecutive implementations of co-designed lessons. Responsive teaching was made an explicit focus of co-design before the second implementation. We investigate the instructional moves of the teacher and present evidence that making responsive teaching the focus of teacher-researcher co-design causes a shift in the instructional moves of a teacher.

papers.title: Constraints and Boundaries for Collective Agency in Co-Design
papers.authors: Gavin Tierney, Kristina Stamatis
papers.design_stakeholders: Teachers; Educators & Practitioners; Youth & Adolescents; Educational Researchers & Designers; Community Members & Partners
papers.abstract: Co-design in education has emerged as an avenue for including broader perspectives into the creation of curriculum and learning environments, while also positively impacting learning and identity development. This kind of co-design requires designers’ collective agentic participation. In this paper, we look across several sets of data to build understandings of the ways collective agency emerges and is constrained within co-design. While research has pointed to the ways that participation in co-design has potential to increase feelings of agency in practitioners and youth, there is still a need to understand the ways communities of designers build and use collective agency. Without theories that describe the ways that co-design teams leverage their collective identities toward common outcomes, we fear that the power of this kind of work can fall short of its potential.

The study reveals educators' perceptions and the limitations of current narratives about AIed. papers.abstract: The Connective and Productive Disciplinary Engagement framework provides design and analysis tools to explore the affordances of foregrounding power dynamics as students learn about climate change. I suggest these youths’ critical awareness be foregrounded in science education to support critical and equitable learning opportunities.

papers.abstract: In the Learning Sciences and CSCL communities, interaction analysis (IA) is an important methodological approach to studying teaching and learning. IA relies on transcripts to selectively encode, represent, and experience video. However, researchers using IA continue to highlight the need for more dynamic and interactive transcription techniques to interpret, experience, and even speculate about data in context. In this paper, we use a comparative case study to introduce a transcription technique we call turn charts. Turn charts integrate ideas in IA with interactive and alternative visualization to visually map conversation over time, while also providing dynamic ways to select and experience audio and video data. papers.authors: Michael Schneider, Jessie Nixon, Srinjita Bhaduri, Colin Hennessy Elliott

papers.abstract: Debugging has long been considered an important skill in computer programming but one that students often struggle to master. While there are existing resources for supporting students in debugging, they have typically been designed to address the needs of undergraduates training to be software engineers. This focus on industry preparation can make adoption of resources difficult for the growing number of K-12 educators who are incorporating programming into non-CS classrooms. papers.authors: Lydia Y. Cao, Rupert Wegerif, Sara Hennessy, Chris Dede
papers.design_stakeholders: Teachers; Educators & Practitioners; Students & Learners; Educational Researchers & Designers
papers.abstract: Orchestrating productive science discussions is challenging for teachers. Little is known about how to support teachers to develop contingent responsiveness (CR), the adaptive expertise in responding to student ideas in the moment to improve the collective dialogue. Using a design-based research method, a professional development (PD) programme that incorporates mixed-reality simulation (Mursion) was co-designed remotely by researchers and practitioners in Pakistan during the pandemic over four iterations. papers.authors: LuEttaMae Lawrence, Vanessa Echeverria, Nikol Rummel
papers.design_stakeholders: Math Teachers; Middle School Students; Educational Researchers & Designers
papers.abstract: Classrooms are historically situated within hierarchical power structures. In traditional K-12 classrooms, teachers are positioned as the experts who makes decisions about learning, and students follow their instruction. This contrasts with approaches wherein teachers position students as having agency in how they learn and with whom. One way to disrupt more traditional power structures and support mutuality in the classroom is to leverage technology to provide an avenue to communicate and make decisions about learning. In this paper, we examine teachers’ views of shared control while designing an orchestration tool which it aimed at distributing power across teachers, students, and technology while students are moving between individual and collaborative activities. We discuss two case studies that highlight teachers’ nuanced views of how AI can be leveraged to support dynamic transitions for learning. Our contribution highlights a need to account for the range of teachers’ views about power structures when designing AI-based orchestration tools.

papers.abstract: This paper explores how MoDa, an integrated computational modeling and data environment, enabled students to express their ideas about diffusion and shift them toward canonical ideas. Drawing on data from an 8-day unit with two 6th-grade science classes, we analyze students' utterances in presentations, drawings, and written responses to document their diverse ideas about diffusion We present three case studies to illustrate how engaging with computational modeling in MoDa and the unit around it enabled students to shift from non-canonical ideas towards more canonical explanations of diffusion. papers.abstract: Collaborative design is a research-practice partnership with partners having equal decision-making power. However, creating and sustaining equitable participation in codesign partnerships is a significant challenge for further research efforts. Thus, this exploratory research investigates a trajectory from imbalanced participation to an increasingly equitable and collaborative one in a three-year research-practice partnership that aimed to design and implement a STEM-integrated bioinformatics high-school curriculum through the lens of relational trust. We adapted a multidimensional relational trust framework and followed an inductive approach to analyze a corpus of interviews with two teachers who participated in the codesign sessions and three researchers who facilitated the curriculum implementation and codesign processes. Our results suggested the partners shared authority as they collaboratively redesigned the curriculum and, by further reframing the relational trust dimensions intersected with the shifts in partners’ participation, offered a preliminary conceptualization of multidimensional and multifaceted relational trust for equitable participation in codesign partnerships.

papers.abstract: When using learning technologies within classrooms, teachers often face challenges around supporting their students’ learning within a digital space. To address this, prior work typically augments learning technologies with teacher dashboards that display real-time student data. Although common similarities in dashboard designs can be found, not all dashboards are designed similarly as teachers and learning technologies vary greatly. There is a lack of prior work around what design principles offer best practices for designing teacher dashboards. Our work addresses this gap through a systematic literature review of research on K-12 dashboards. Our review yielded (a) a concrete list of teacher tasks that teacher dashboards should support and (b) design principles that best support the design and development of teacher dashboards.

The PAT had two parts, a reporting part in which students were asked to self-assess their participation, and a visualization part in which students were presented with a graph representing the distribution of participation together with an indicator of the level of inequality in participation. Students used the PAT for four weeks. Results support a positive effect of the tool. Students benefit more from the visualization than from the self-assessment activity. The influence of the visualization on the regulation of participation seems to be more important for the most active students. Case study analyses of teacher and caregiver interviews reveal four dimensions of effective family-school partnerships: 1) having the “classroom in the living room,” 2) open strengths-based communication, 3) social and emotional support, and 4) active partnership. This work has significant implications for how families and schools can move forward to leverage these practices to have more equitable, collaborative, and authentic family-school partnerships in distance learning and beyond.

To explore ways to design technologies to allow teacher to provide effective homework guidance, we interviewed and conducted co-design sessions with middle school science teachers about their views on supporting student learning in the classroom and during homework. papers.abstract: Data literacy is important for supporting individuals to incorporate information from research studies into their own perspectives and decision-making processes. Students have to be able to traverse the representational forms that data takes on (i.e., numerical, graphical, etc.) and connect it to their understanding of a topic.
